Alternative farms also found that building social capital within their community offset the need for seeking extra hired help, as well as using those community connections to better navigate economic challenges by sharing useful knowledge among their networks. They also described the benefit of increasing their temporal diversity, setting up their agroecosystem so that it is functioning and bringing in income for as many months of the year as possible. One farm used strong natural capital, represented by a picturesque apple orchard, and social capital, represented by integration into community networks such as providing field trips for local schools, to make ecotourism a central part of their income during the farm ' s offseason. This is a prime example of natural and social capital characteristics influencing one of the selected indicators.

Although the sampled alternative farms match up well with many of the selected indicators of resilience, there are still limitations to this form of farming. The first limitation is the systemic struggle to make this form of farming a reasonably profitable way to make a living. It was noted in the interviews that most farmers who farm this way require a direct household member with a secure second job, although this type of split livelihood was in no way confined solely to alternative agriculture. Some alternative farmers who do not require a second job are in a financial position where they are not currently relying on producing a steady income. Farmers in this situation might be retired or pursuing alternative farming more as a hobby than as a job to make a living because they are already financially comfortable. Overall, there is a diversity of financial situations for these types of farmers. There are farmers who operate as a business for profit and do not require second jobs, there are farmers who are reliant on diversified streams of income, and there are farmers who have built financial capacity from their previous careers to have flexibility in their operations.

Conventional farmers ' responses to financial and labor issues generally relied on using new technology to increase efficiency on the farm. Efficiency through mechanization was identified to both save money by using fewer inputs and reduce reliance on labor by introducing automation. All of the surveyed dairy farms have either upgraded to robotic milking systems or, in the case of one farm, have started using heat and motion tracking collars for their livestock. All dairy farms also have heavily relied on artificial insemination (AI) breeding to develop stronger and more productive animals, which has been noted by all to be a useful endeavor. Each farm also makes use of new technology through relying on genetically modified organism (GMO) seeds for their cash cropping operations. Improved efficiency is especially desirable for these farmers given their strong reliance on high-input farming. Knowledge of new technology was primarily initiated through informal network discussions between dairy farmers. Several dairy farmers mentioned that they learn about which technologies are useful and which are not by sharing knowledge with each other. One farmer specifically noted this as being critical, citing examples of how input dealers are not the best source of finding accurate unbiased information for new technology.

Whereas conventional farms are generally responding in a uniform way to short-term socioeconomic threats, long-term threats are being handled differently. To deal with shifting liberalized markets, some farms have shifted toward specialization and other have shifted toward diversification. Other farms are settled in between. For example, one farm is continually diversifying their farm away from solely cash cropping by introducing new ventures through greenhouses and growing several different products to be sold both locally as well as overseas. This diversification is a result of the farmer ' s hesitancy to continue participating in global markets owing to price volatility. Conversely, another farm is specializing in sheep production and

has no intentions of diversifying away from this mission. Everything on the farm is designed to support lamb production, as it is their only income. This relies on expanding urban markets that purchase their product, but issues will arise if those markets decline.

Four other conventional farms are working on a hybrid specialization model. On each farm, dairy is the focus and most of the farm ' s operation works toward supporting the cows. Each farm within the last -ten to fifteen years, however, has diversified into growing cash crops as a secondary feature to earn supplemental income. Although not the focus of the farm, this diversification adds a cushion toward both short-term shocks through seasonal market disruption and long-term stresses if market forces or political forces, such as the disappearance of supply management, start to favor cash cropping over dairy farming. Diversification in this vein introduces spatial diversity, which was nonexistent prior to diversifying. Although these farms have pivoted from solely producing dairy products, the farmers still maintain that they are dairy farms. In essence, their identity as dairy farms is preserved because they now have extra incomes from cash cropping to support their dairy endeavors. Shifts in farming approach toward hybrid specialization strongly rely on natural capital, primarily by having the land to plant new crops. Of the three dairy farmers who have recently started growing cash crops, one farmer already owned the land to be set aside for growing crops, whereas the other two had to start renting land to begin their cash crop endeavor. Financial capital in the form of investment, as well as upgrades to physical capital were also precursors toward hybrid specialization. Investing in these capitals to create this new farming model resulted in examples of the farms demonstrating spatial diversity and response diversity by having a more spatially diverse farm that produces multiple products, as well as earning supplemental income to be used to address future threats.

In contrast to alternative farms, conventional farms are more uniform in their approaches to resilience building. This is likely due to their participation in conventional food systems that provide farmers with less autonomy over farm operations and, therein, restricting their potential resiliencebuilding pathways. The dominant short-term issue voiced by these farmers was rising prices for the inputs that they have become dependent on, such as fertilizers, fuels, and seeds. Equally, farmers have felt overworked because of the extreme difficulty in finding reliable sources of farm labor. These two issues combined have prompted a strong response in the form of searching for ways to improve efficiency on the farm at all costs. Efficiency reduces costs by using fewer inputs, which saves money, and efficiency also reduces the need to find labor by integrating automation into the system. Efficiency through mechanization, however, reduces resilience in agricultural systems because it leads to homogenized production and results in fewer people involved to make decisions or contribute their knowledge (Hendrickson 2015; Bennett et al. 2021).

Where these conventional farms diverge is how they approach long-term stresses. For the farms who diversified, the farmers noted the benefit of having multiple income streams to buffer against market volatility. The farm that diversified the most noted they can by virtue of having the financial resources -including stable access to bank credit -try out new ventures. The other farms maintain a focus on dairy in part because dairy is what they know best, so they do not want to risk moving away from their primary areas of expertise. Additionally, the infrastructure for dairy is so demanding that pivoting away from it would require a degree of operational flexibility that many conventional farmers do not possess.

One common theme in dealing with several of the threats in Table 2 was reliance on the ' family farm ' aspect of each farm by using existing social capital to integrate local knowledge and reflective and shared learning values into the farm management plan. Whereas the tightening of operating costs is threatening the longevity of each farm, the internal local knowledge possessed by each family acts to keep motivation high to carry on the family farm ' s tradition. All farmers noted that farms are going out of business in their region, but they all still argue that there exists a sense of farming community. Each farmer has strong social capital where they have existing relationships with several other farmers in the region, which offers several benefits both in the short term and long term. Short-term issues that rely on strong social capital, such as needing help with machinery or someone to watch the farm while the primary operator takes some time off, or long-term issues such as maintaining a presence in local agricultural organizations to lobby for long-term health of the area, were all highlighted by farmers as solutions toward preserving the longevity and intergenerational potential of family farms.

title: Love Actually: Youth Mediators and Advisors in North India
abstract: This article uses ethnographic research conducted in Bemni, a village in Uttarakhand, north India, to make a distinctive contribution to geographies of love. Building on fieldwork with young people between sixteen and thirty years old who work as mediators or advisors in Bemni in relation to premarital or extramarital affairs, I argue that practices and narratives of romantic love are strongly implicated in processes of social change. In the rural Uttarakhandi context, young people often use the idea of being specialists in love to bolster their own position and resolve conflict. I also provide a counterpoint to geographical youth research stressing the reactionary politics of marginalized young people. I show instead that in a region relatively unaffected by strong religious- or caste-based conflict, youth are able to ameliorate rather than exacerbate violent action, even while they reproduce aspects of caste, class, and gender inequality.

sections.Bemni, Uttarakhand:
Uttarakhand was established as a separate state in 2000. It contained approximately 10 million people in 2011. Uttarakhand ranks near the bottom of the table of states in India in terms of infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy, death rate, birth rate, percapita income, and electrification of villages. Poor governance, especially a poor record of policing, exacerbates problems of economic growth and human development.

Two thirds of the Uttarakhand population are upper caste (Brahmins and Kshatriyas, also called general castes [GCs]), with 17 percent scheduled caste (SC) in 2011 (Office of the Registrar General [ORG] 2011). There is close overlap between people's caste status and access to land, social contacts, and salaried work in Uttarakhand (see Dyson 2008, 2010). Strong gender norms are characteristic of rural Uttarakhand such that women are not expected to engage in paid work outside the household. In other cases they are permitted to do so but only in a narrow range of areas, such as teaching and work in government nurseries (Klenk 2010). In addition, cultural prescriptions surround the sexual activity of girls and young women. In rural areas in particular, people typically regard a girl or woman

entering sexual relations prior to marriage or outside the conjugal relationship as having transgressed social mores (see Chowdhry 2004).

NGOs have emerged to address gender issues, and scholars are beginning to show how, at the everyday level, rural women in Uttarakhand find ways to challenge or transform relationships of gender dominance (Klenk 2010; Dyson 2008, 2014). Women, however, and especially young women, are typically subordinated in local and regional gender hierarchies.

The village of Bemni is located in Chamoli district in a relatively remote part of Uttarakhand, bordering Tibet, at an altitude of about 2,500 m. Chamoli district is overwhelmingly rural and agricultural in character, as 90 percent of people lived in rural areas in 2011 according to the national census (ORG 2011). People in Bemni typically practice a form of agro-pastoralism. They plant wheat, barley, and millet in fields around the village while also using the surrounding forest to graze cattle and goats. In 2012, Bemni had a population of 940, of which 69 percent were GCs and 31 percent were SCs (author's household census 2012).

Between March 2012 and March 2015, I conducted seven months of research in Bemni, which built on fifteen months of doctoral research that I conducted in the same village in 2003 and 2004. Between 2012 and 2015, I examined the economic, social, and political practices of marginalized youth, especially those who were educated but unemployed or underemployed in the sense of being confined to work that did not reflect their educational qualifications or ambitions. In addition to the village census that I conducted, I carried out semistructured interviews concerning young people's educational and employment experiences, marriage, views on politics, social life, and intimacy. I interviewed forty-five of the fifty young people (ages sixteen to thirty) who had at least a Tenth Class (high school) pass and defined themselves as unemployed or underemployed. I also carried out participant observation that involved a wider set of youth.

The village changed dramatically between 2003 and 2012. The government greatly increased its development assistance to rural areas of Uttarakhand between 2003 and 2004. The introduction of a state employment program-the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS)-in 2005 resulted in a threefold increase in the money arriving annually with the village council ( panchayat ) and substantially enhanced the capacity of the village council to provide work to local people and construct village facilities, such as irrigation channels, paths, and recreational facilities. The government's increased assistance also took the form of stand-alone projects: Ninth and Tenth Classes were added to the local secondary school in 2005; a communications tower was constructed in the village in 2009; electricity arrived in the village in 2010; and a dirt road connecting the village to the local town became usable in 2012.

Between 2003 and 2012, Bemni was absorbed into wider circuits of knowledge and information, especially as a result of rising phone ownership: 60 percent of households had at least one mobile phone in 2012, compared to just 4 percent in 2003 (author's household census 2012). Schooling levels rose sharply, too. For example, 90 percent of men and 69 percent of women age sixteen to twenty-five in Bemni had at least an Eighth Class pass in 2012 compared to 64 percent of men and 10 percent of women age thirty-six to forty-five, even though girls' and SCs' education continues to lag behind that of boys and GCs.

As young people are increasingly educated, their employment aspirations have shifted away from farming. Moreover, climate change and declining prices for key crops have undermined the viability of agriculture. There are very few formal jobs for school and university graduates, however. Over two thirds of the young men twenty to thirty-four years old who live and work the land in Bemni describe themselves as unemployed or underemployed.

These shifts had led to attitudinal changes, especially evident in relation to love. Between 2003 and 2012, there was a marked increase in instances in which people referred to love, often using the English word love , which has the specific sense of romantic love, or the more general Hindi terms for love, prem and pyar , frequently employed to describe close attachment to family members (see also Abraham 2002). By the early 2010s, a series of new practices connected to love had also emerged, including couples taking trips without their children to scenic parts of the mountains and the inclusion of a double bed in the dowries provided by a girl's parents at the point of marriage.

At the same time, villagers continued to expect that young people would not enter sexual relationships until marriage. Moreover, people continued to believe that it was parents' responsibility to arrange the marriage of children and that young people should have limited opportunities to meet prior to an alliance. A young man's parents typically assume responsibility for searching for a bride, assisted sometimes by the young

man's maternal uncle or uncles. They usually approach the parents of a prospective bride to discuss the suitability of the match.

Traditional forms of marriage are nevertheless fluid. Until the late 1990s, a brideprice system operated in Bemni. Reflecting the importance and value of women's agricultural labor to a household, a groom's family made a token payment to a bride's family. In this system, young women had some autonomy after marriage to return to their natal homes, partly reflecting the low cost of marriage. In addition, secondary marriage-wherein a husband took a second wife-was common in the region in the mid-twentieth century (Berreman 1963).

The perceived declining value of women's agricultural work in the 2000s led to a transition in this period to a dowry system of arranged marriage. Parents remained primarily responsible for negotiating alliances in the dowry system of arranged marriage, but in this new system a bride's family paid a small dowry in kind to a groom's family. In 2012, the costs of marriage had increased tenfold in real terms from a decade earlier. Commentators have pointed to the negative implications of this system for young women's agency. Women sometimes become bargaining counters in the efforts of a groom's family after marriage to continue dowry payments, exposing them to violence (see Chowdhry 2004, 2007). More broadly, the dowry system is associated with a relatively narrow strategic approach to arranging the marriage of young people, such that considerations of economic and social profit frequently take precedence over questions of compatibility, women's safety after marriage, and romantic attachment. At the same time, however, the notion that a marriage requires people to be companions and to love one another featured in parental discussions about marriage, reflecting the influence of ideas of companionate marriage circulating in Bemni by the late 2000s and early 2010s and perhaps also the influence of notions of romantic compatibility that were discussed in the previous brideprice system.
sections.Youth in Bemni:
Several young people said that they had become downhearted as a result of rising unemployment. At the same time, many reflected on their position in more positive terms. They said that they constituted a new generation in Bemni of youth ( yuwa or jawaani ). Until the 1980s, young people married in their midteens, moving directly from childhood ( bachpan ) to adulthood ( bare ). Rising education among men and later women, however, led to a delay in marriage. By 2012, the average age of young women at marriage was around twenty-three and for young men around twenty-seven (author's household census 2012). This shift created a new period of 'youth' that had not previously existed in the village. In Bemni, youth ( jawaani ) is commonly imagined as a period that lasts from puberty until marriage. For men, the notion of youth has extended still further. As many men and some young women continue education into their late twenties and even thirties, and after getting married, the category of youth has become partially detached from its former association with a premarital period.

Young people also maintained that a social revolution in India associated with improved communication, rising education, and increasing understanding of citizenship meant that youth are able to serve wider society. Several young men and young women provided children with tutorials free of charge, volunteered in government schools, offered health advice to villagers, assisted neighbors or relatives in times of medical crisis, campaigned vis- a-vis the state on issues of corruption and welfare provision, and helped to resolve political conflicts in the village-all practices more prevalent in the 2010s than in the 1990s or 2000s (see Jeffrey and Dyson 2014). As Naafs and White (2012) found in an Indonesian context, young people often argued that they are particularly well placed to perform this work because as youth they have a closer knowledge of education, health, relationship, and work issues than do people in their forties and fifties. Young people sometimes explicitly referred to themselves as an 'in-between generation' ( beech ki pithi ) who could assist children in a context in which those children's parents lacked recent knowledge of the spheres of education, health, work, and relationships.

The claim to be able to assist effectively in resolving disputes related to love and especially extramarital affairs was crucially important in young people's wider assertion to be a distinctively skilled in-between generation. The rise of romantic love alongside other social changes, such as young people's increasing propensity to study in local towns, was leading to the growing frequency of premarital sexual relationships or sexual relations outside of marriage. Young people's work as mediators and advisors in the village was often focused on coordinating a response to these contested events.

Young people argued strongly that their involvement in the resolution of affairs in Bemni, as mediators

or advisors, was important in preventing violence, conflict, and social suffering among those directly affected by the situation at hand. The weight of the evidence that I collected in Bemni provided qualified support for this assertion. Between 2012 and 2015, I encountered twenty cases of premarital elopement or extramarital romantic relationships, all of which villagers described as affairs, using the English word. In five of the twenty cases I encountered, young people were not closely involved in managing the fallout of the affairs. In all five of these cases, the affairs led to conflict and prolonged hardship for several of those involved. By contrast, of the fifteen cases in which young people were closely involved in resolving the affair, nine were settled relatively peaceably, largely reflecting the role of youth as mediators or advisors. Qualitative analysis of specific cases in which young people did not participate or were closely involved in assisting in the fallout of affairs illuminates why young people's involvement might have some constructive effect. In each instance that follows, I use a particular case study to exemplify key aspects of a wider 'analytic set' of incidents that I collected in the field.

title: Oil and Gas Production in the Russian Sector of the Caspian Sea: Public Opinion on Development Paths and Consequences
abstract: This article considers public opinion in the republic of Dagestan on the expansion of hydrocarbon production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea. The article reports the findings of a survey (N = 956) conducted in 2010 in fourteen rural locations in the republic. Overall, respondents uniformly oppose the proposed expansion of offshore oil and gas production in the Russian sector of the Caspian Sea, seeing little economic benefit from this development and expressing concern about the environmental consequences. These findings resonate with work in geography on resource peripheries and development alternatives available in these locations.
picked: Opinions on Resource Development in Dagestan

sections.Opinions on Resource Development in Dage:
To evaluate the potential impact of hydrocarbon development on the rural residents of Dagestan, in the summer of 2010 two of the article's coauthors conducted a survey ( N = 956) among residents living near Dagestan's Caspian Sea coast. The survey consisted of a structured questionnaire with twenty-three questions that queried respondents on the following subjects: demographic information such as age, gender, and educational level; baseline economic statistics such as employment status, socioeconomic condition, and migration preferences; opinions on the economic situation in Dagestan; and prospects for expanded oil and gas production (Eldarov et al. 2011). Broadly stated, the survey had two aims to (1) evaluate economic and environmental conditions in rural Dagestan; and (2) gauge residents' positions on nascent oil and gas development in Dagestan's coastal region.

The survey used convenience sampling at fourteen rural locations. Local contacts at each site distributed the survey among their social and employment networks. 3 Acknowledging the nonrepresentative nature of the sample, we do not perform more advanced statistical analysis on the data. Given the large sample size and the targeted nature of the survey, however, and its questions at locations that will be affected by increased oil and gas production (both offshore in the north Caspian and near Dagestan's southern coast), these data provide valuable insight into receptiveness to the proposed longer term expansion of such production.

The fourteen villages and urban-type settlements ( poselki gorodskogo tipa ) that were surveyed are sited either near or along the republic's coast (see Figure 2). 4 In the south, this included the villages of Kayakent, Novokayakent, Berikey, Mamedkala, Belidzhi, and Samur; in the republic's central region, it included Dakhadaevka, Zelenomorsk, Manaskent, and the urban-type settlement of Glavniy Sulak. The southern section of the republic's coastline is a site for industrial facilities but also an area for recreation, with large urban settlements. Roughly one third of the sample was drawn from the north of the republic, an area of comparatively less economic development. The primary economic activities in this section are tied to the fisheries sector and include fishing and the processing of the catch. The hydrocarbon potential of much of this northern section has yet to be evaluated for recoverable reserves, although these villages would be impacted by any spills occurring further out in the Caspian Sea. The sample points in this area were the villages of Kochubey, Bryansk, and Kraynovka, as well as the settlement of Staroterechnoe.

A majority of respondents to the survey were men (64 percent). With respect to age, roughly three fifths of those surveyed reported that they are older than thirty years of age. Similarly, approximately 60 percent of the sample reported that they were born in Dagestan's lowlands; the remainder have resettled there from other parts of the republic, specifically the mountainous regions of the republic's south and west (on this process of resettlement, see Eldarov et al. 2007). The overall educational level was lower than expected given the convenient nature of the sampling and its reliance on employment and social networks, with only a quarter of respondents reporting some university-level work.

title: Waves of rural brides: Female marriage migration in China
abstract: Conventional views on marriage migration consider it primarily family-related and portray female marriage migrants as mostly passive, tied movers. Marriage as an economic strategy is seldom studied. We argue that a structural framework enables analysis of the complexities underlying female marriage migration, stressing institutional, economic, and sociocultural factors that impose constraints on and provide opportunities for women's mobility. A review of the historical and social roles of marriage in China shows that its transactional nature undermines women's status but offers disadvantaged women an opportunity to achieve social and economic mobility. Based on statistical analyses of a one-percent sample of China's 1990 Census, we show that peasant women in poor areas are constrained by their institutional positions, rural origins, and low education and status, shutting them out from cities and the urban labor market. Yet in the face of these constraints, many women, in exchange for economic opportunities and agricultural work, pursue migration by marrying into rural areas in more developed regions and by moving over long distances. These rural brides in well-defined migration streams are testimony to the roles of social and kinship networks and of brokers in the marriage market. Men who are socially and/or economically disadvantaged but locationally privileged are able to draw brides from afar. Despite the neoclassical overtone of the notion that marriage migration is an economic strategy, we argue that a structural approach is necessary for understanding the complexities underlying female migration and for explaining the recent phenomenon of long-distance female marriage migration in China.
picked: Assessing the Determinants of Marriage Migration

sections.Empirical Analysis:
Recent census and population surveys in China have inquired as to the primary 'reason of migration.' Both the 1987 one-percent Sample Survey and the 1990 Census offered nine options for reasons of migration: 'job transfer,' 'job assignment,' 'industry/business,' 'seek help from friends/relatives,' 'retirement,' 'joining family,' 'marriage,' 'study/training,' and 'other.' 13 The empirical analysis in this paper mainly employs a one-percent village-level sample of the 1990 Census 14 (SSB 1994). It contains information about every individual in all households of the sampled village-level units (villages, towns, or urban neighborhoods in cities). The 1990 Census defines a migrant as an individual five years or older whose usual place of residence on July 1, 1985 was in a different city, town, or county than that on July 1, 1990. Although this definition underestimates the actual volume of migration by excluding multiple moves, return migrants, migrants younger than five years old, and moves within the same city, town, or county, the census remains by far the most comprehensive source of

migration data in China. W e will first describe the pattern of female migration, then analyze the characteristics of these migrants and their husbands, and, third, investigate the spatial features of  this migration. We conclude the empirical analysis with a logistic regression analysis that examines the relative contributions of structural, sociocultural, and economic factors to explaining the patterns of interprovincial female marriage migration.
sections.Assessing the Determinants of Marriage M:
Theaboveanalyses provide general support for the importance of institutional, economic, and sociocultural factors in shaping female marriage migration. They also give weight to the argument that women in disadvantaged positions are more likely to pursue marriage as a strategy to achieve migration and to improve their social and economicmobility. In what follows, we further exami ne the effects of the above factors on interprovincial female marriage migration, using a logistic regression analysis in an effort to assess the relative significance of the factors thus far investigated.

The dependent variable in our analysis takes the value of 1 for marriage migration and 0 for other types of migration. There are four sets of independent variables variously referencing individual- and provincial-level data (T able 4). The second set of independent variables  examines  the  status  of female migrants. Among demographic variables reported in the census, education is the most appropriate indicator of women's status. We use three education variables to examine possible nonlinear effects of education on migration (Ortiz 1996): (5) education 1 (primary and junior high); (6) education 2 (senior high); and (7) college or above. W e expect more women with lower education to be marriage migrants. The third set of independent variables represents economic factors: (8) income of origin is measured by agricultural household income per capita 25 of migrants' province (before migration), and is  evaluated for  the year  1988, near  the midpoint of the period 1985-1990; and (9) destination 3 (coastal provinces versus inland provinces). We expect income of the originating provinces to be negatively related, and income of the coastal destinations to be positively related, to the likelihood of marriage migration. Finally, the sex-ratio variable (10) compares, at the provincial level, the number of single men over 30 years old with their female counterparts and aims at testing the effect of demographic structure on marriage migration. W e expect high sex ratios to be positively related to high propensities of female marriage inmigration.

Estimates of the model are reported in T able 4. The goodness of fit measure r 2 is 0.28, suggesting that the model is a relatively good fit for the data (Hensher and Johnson 1981: 51). The results are generally consistent with our expectations. Female migrants with agricultural hukou classification were 5.0 (odds ratio) times more likely to be marriage migrants than those with nonagricultural hukou. Female migrants with rural hukou location were 1.7 times more likely to be marriage migrants than those with urban hukou location. In terms of destination, female marriage migrants to rural destinations were 3.0 times more likely than those to urban  destinations, and  female marriage migrants to nonmunicipality provinces were 1.2 times more likely than those to the three centrally administered municipalities (Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai). The parameter estimates and odds ratios confirm the importance of institutional and structural factors. Peasant women are constrained by their hukou status and location and are likely to migrate through marriage into other rural areas, but they continue to be shut out from urban areas and large cities that have stricter controls over permanent migration.

Odds ratios for the education variables suggest that women with higher education are less likely than those with lower education to engage in marriage migration. Specifically, female migrants with college or above level of education were 77.3 percent (1 - odds ratio = 1 - 0.227) less likely to be marriage migrants than those without. But the effect of education seems to be curvilinear. Female migrants with primary and juniorhigh education were 1.6 times, and those with senior-high education 1.4 times, more likely to be marriage migrants than those with either lower or higher education. What these estimates suggest is that some degree of education facilitates the gathering of resources  and information (Ortiz 1996) and motivates women to pursue marriage migration. Interprovincial marriage migration is not traditional, and the long distance and many intervening obstacles involved demand a certain spirit of adventure and creativity that women with very little or no education may not possess. On the other hand, those with the highest education were more likely to pursue other types of migration, including to urban areas where they may be more competitive in the labor market.

As expected, estimates of the economic variables suggest that female migrants from wealthier provinces were less likely (58.7 percent, or 1 0.413), and female migrants to coastal provinces more likely (1.2 times), to be marriage migrants. A positive parameter estimate for the sex-ratio variable suggests that a large relative proportion of older single men was conducive to marriage migration, yet an odds ratio of 1.0 also indicates that its effect was weak. title: SHIFTING SYNANTHROPY OF THE CROW IN EASTERN NORTH AMERICA
abstract: P>The American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) falls into a category of wild organisms, called synanthropes, that have developed an affinity for, or dependency on, human interventions in the landscape. The distribution and numbers of crows in North America east of the Mississippi River have been largely tied to the anthropogenic fragmentation of the forest. As ground feeders, crows need open space for foraging, but they also need trees for nesting and roosting. Conflicts between corvids and people centered on the former's damage to agriculture. Both Native American peoples and Euro-American settlers sought to thwart corvine preference for maize through a series of ingenious measures. After 1950 rural concern about corvine depredations greatly diminished. The appearance of large winter roosts in cities shifted the conflict with crows. Like humans, crows have undergone change, and their synanthropic character can be seen as fundamental to their biogeography.

title: Toward Postsecular Feminism: Intersectionality and the Religious Subjectivities of Women Migrant Workers in China
abstract: This article investigates the subjectivities of Christian women migrant workers within the context of China's social transformation, characterized by the interactive advancement of global capitalism, rural-to-urban migration, and Christian fever. Despite the burgeoning literature on women migrant workers in global capitalism within geographical scholarship, there has been less focus on women migrants' religious subjectivity and agency. Drawing on empirical research on the intersectional experiences of women migrant workers, this article seeks to advance a postsecular feminism by bringing intersectionality into conversation with debates on postsecularity and gender inequalities. First, we examine the intersectional matrix of domination imposed through state power, Chinese patriarchal culture, and the gendered and class-based disciplinary labor regime under global capitalism, which serves as an ontological condition in which women migrants' religious subjectivities form and are shaped. Second, we use intersectionality to help understand the process of becoming and a relation of emergence, wherein multiple agential qualities of women migrants-manifesting as counterpatriarchal subjects or through docile, tolerant, self-sacrificial, and pious femininity-arise at the intersections of religion, class, gender, and family. We therefore argue that postsecular feminist critique needs to carefully consider the patterns and diverse effects of intersectionality where both domination and religious agency are engendered and interwoven.
picked: An Intersectional Approach to Postsecular Feminism

sections.The Study:
This article is based on a project that examines the religious subjectivity of Christian rural migrant workers in Shenzhen, China. It deploys an intersectional analytical frame to explore how migrant workers ' religion, gender, age, and class subjectivities mutually shape one another. The field work was conducted between 2014 and 2018 in Shenzhen ' s nine Protestant churches (including state-sanctioned

churches and house or underground churches). We interviewed fifty-two Christian migrant workers (thirty-two males and twenty females) and eight leaders, pastors, and preachers. Although this article primarily draws on the experiences of twenty women migrant workers between the ages of eighteen and forty-six, it also considers the perspectives of male Christians and their non-Christian family members or workmates to provide a relational account of gender subjectivities. The churches that migrant workers attend can be classified as either state-sanctioned or house or underground churches, the latter of which operate without the recognition of the state. The epistemological style of the former is often labeled as evangelism, characterized by a more intellectual and text-centric understanding of Christianity. Although some evangelist churches also operate in an underground manner, the house churches in the city organized by rural Christians often embrace Pentecostal styles that are more emotional and practice-centric (Huang 2014). This distinction is not fixed, however, as migrant workers often attend both types of churches interchangeably.

Methods used in this study included in-depth interviews and participant observation. Following McCall (2005) and Hopkins (2019), who considered story narrative and open interviews as the most effective method to research intersectionality as multiple experiences in subjects ' everyday lives, we use these methods to provide spaces for participants to freely narrate the social divisions most significant to them. The first author also followed Christian migrant workers ' everyday routines and practices in their churches, factories, and living spaces and participated in sermon sessions and fellowships inside and outside the churches. The third author closely traced the life trajectory of women migrant workers and their marginalized experiences during the process of out-migration. Each interview lasted between forty minutes and three hours. All the informant names appearing in the article are pseudonyms.
sections.An Intersectional Approach to Postsecula:
Despite the acknowledgment of various power structures that shape and condition the subjectivities of women migrants, relatively little research has focused on how religion interacts with migrants ' constitution of gender subjectivities, and in particular, how religious resources and ethics enable women migrants to negotiate these multiple inequalities. Migrants ' religious lives not only allow them to imagine alternative subjectivities beyond those normalized by material and discursive power relations, but also provide support and a sense of community that enables them to materially and emotionally settle in new socioeconomic environments (Silvey 2013). The extent to which women ' s subjectivity and agency can be conveyed through and supported by religious ethics and piety, however, is debatable (Mahmood 2005; Braidotti 2008; Vasilaki 2016; Cloke et al. 2019). Religion might open up new spaces for the restoration of spiritual and sacred sources of agency for migrant women and thus reconstruct their subaltern subjectivities, or reproduce the gender- or class-based hierarchies that can thwart their agency (Gao and Qian 2019). Therefore, attention to religious practices can enable a more nuanced understanding of women migrants ' gender subjectivities as malleable and culturally conditioned.

Nilsson and Tesfahuney (2019) noted that religion has not been seriously taken into account in the analysis of women ' s subjectivities and agency, as ' the traditional and the religious have been equated with female oppression, patriarchy and hierarchy ' (2). In response, the postsecular turn in feminism calls for a critical rethinking of religion, gender, and the secular, beyond secularist accounts of religion as a space that restricts women ' s agency, as well as the assumption of women ' s agency in terms of emancipatory and resisting subjects (Mahmood 2005; Braidotti 2008; Vasilaki 2016). This emerging approach of postsecular feminism has prioritized religious ethics as an important impetus that brings forth an alternative notion of the feminine self and feminist consciousness beyond the femininity defined by the ethos of secularism (Mahmood 2005; Braidotti 2008; Vasilaki 2016). In this regard, the feminist scholar Braidotti (2008) proposed a ' non-oppositional ' understanding of woman ' s agency that contests the normative liberal-feminist assumption that agency primarily manifests in practices of resisting or subverting social norms. In other words, women ' s agency can also be achieved through strategically reconstituting their subjectivities by drawing on existing cultural resources rather than socially, ethically, or political opposing hegemonic norms. Mahmood (2005) therefore emphasized the ethical formation of religious agency, arguing that ' agentival capacity is entailed not only in those acts that resist norms but also in the multiple ways in which one inhabits norms ' (15). Nevertheless, research on gender and religion should abandon a zero-sum stance with a simple dichotomy between domination and resistance that omits the complex and ambiguous relationship between gender and religion.

The ' postsecular turn ' that moves toward an affective and ethical engagement with religion, though, might also risk adopting an apolitical account of religion per se, overlooking religion as ideologies that sustain women ' s ' natural ' status (Vasilaki 2016). For instance, in Ammerman ' s (1987) study of a North American conservative Christian community, ' most women learn to influence family decision making while still deferring to their husbands ' authority, and that both they and their husbands find ways to live with the tension between Fundamentalist norms for

family structure and modern norms of individuality and equality ' (146). In general, there is still a theoretical tension that researchers seek to discern the ' progressive ' and ' dark ' sides of religion and how they have different effects on women ' s subjectivities.

To overcome this theoretical difficulty, this article advances a postsecular feminism by introducing an intersectional approach to women ' s religious subjectivities. Intersectionality explores how different categories and social inequalities (e.g., gender, race, and class) mutually form one another in a way that constitutes a ' matrix of domination ' or new ontological conditions that cannot be challenged by singular antioppression power (Collins 2002; Cho, Crenshaw, and McCall 2013). Methodologically, developing an intersectional approach to religious subjectivities requires focusing on multiple categorizations as well as the relational, contextualized, and mutually constitutive nature of social dominations (Hopkins 2019). Here, McCall ' s (2005) conceptualization of the three dimensions of intersectionality -namely anticategorical, intracategorical, and intercategorical complexities -offers crucial insights for exploring the religious subjectivity of women migrants. Whereas anticategorical complexity provides a poststructural deconstruction of analytical categories and the inequalities they sustain, intracategorical complexity aims to examine ' particular social groups at neglected points of intersection [ … and] to reveal the complexity of lived experience within such groups ' (McCall 2005, 1773). The idea of intercategorical complexity attends to the ' relationships of inequality among social groups and changing configurations of inequality along multiple and conflicting dimensions ' (McCall 2005, 1773).

Drawing on the theoretical advances of intersectionality (McCall 2005; Collins 2019), we suggest that intersectionality can help us reflect on postsecular feminism in two ways. First, theorizing women ' s religious agency as a process of ethical formation (Mahmood 2005) needs to be understood within the existential intersectional condition in which religion is felt, inhabited, and performed. This is in line with the recent theoretical shift of intersectionality studies away from identity politics to a structural critique of power (Singh 2015). In other words, an intersectional approach not only acknowledges the multiple layers of identity and their politics but also discerns the intersectional structure and process that produce domination and (religious) identity. In particular, although different forms of inequalities can mutually constitute one another, McCall (2005) also argued that ' some forms of inequality seem to arise from the same conditions that might reduce other forms ' (1791). That is, the intersections of some social inequalities might be more ontological in structuring the effects of other social experiences. In this sense, we do not simply look at the religious institutions and practices themselves, but delve into the intersectional system of powers, which serves as an ontological condition through which individuals interpret, use, or inhabit religion. As we show in this article, the intersection of class-based exploitation and state power structures other categorizations of religion and gender.

Second, intersectionality is not a fixed power structure but also implies a process of becoming that might open up spaces of ethical aspiration and existential freedom that cut against the social inequalities (Collins 2019). As Collins (2019) revealed, ' The idea of intersectionality works in multiple registers of recognizing the significance of social structural arrangements of power, how individual and group experiences reflect those structural intersections, and how political marginality might engender new subjectivities and agency ' (26). In this vein, religious agency cannot be simply defined or captured in a singular way; instead, it is more likely to be a relation of emergence , where new religious subjectivities emerge from the interaction among different forms of lived experience in particular sociospatial conditions. In this article, although not necessarily functioning as a resisting force, the intersection of religion, class, and gender nonetheless help women migrants reclaim the intimate within the matrix of dominations. This theorization therefore can help have a broader horizon of ethical-political concerns and postsecular possibilities beyond the simplistic division of progressive and dark sides of religion.

title: Circular migration and the spaces of cultural assertion
abstract: Harnessing primary and secondary evidence from India, our essay conceptualizes the cultural dynamics of migration. In so doing, it demonstrates the incompleteness of standard marginalist and Marxist accounts of labor circulation. As a corrective, we examine the linkages between culture, politics, space, and labor mobility and offer a way to think about them by building on poststructural critiques of development and postcolonial theories of migrant subjectivity. The proverbial compression of space-time not only has made extralocal work more viable for members of proletarianized groups but, more importantly, has allowed them to transfer their experiences of new ways of being into local contexts through acts of consumption and labor deployment that can become elements of a Gramscian counterhegemonic praxis. We argue that the possibility of this sort of body politics compels not merely a critique of the modernization paradigm that has organized classical migration studies but, more profoundly, a reassessment of the way we understand modernity itself We advocate an approach that provincializes the Eurowest and foregrounds the existence of pluritopic regional modernities.

In giving empirical substance to our theoretical arguments on migration and modernity, we focus on two categories of subordinated groups in rural India: tribals and dalits. 13 Wedraw evidence from secondary materials, as well as fieldwork conducted by the authors between 1993 and 2001 in the Kheda and Baroda districts of Gujarat, Tiruvannamalai District of Tamil Nadu, and Midnapore District of West Bengal (Figure 1).

Abriefnoteonthegenesisofthisarticleseemsnecessary. Our initial projects were independent evaluations of the distributive and political impacts of development programs in two different agrarian settings (Gidwani studied how the introduction of a large surface-irrigation scheme transformed agrarian social relations in central Gujarat, particularly the bargaining power and political consciousness of low caste workers; Sivaramakrishnan examined how the introduction of joint forest management (JFM) schemes in eastern West Bengal intersected with regional tribal politics, and whether JFM marked a devolution in state control or a new form of governmentality). Although the link between circular migration and changes in the cultural assertiveness of subordinated caste and tribal groups was not the explicit focus of our initial research programs, the parallels between these geographically dispersed research sites soon became evident to us. And while we were clearly struck by the upsurge in intercaste tensions and the rise of regional identity (caste, dalit, and tribal) politics in the 1990s, we were also intrigued by microstudies of migration (notably the work of Dutch anthropologist Jan Breman) that suggested a rising trend in labor mobility in rural India, particularly after 1991-the year when the Indian government formally adopted the macroeconomic tenets of ''economic liberalization'' and ''structural adjustment.'' We decided it was important to explore whether there was a relationship between rising labor circulation and the intensification of regional identity politics.

title: Nature, Agriculture, and Black Space-Making in Serra dos Tapes, Brazil
abstract: In this work, I focus on how Quilombolas in southern Brazil create territorial conceptions and practices. Contemporary quilombos constitute complex forms of social organization composed of different collectivities and political subjectivities whose ancestors resisted colonial slavery by creating free communities in urban and rural spaces. In Serra dos Tapes, rural Black Quilombola communities have struggled with geographic dispossession, socioeconomic inequalities, and everyday racism. At the same time, they have created space-making practices, thinking of their territory as a lived space. Agriculture plays an essential role in this process, articulating knowledge, creativity, and a unique relationship to nature. Black people in Serra dos Tapes consider the cultivation and their relation to nature meaningful in the constitution of their identities, food security, and autonomy. Results of this study were gained through the life history method. Taking Quilombolas' practices, narratives, and trajectories seriously in their political and epistemological importance, this article aims to offer some insights to advance discussions concerning the entanglement of race, nature, and environment within geographical studies.

sections.Serra Dos Tapes:
Serra dos Tapes is a region in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil, which covers the mountainous areas of the municipalities of Pelotas, S ~ ao Lourenc ¸o do Sul, Morro Redondo, Canguc ¸u, Turuc ¸u, and Arroio do Padre (Salamoni et al. 2021). Currently, in this mountain range, there are agricultural colonies of German and Italian origin represented by family farmers -also known as Colonos -in varied socioeconomic situations (Salamoni and Waskievicz 2013). There are also many rural Black communities, some of them presently recognized by the Brazilian state as quilombo remnants (Pinheiro 2014).

Part of the history of this region -which has the city of Pelotas as its main urban center -dates back to Portuguese colonization throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and to colonial slavery employed in cattle raising and jerky meat ( charque ) production (Gutierrez 2001). The headquarters of colonial properties, and the main economic activities, were located in the lowlands, as the flat terrain facilitated the raising of cattle and the installation of jerky farms, or charqueadas (Salamoni and Waskievicz 2013). In the vicinity of the flatlands are the sierras -which officially belonged to Portuguese landowners but were not often explored by them -defined by the undulating relief and dense vegetation. The natural characteristics of these sierras made them geographic allies for people who wanted to escape from the forced labor and the violence imposed by the slavery system (Pinheiro 2014, 2016).

In this sense, the formation of rural Black Quilombola communities in Serra dos Tapes dates back to slavery but is not limited to it. B. Nascimento considered historical quilombos as a search for an own and independent life, during slavery but beyond it. She challenged us to think of

Quilombola ' s articulations as possibilities to conceive and build other forms of social and spatial relations (B. Nascimento 1985, 2018, 2021). This understanding proposed by Nascimento guides my discussion in this article.

In the second half of the nineteenth century, the Brazilian state implemented non-Iberian European colonization projects in Serra dos Tapes (Salamoni and Waskievicz 2013), which strained racial and territorial relations in the region (Rubert 2009). These projects stimulated an articulation between public and private colonization initiatives, as Portuguese settlers started to divide the lands into lots for commercialization (Grando 1989). Among the motivations for this new colonization project were the replacement of enslaved labor that, in a few decades, would be formally emancipated; the land occupation with the production of foodstuffs for internal supply; and the whitening of the population that was primarily Black (Santos 2002; Costa 2011).

The Southern region, specifically the state of Rio Grande do Sul, seeks to position itself as a fragment of Europe in Brazil, racially differentiating it from the rest of the country. This phenomenon is due to spatial, social, and cultural processes privileged by hegemonic history, which neglects the Black and Indigenous populations (Torres 1994). Paradoxically, Rio Grande do Sul has the largest Quilombola population in the Southern region (Fundac ¸ ~ ao Cultural Palmares 2021). The capital, Porto Alegre, is the city with the most significant number of urban quilombos in Brazil (Fundac ¸ ~ ao Cultural Palmares 2021). Of the 137 quilombos formally recognized in the Rio Grande do Sul, 20 percent are in Serra dos Tapes. Nevertheless, this region is noted for its Germanic and Italian cultural heritage. It has also been contemplated by rural development projects aimed at promoting colonial agricultural production and tourism focused on appreciating the landscape, the region ' s natural environment, and the Euro-descendant material and intangible patrimony.

Grisa and Schneider (2014) identified three ongoing generations of public policies for family farming in Brazil that emerged in different economic and political contexts. The first generation has an agricultural focus interested in expanding production, consolidating this type of agriculture in the market, and encouraging agrarian reform; the second generation has an assistance approach, creating social programs for underprivileged farmers; and the third aims

to build institutional markets to purchase family farming products, focusing on food security and sustainability. Those policies result from peasant political mobilizations for agrarian reform, better economic conditions, and quality of life in rural spaces (Aquino and Schneider 2015). Although being increasingly scarce due to the economic and political crisis that has affected Brazil since 2016, those public policies paved the way for strengthening family farming as a productive sector and as a normative and analytical social category in the Brazilian rural space (Grisa and Schneider 2014).

In Serra dos Tapes, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), rural extension workers, and cooperatives are responsible for mediating the interaction between the farmer and the state and executing the programs. Colonial family farming has been aided with rural credit programs, expanded its relations with industries, and changed its technical and productive bases. Presently, the Colonos cultivate a variety of agricultural goods, specializing in peach and tobacco production and transforming the Rio Grande do Sul into the largest purveyor of those products in Brazil (Secretaria de Planejamento and Governanc ¸a e Gest ~ ao 2021). Also, with rural tourism, those farmers have played a leading role in revealing that rural spaces can transcend their agricultural function, demonstrating a potential for sustainability and conserving rural communities ' social networks (Salamoni et al. 2021).

In the case of rural Black communities, many of them are composed of farming families. They struggle, however, with historical difficulties in accessing land. Furthermore, they navigate different experiences of political articulation and negotiations with the Brazilian state. As a result of Black political mobilizations in Brazil, recent public policies for quilombos aim to promote racial equality. To execute these policies in the local context, the federal government compartmentalized them into programs related to issues such as housing, social development, and productive inclusion. In the case of Serra dos Tapes, those social policies have been disconnected from territorial claims, practices, and social experiences of Black people in the region.

Regarding initiatives to encourage agricultural production, families of Quilombo Alto do Caix ~ ao -the community where this research took place -reported that technical and rural extension services are designed from the reality of the colonial farming production system. Seu Ademir, one of my interlocutors, said that the technical recommendations often do not consider his knowledge and practices, his artisanal tools for agricultural work, or even the fact that he does not have enough space or the proper type of soil for some procedures.

Personal and familial narratives also indicate that Black communities in Serra dos Tapes have experienced a silent territorial tension since nonIberian European colonization projects. The historical processes briefly described in this section reveal that Serra dos Tapes does not present the typical scenario in Brazil of social contrast between peasant communities and large agricultural companies, landowners, or extractive industries, where territorial conflicts are visible. The coexistence of Indigenous, Afro-descendants, and Colonos communities is a particularity that partially defines Serra dos Tapes ' s social and territorial relations. This social aspect of the region is one reason a narrative of an ' ethnic mosaic ' (Cerqueira 2010) in a certain sociospatial harmony predominates in the literature. This point of view prevails as a background in geographical studies about this region. Similarly, local authorities and policymakers ' discourses do not critique Serra dos Tapes ' s deeprooted social and racial hierarchies that affect everyday life in the quilombos.

Reading anthropological studies about the region (Rubert 2009, 2011; Pinheiro 2014, 2016) and listening to personal narratives, my analysis shows that the territorial tension is silent and connects to the ethnic-racial relations between Quilombolas and Colonos. After Black communities started to organize themselves politically, demanding their social rights and official recognition as quilombos, they faced persistent questions from the White settlers about whether they would initiate territorial claims. Charles, son of Seu Ademir, remembered being questioned by a neighbor:

There was a rumor running that the government would demarcate the territory. That wasn ' t even true, and they bothered me a lot: ' Oh, because you ' ll have to reimburse me … . ' I had gone out to buy a snack and, at the end of the day, I had to explain something that wasn ' t even going to happen.

Seu Ademir reported that the expansion of the colonial agricultural frontier displaced Quilombolas from cultivable lands: ' Where are the Quilombolas today?

They are on the top of the hill, where planting machines do not enter, where we wouldn ' t be able to plant. But we plant anyway. '

The Quilombo Alto do Caix ~ ao is surrounded and crossed by Colonos ' properties. This Black community avoids discussing the territorial claim issue due to the neighborship and work relations with the Colonos. Many Quilombolas have limited market access to sell their agricultural goods, or they do not have space to plant in an amount that is sufficient to sell, thus prioritizing domestic consumption (Gois and Miguel 2019). Therefore, they work for the Colonos in tobacco and peach plantations to increase their family income. Because of the worry of losing work opportunities offered by those settlers or creating a conflicting relationship with them, some people from the quilombo prefer not to pursue the territorial official recognition and demarcation, even though it is a right guaranteed by the Brazilian constitution.

In her studies about historical quilombos, B. Nascimento considered the connection between territory, nature, and broader socioeconomic dynamics with the Quilombola ubiquity in Brazil and the multiplicity of strategies they employed to confront slavery and build other forms of living (B. Nascimento 1985). Nascimento acknowledged the significance of Quilombolas ' narratives. According to her, oral histories encourage researchers not to essentialize those Black communities and to realize that ' the complexity of their institutions and the evolution of global society must be comprehended as interactional processes ' (B. Nascimento 2021, 114).

Thinking with Nascimento about the simultaneousness of changes and continuities of quilombos ' sociospatial practices over time, I understand that, in Serra dos Tapes, the Quilombolas scrutinize the region ' s social and economic circumstances, reflect on their situations, and organize their plans for social, economic, and territorial reproduction. Despite the adverse conditions -like insufficient space for planting and unequal access to the market -those Black families have sought to affirm themselves as food producers in the region to ensure their economic survival. At the same time, they preserve inherited cultural and territorial practices to confront everyday discrimination and sociospatial inequalities.

Navigating historical dispossessions, the Quilombolas in Alto do Caix ~ ao are, through inventiveness, building their conceptions of territory. The idea of territory that they carry forward in their sociospatial relations is that of a lived space. In this way, the territory is not just an analytical spatial category valuable for reflecting on Latin American geographies, nor is it reduced to the idea of the nation-state and political-administrative powers. The Quilombola territory in Serra dos Tapes has a physical and an existential quality (B. Nascimento 2018), and Black families mobilize it in their social, political, and daily lives.

title: Translocal Precarity: Labor and Social Reproduction in Cambodia
abstract: Many people in the Global South have left behind rural homes in search of employment in urban and transnational labor markets often defined by precarious work. Employment is insecure, uncertain, and temporary, and for transnational migrants, there is the constant risk of deportation. Although geographers have studied such migrant precarity, there is an increasing interest in its translocal dimensions, particularly related to how precarious work travels home and affects left-behind family members. This scholarship, however, tends to assume that precarity arises primarily in the spaces of production. Drawing on twenty months of ethnographic fieldwork in rural Cambodia, we argue that precarity simultaneously emerges from the challenges of social reproduction faced by kin in rural communities. As such, we further develop the concept of translocal precarity to capture the fragility of social reproduction strategies that migrant households employ across space. Translocal precarity is the looming threat that family members' efforts to support one another might fall apart due to the instability of urban labor markets in tandem with a lack of sustaining infrastructures in rural areas. Our argument advances geographic scholarship on precarity by explaining how it is experienced across the translocal relations that connect the productive and reproductive labor of household members living in different locations.

title: A LIFE-STAGE APPROACH FOR DECOMPOSING SPATIOTEMPORAL POPULATION CHANGES ALONG AN URBAN-RURAL GRADIENT: IMPLICATIONS FOR REGIONAL PLANNING
abstract: The study of population changes across space and time of cohorts at different life stages is relevant for regional planning, but it is often not taken into account. We focus on a case study along the urban-rural gradient of continental Spain from 2002 to 2017 at a municipal scale. Making use of longitudinal data from the municipal registers, we studied changes in total population and three birth cohorts: the cohort joining the workforce, the cohort at a mature working age and the cohort reaching retirement during the study period. The results showed key spatiotemporal population variations. The absolute population increased in 36% of the municipalities, but at least one of the study cohorts showed an increase in 75% of the municipalities. While the cohort joining workforce tended to concentrate in urban and suburban areas, the retiring cohort tended to move to small suburban and rural municipalities. In the next decades the retirement of large birth cohorts in Spain will be a relevant issue for planning. This methodological approach allows us to understand life cycle residential movements across urban, suburban and rural areas and better enables spatial planning decisions. The method can be applied to other study areas at different spatial and temporal scales.
picked: STUDY  BIRTH  COHORTS  AND  POPULATION  CHANGE  TYPOLOGIES

sections.DATA: Demographic data was obtained from the Spanish Continuous Municipal Register of the Spanish Statistical Office (INE), which indicates each municipality's official population by age on January 1 st  of  each year. The INE is an official and reliable source, however the data is not always precise because in some cases migrants take time  to  register  in  their  new  place  of  residence  and  inform  their  previous  local registry. The three birth cohorts for the study were obtained by combining the year of the registry and the age of the registered inhabitants.
sections.STUDY AREA AND URBAN-RURAL GRADIENT:
The  area  of  this  case  study  comprises  continental  Spain  (Iberian  Peninsula, Southwest  Europe),  yielding 47 provinces  (Figure 1 ).  In  the  study  area,  we

4

FIG. 1 -Map of the study area.

<!-- image -->

worked  with  complete  longitudinal  population  data  for 7 , 914 of  the  municipalities,  with a total population of 43 . 12 million inhabitants in 2017 (INE 2018 ).

Municipalities were ranked by demographic size and distance to urban centers to classify them along an urban-rural gradient. The population-size-based classification of municipalities varies from one country to another and may even vary from one official body to another within the same country. In the case of this study, the criterion used was based on the same one established by Spanish law 45 / 2007 for the sustainable development of the rural environment, which categorizes municipalities with more than 30 , 000 inhabitants as urban and with less than 30 , 000 inhabitants as nonurban.  This  law  seeks  to  establish  measures  to  improve  the  socioeconomic situation of the nonurban population and improve access to quality services. Four types of municipalities were isolated as a function of their absolute population size in 2017 :  urban  (more  than 30 , 000 inhabitants),  large  ( 10 , 000 -30 , 000 inhabitants), medium-sized ( 2 , 000 -10 , 000 ), and small (less than 2 , 000 ) (Figure 1 ). Municipalities thus categorized according to population size were then further classified in terms of their distance from urban municipalities (Salvati 2014 ). Two categories of nonurban municipalities  were  used,  calculated  by  GIS  from  the  urban  municipalities:  suburban (less than 20 km) and rural (more than 20 km). By combining demographic size  with  distance  from  urban  municipalities  we  obtained  an  urban-rural  spatial gradient consisting of seven municipality classes.
sections.STUDY BIRTH COHORTS AND POPULATION:
The  percentage  of  change  in  the  population  in  each  municipality  during  the study period was calculated based on the following population groups: absolute population;  the  birth  cohort  of  individuals  born  between 1973 and 1992 ,  who reached employment age during the study period and gained access to their first occupations  in  the  labor  market  (aged  between 25 and 44 in 2017 )-this  range was selected for this concrete case study of Spain (on average, young people take longer  to  enter  the  labor  market  and  do  so  with  less  stability  in  Spain  than  in other  developed  countries)  (Wölfl 2013 )- the  birth  cohort  of  individuals  born between 1953 and 1972 ,  comprising  individuals  that  have  remained  at  a  mature working age during the study period (aged between 45 and 64 in 2017 );  and the birth cohort of individuals born between 1943 and 1952 ,  who reached retirement age during the study period (aged between 65 and 74 in 2017 ).

The  number  of  inhabitants  and  their  percent  variation  during  the  study period  of  the  four  population  groups  were  calculated  in  each  of  the  seven municipality  classes  within  the  urban-rural  spatial  gradient.  Also,  the  number and  percentage  of  municipalities  which  experienced  an  increase  or  decrease  in their  absolute  population  was  analyzed,  resulting  in  two  population  change typologies.  In  addition,  the  analysis  included  the  number  and  percentage  of municipalities of each class of the urban-rural gradient in which the population of  the  study  birth  cohorts  increased  or  decreased  during  the  study  period, resulting in another eight population change typologies.
