For instance, the cumulative frequency of negative precipitation anomalies (60 mm less than the monthly average) for each county or district was ten for 1990 to 2000 and thirteen for 2000 to 2010. Third, although data on urban land use (MODIS) and weather shocks from 1990 to 2000 are publicly available, detailed urban population data at the district or county level are unavailable for most regions such as Guangxi, Yunnan, Lao PDR, and Myanmar before 2000. Studies of longer periods are mainly conducted at the subnational level (the second-level administrative division), rather than the county or district level (the third- or fourth-level administrative division; Henderson, Storeygard, and Deichmann 2017). Accordingly, we restrict our analyses mainly to the period of 2000 to 2010.
sections.Data Sources and Variables:
To examine how urbanization and urban expansion are affected by weather extremes, we rely on three types of data -urbanization, climatology, and local geographical and socioeconomic data. The dependent variables are the urban population change rate and the built-up area change rate in percentage, capturing urbanization and the urban expansion process between 2000 and 2010 in the GMR (Table 1). The data on urban population and the built-up areas are provided by the World Bank East Asia and Pacific Urban Flagship Study (PUMA; Mertes et al. 2015). To identify the extreme weather events and their impact on urbanization, multiple data sets of precipitation, TCs, and temperature from January 2000 to December 2010 are incorporated to construct an eleven-year climatological record for each county and district. Moreover, to control local climate, geographical, and socioeconomic differences, several groups of control variables such as baseline climate variables and local accessibility are also considered in this study.

Precipitation Anomalies. The precipitation anomaly is one of the direct indexes of the deficit or surplus of rainfall, which measure the difference between the observational data and the long-term climatological mean. In this study, the frequencies of monthly precipitation anomalies with values greater than 60 mm ( PM60 ) or less than -60mm ( NM60 ) are calculated to capture the precipitation extremes for each county or district (Manton et al. 2001). We use absolute monthly rainfall anomalies to estimate the rainfall conditions for two reasons. First, the absolute rainfall anomaly is easy to interpret and has been used in previous climatological studies and several agriculture organizations, such as the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS-NET; Dai and Wigley 2000; Feng et al. 2010). Second, previous studies defined climatic anomalies as occasions when precipitation exceeds one to three times the standard deviation or falls below one to three times the standard deviation (Hansen, Sato, and Ruedy 2012). The mean standard deviation of the elevenyear precipitation across our observations is 40 mm. Thus, in this study, we use 1.5 times the standard deviation as the threshold, which is 60 mm.

The monthly precipitation from January 2000 to December 2010, as well as the monthly average precipitation for the eleven-year period, is extracted and calculated from Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data (CHIRPS; Mason and Goddard 2001). Developed by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the Climate Hazards Group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, the CHIRPS data set covers the quasi-global region from 50  N to 50  S, with a resolution of 0.05  latitude -longitude grids (Funk et al. 2015). It offers daily and monthly precipitation from 1981 to the present by combining in situ rain gauge observations and observations from geostationary weather satellites. Because it provides complete spatial and temporal coverage of precipitation with high resolutions, the CHIRPS data set has been used by many regional and global studies that have shown that it does an excellent job in combination with socioeconomic data (Funk et al. 2014; Grace et al. 2015).

Tropical Cyclones. We employ the cumulative frequency of direct hits by storms ( TC ), the total precipitation from TCs for each county or district ( TCP ), and the total frequency of receiving rainfall ( TCAR ) and wind ( TCAW ) from TCs for each county or district to capture the influence from TCs. The TC tracks are obtained from International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS/ National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration), which provides TC center locations and storm intensity every six hours at the standard synoptic times for each day since 1851 (Knapp et al. 2010). We plot the track data in a geographic information system (GIS) to identify TCs originating from the Western Pacific Ocean and

Indian Ocean located within 100km of the GMR during the study period. To determine the possible extent of wind damage during the TCs, the radius of storm-force winds (17 m/s) every six hours is obtained from IBTrACS (Kruk et al. 2010). Asymmetric buffers of wind radius are created to determine whether or not a county or district is affected by TC wind. To estimate the precipitation associated with TCs, we obtain gridded daily precipitation data from the CHIRPS data set. For each TC, the storm period begins on the day when the TC first entered the 500-km range of GMR coastline and ends on the day it exited the 500-km range or dissipated over land. To measure the storm-total precipitation of each TC, we extract the daily precipitation grids within 500 km of track on that day. This 500-km radius is employed because it has been widely used in previous studies to separate TC precipitation from rainfall generated by other weather systems (Villarini et al. 2014). All of the grid cells located within 500-km radius are extracted and identified as daily TC rainfall. All daily precipitation cells during the storm period are summed to calculate storm-total rainfall (Zhou and Matyas 2017).

Temperature Extremes. Because previous studies have used 313.15 K as a threshold to define boiling days, our primary constructed measure of hot days is the cumulative count of days with the maximum daytime temperature greater than 313.15 K ( TM40 ; 40  C) from 2000 to 2010 (Harlan et al. 2006; Grace et al. 2015). To capture the cold waves, we count the total frequency of daily minimum temperature lower than 273.15 K ( TN00 ; 0  C; Powell and Keim 2015). The temperature data set used in this research is developed by Global Meteorological Forcing Dataset (GMFD) for land surface modeling (Sheffield, Goteti, and Wood 2006). This temperature data set is primarily derived from the National Center for Environmental Prediction ' s reanalysis (Kistler et al. 2001), which is currently available at various spatial resolutions (0.25  , 0.5  , and 1.0  latitude -longitude grids) and temporal resolutions (three-hourly, daily, and monthly) globally for the period since 1948. It is generated by assimilating a long-term quality-controlled database of land, oceanic, and atmospheric observations into a global climate model simulation and has been widely used in various global studies (Sheffield and Wood 2008).

Baseline Climate Variables. Baseline climate is widely used to determine a reference period or

' normal ' conditions in research on climate change and extreme weather events (IPCC 2001). Also, the baseline climate indirectly reflects the local human society ' s capability and tolerance for coping with weather extremes. Previous studies employed baseline climate data derived from observation records, usually with average climatic data over a twenty-year or thirty-year period to define the baseline climate (Kennedy, Morice, and Parker 2014; Baker et al. 2016). For precipitation, we calculate monthly average precipitation in the dry season (November -April) and the wet season (May -October) from 1981 to 1999 (Nguyen, Renwick, and McGregor 2014). The temperature control variables are the average daily maximum temperature in summer (June -August) and the average daily minimum temperature in winter (December -February) from 1970 to 1999 (Choi et al. 2009). Last, for each county, we calculate the average annual frequency of direct hits by a TC from the western Pacific Ocean and the north Indian Ocean from 1970 to 1999 (246 TCs total). To maintain data consistency, all of the baseline climate variables are extracted from the same data sets for calculating weather extremes: CHIRPS for precipitation, GMFD for temperature, and IBTrACS for TC tracks.

Local Accessibility. Previous studies have extensively demonstrated that local transportation accessibility has a significant influence on rural -urban and urban -urban migration and the process of urban expansion. The development of highways, major roads, and railways significantly enhances cities ' economic growth and urban expansion. Location close to a major river could be interpreted as a positive factor for urban growth, as the proximity to the river might supply more resources for people ' s lives, such as flows of freight and passengers (Christensen and McCord 2016). Therefore, we introduce four widely used factors to control for the differences in accessibility and reflect the relationship between weather shocks and urbanization more precisely. The distance variables for proximities to the nearest highway ( DH ), major road ( DMR ), railway ( DRL ), and a major river ( DRV ) are employed to capture the influence of accessibility. The data for railways, highways, and major roads are primarily extracted and digitized based on the network maps of roads and railways from the ADB. The streams of the Mekong River, Irrawaddy River, Hong River, Chao Phraya River, and Salween River, as well as their major tributaries, are obtained through the physical

layers at 1:10 m scale from the Web site of Natural Earth (see www.naturalearthdata.com).

Geographical Control Variables. With respect to geographical variables, we use the average elevation ( EL ) overlapping the polygons of each county or district derived from the digital elevation model (DEM) to monitor the association between temperature, precipitation, and elevation, as well as to capture the construction cost associated with increasing built-up area and the area ' s suitability for human activities. The raster data of DEM are collected from the USGS. Globally, cities are more likely to concentrate in coastal areas that have greater penetration of globalization and more job opportunities. Thus, the variable of distance to the coastline ( DC ) is included to assess whether the coastal areas have more urban land development. Moreover, the Mekong River Basin is subject to frequent flooding and water quality issues, including acid sulfate soils and salinity intrusion. To test whether a county located in the Mekong River Basin will have a relatively slower urbanization process, we add a dummy variable ( MRB ) to check whether the county or district is located in the Mekong River Basin. The area polygon of the Mekong River Basin is constructed based on a database of the World Resource Institute (WRI).

Socioeconomic Control Variables. In the process of urbanization in Southeast Asia, the most productive economic activities and the bulk of the urban population are mainly concentrated in the capital areas (Bracken 2015). For instance, the population living in the Bangkok metropolitan area accounted for about 54 percent of Thailand ' s total population in 2000. Therefore, to avoid the deviation caused by urban primacy, we include a dummy variable ( CA ) in the models indicating whether a particular county included a capital region. The level of economic development profoundly affects people ' s and cities ' responses to weather extremes (Cattaneo and Peri 2016). Because the gross domestic product per capita is unavailable for each county or district, we add the gross domestic product per capita in 2000 measured by dollars at the country level for Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, and Lao PDR and the province level for Yunnan and Guangxi into the analysis to capture local economic status. The country-level data for Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, and Lao PDR are gathered from the International Monetary Fund, whereas province-level data for Yunnan and Guangxi are collected from the Statistical Yearbook for Regional Economy of China (China State Statistical Bureau 2001).

As we mentioned in the literature review, due to a more centralized administrative system, socialist countries have a better performance in mobilizing resources for disaster relief and local reconstruction (Moore et al. 2007; Petz 2014; Chen, Zhang, and Hsu 2016). Existing studies have also pointed out that institutional variation across the GMR countries is likely to result in different patterns of urban development, and socialist countries in recent decades tend to urbanize more rapidly than nonsocialist countries (Li, Wei, and Korinek 2018). To isolate the influence of institutional variations and determine whether the centralized socialist countries have better risk management and disaster relief and therefore suffer less from weather extremes, we add a dummy variable for the transitional socialist countries in the model ( TSC ). For the counties belonging to China, Lao PDR, and Vietnam, we assign the variable a value of 1, and for the other countries ' counties, the value is 0. Moreover, to consider the influence of initial advantages, urban population ( P00 ) and built-up area ( B00 ) in 2000 are applied to capture each county or district ' s base condition in urban development.
sections.Regression Methods: Spatial Autocorrelat:
The spatial effects of urbanization and urban expansion have been widely identified in the literature based on the theories of regional spillover and competition (Li et al. 2015). In this study, the values of global Moran ' s I of urban population growth rate and construction land expansion rate are 0.142 and 0.250, with a significant p -value, respectively. Meanwhile, values of Moran ' s I for residuals in simple ordinary least squares (OLS) regression are 0.107 for the urbanization model and 0.202 for the urban expansion model with a p -value at the significance level of 1 percent. Thus, four types of spatial econometrics are employed to control the biased estimation caused by spatial autocorrelation and heterogeneity.

Spatial Autocorrelation. We introduce a spatial autoregressive model and spatial filtering regression to mitigate the problem of spatial autocorrelation. For the spatial autoregressive model, the result of the Lagrange multiplier test suggests the need for a

Spatial Heterogeneity. The mean value of the intragroup test between six nations (the function of RWG in R) with the expected random variance as 2 for urban population growth rate is 0.76, and the number for built-up area change rate is 0.91. Both of these outputs are larger than 0.70, which suggests that there is a high within-group similarity in nations. Therefore, there is a significant gap or heterogeneity in urbanization and urban expansion between six national groups. Therefore, we employ multilevel and spatial regime regressions to control the spatial heterogeneity (Anselin 2010).

Because we aim to investigate differences between nations with regard to the effects of weather shocks on urbanization, it is necessary to assume that effects vary randomly within the counties or districts of nations, which means that country-specific effects are uncorrelated with urbanization and urban expansion at the county or district level (Gelman and Hill 2007). Therefore, random intercept multilevel models are adapted to control the effects within the six national groups.

To examine different responses of urbanization to weather extremes across the divergent political systems with their related disaster management and relief capabilities, we use the spatial regime model, which can explicitly recognize the heterogeneity of determinants across groups. More specifically, the spatial regime model is a technique that can derive the parameters that are specific to counties and districts in particular groups or spatial regimes. This model has been widely used in planning, political, urban, and geographical studies (Li et al. 2015). In our model, by addressing the variance between socialist nations and nonsocialist countries in the GMR, the effects of extreme weather are assumed to be sensitive to their political systems (Chen, Zhang, and Hsu 2016). title: We Plant Only Cotton to Maximize Our Earnings: The Paradox of Food Sovereignty in Rural Telengana, India
abstract: This article critically examines the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints to the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security to exercise truefood sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods. ???????, ?????????????????????????????, ?????????????????????????????????????, ???????????, ??????????????, ????????????????????????????????????, ??????????????, ????????????????????????, ???????????????????????, ?????????????, ?????????????????????? Este articulo examina criticamente el papel de las intervenciones de la soberania alimentaria en la mitigacion de los impactos ejercidos por politicas economicas neoliberales sobre los agricultores pobres de la region Telengana, en la India. Los hallazgos logrados con base en dieciocho meses de investigacion etnografica en esa region revelan que los agricultores pequenos y pobres tienen que enfrentar restricciones socioeconomicas y culturales para la adopcion de las practicas e ideales de la soberania alimentaria. Las prescripciones de la soberania alimentaria basada en una agricultura localizada, sostenible y de subsistencia paradojicamente restringen las oportunidades de los agricultores de mantener un sistema de vida rural viable en medio de un clima economico dificil. Basandome en estos hallazgos, sostengo que al contrario de lo que proclaman sus mentores, en el sentido de ver la soberania alimentaria como condicion previa para una genuina seguridad alimentaria, los agricultores primero deben tener comida y seguridad de medios de vida para ejercer una verdadera soberania alimentaria que les permita mayor control sobre su subsistencia.

sections.The Telengana Context:
Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

The Telengana region (see Figure 1) forms part of a contiguous semi-arid belt and is considered 'backward' in terms of its human development (Nagaraj 2008). The region is characterized by rain-fed agriculture, poor soils, drought, and cultural and economic marginalization. Since India adopted neoliberal economic policies, already vulnerable farming systems have given way to widespread agrarian distress in the form of farmer suicides (Nagaraj 2008).

The region still primarily cultivates food crops such as sorghum, lentils, and oilseeds in nonirrigated lands and commercial crops such as sugarcane, potato, and banana in irrigated lands. Genetically modified (GM) cotton, considered by local farmers to be a high-risk crop, has in the past been cultivated by mainly large farmers. Yet, within the last seven to eight years, GM cotton and hybrid corn sold by Monsanto's local affiliates have been adopted on a large scale, even by small and marginal farmers.

Distress is not new to small and marginal farmers 2 in the region. Historically, lower castes have dealt with extreme oppression, exploitation, and hunger. Under late-Mughal rule, land and power were highly concentrated among the high castes, while untouchables and lower castes provided wage and unfree labor (Pavier 1981). Examples of earlier hardships were recounted several times during life history interviews by Dalit and lower caste families at the field site. They talked about the indignity of being hungry into the 1970s and 1980s, of having to beg for food and the compulsory unpaid labor called vetti.

The era of state-led development after independence brought some positive changes with land reforms, abolition of feudal institutions, investments in agriculture, the provision of safety nets resulting in agricultural growth, and increased food security. Many interviewees benefited from land reforms and became owner-cultivators. They reported that the availability of subsidized rice and rural employment programs greatly contributed to their food security. For the lower castes, these developments brought self-respect as culturally sanctioned poverty and social exclusion lessened.

The adoption of neoliberal economic reforms in the 1990s led to massive cuts in farming subsidies, reduced safety nets, and privatization and disinvestment in several key institutions for agriculture including credit, seeds, research, and extension services (Ghosh 2005). Costs of cultivation rose substantially as a result, leading to high debt. The reforms had differentiated impacts for the poor at the field site. Increased market engagement created new opportunities but also increased vulnerability in the face of ecological and market perturbations. Although most small farmers continued to struggle to meet their basic needs and their lives were extremely vulnerable, a majority of Dalits felt that they were better off than the past. Maniamma, an elder Dalit farmer who recounted hardships during a life history interview in 2009, explained:

Figure 1 Map of study site, Medak District in Andhra Pradesh State of India. Map credit: Charles Daveny, Cartographer, Department of Geography, University of Hawai'i at M¯ anoa. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

Things are better now. We are eating well because of subsidized rice, state-provided rural employment, and the ability to cultivate our land. Our own hard work brings in wages that are high. Before we could not work in our own fields and had to work the landlord's fields. If we did not work for them they would not give us the grain we needed to survive.

This comment suggests that a combination of higher wages that came with neoliberal reforms, state welfare measures, and the breaking down of traditional feudal institutions have allowed them to cultivate their own land and sell their labor freely. These have been key to their improved food security. Small farmers are still up against insurmountable obstacles in their quest to eke out a livelihood in the Telengana region, however.

It is within this context of historical vulnerability, hunger, and marginalization and rapid commercialization that food sovereignty interventions have been promoted by RDI among small and marginal mainly Dalit women farmers. Their strategies reflect food sovereignty's overarching model for resisting the neoliberal agro-food regime, promoting localized agroecological farming that intends to improve farmers' capacity to subsist, focusing on traditionally cultivated food crops such as sorghum, millets, oilseeds, and lentils.

The majority of small and poor farmers, however, were unable to adopt localized subsistence-focused agriculture even if it improved their ability to subsist. Farmers faced many constraints including (1) compulsions to participate in an increasingly monetized economy with all the opportunities and risks that markets bring, (2) changing geographies of labor, and (3) changing values and knowledge relating to agriculture.

title: From Labor to Life in Vegetal Geography: Exploring Ontological Marginalization and Critical Externalities in the Plantationscape of a Global South Country
abstract: In the ever-expanding era of urbanization where the dominance of the urban human increasingly defines global society, marginalized subaltern groups in remote rural spaces remain stark reminders of systemic inequities. Nowhere is this more evident than in India, a rising superpower whose rapid growth paradoxically coexists with deep-rooted societal divides. Within its vegetal geographies, such as the tea plantations of the Global South, landscapes of cultivation are not merely sites of production; they are living terrains where plants, labor, and social hierarchies intertwine, reinforcing the very inequities that urban progress claims to transcend. This study explores the ontological marginalization within the tea plantationscape of the Dooars region in India. Ontological marginalization is conceptualized as the systematic exclusion of marginalized ways of being, rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by modern socioeconomic systems. The findings reveal a paradox of livelihood duality. On one hand, subsistence practices rooted in collective labor, seasonal variability in livelihoods, and reciprocal exchange continue to sustain households. On the other, these practices are increasingly enmeshed in exploitative wage economies that define the vegetal geography of tea gardens. In this landscape, the very plants that anchor livelihoods also structure social relations, tying human survival to cycles of cultivation that reproduce dependency and marginality. The research reveals how historical disruptions, contemporary structural inequalities, and gendered dimensions of exclusion have perpetuated intergenerational poverty and systemic vulnerabilities. It argues that addressing ontological marginalization demands rejecting colonial development logics and embracing justice-based frameworks that value diverse ways of being, knowing, and surviving.

title: Who is forest-Dependent? Capturing local variation in forest-product sale, Eastern Honduras
abstract: How researchers describe groups living within or near the world's tropical rain forests has important implications for how and why these groups are targeted for assistance by conservation and development organizations. This article explores how data about market behavior can be used to assess one aspect of forest peoples' liveihoods: their dependence on forest resources as a source of market income. With the intent the importance of methodology, to how we describe forest peoples' livelihoods, I draw from a multiyear survey of market activity among the Tawahka-nested measures of the Tawahkas' engagement in forest-product sale. Results indicate of Honduras and distinguish dicate that whether or not the Tawahka-or any forest group-can be considered financially dependent on forest resources depends on the spatial and temporal scales at which data are aggregated. As a group, the Tawahka earned 18 percent of total market income from forest-product sale, but their group profile masked a high degree of heterogeneity at the village and household level. Similarly multiyear data indicated that while group-level generalizations adhere from year to year, they belie considerable change in households' market behavior across years. I discuss three ways in which the findings are relevant to the theory and practice of conservation and development in the humid tropics. I emphasize the importance of spatial scale in interventions, how market-oriented conservation schemes can benefit from a broader conceptualization of the economic context in which forest-product sale occurs, and how longitudinal analysis can reveal the dynamism of forest peoples' livelihoods.

sections.Study Region:
The Honduran Tawahka, who numbered about 1,000 at the time of the study, are a subgroup of Mayangna, or Sumu, of whom the majority live in Nicaragua. In Honduras, the  Tawahka homeland is centered along the midchannel of the  Patuca  River.  The  area  straddles  three Honduran departamentos (political regions) and lies at the southwestern edge of what is known as the Mosquitia region (Figure 1). Here, the pine-covered coastal plain ( < 75 m) of the Mosquitia  meets  the  Colón  and  Patuca  ranges, which  support  broadleaf  rain  forests  that  include Honduras' most endangered biota (Cruz and Benitez 1994; Harcourt and Sayer 1996).

Most Tawahka live in one of five permanent communities (subsequently referred to in this article as Villages A-E) located along a 40-km stretch of river. Most communities have consolidated around a Catholic church and school, and most Tawahka children receive three years of basic education. Communities differ in size (in 1998, Village A had a population of 624; Village  E,  64)  and  in  the  area  of  adjacent floodplain.  Only  Village  A  had  a  government-funded health clinic during the 1990s.

Figure 1 The location of Tawahka villages within the Tawahka Asangni Biosphere Reserve, eastern Honduras,  1998.  Sources:  Honduras  base-map:  International Travel  Maps,  1997 ,  Herlihy  (1997),  and author's field notes.

<!-- image -->

Most Tawahka households (67 percent) comprise  a  single  nuclear  family,  but  almost  20 percent  included  the  more  traditional  arrangement of extended family, comprising an elder couple and their married children (McSweeney 2000).

Tawahka  livelihoods  are  based  on  permanent,  intensive  polycultural  cultivation  along riverbanks  and  shifting  cultivation  of  poorer uplands (House 1997). Compared to most rural Hondurans, the T awahka live under conditions of  land  abundance. In 1998, households controlled an average of 6.45 ha of land on river terraces ( ± 8.03 ha), in addition to more extensive  upland  fields  and  fallows  (McSweeney 2000). During the study period, land was held in usufruct, and there was no formal land market.  The  T awahka  supplemented  agricultural production with fishing and hunting, and other forest resources provide essential construction materials,  canoes,  medicines,  and  fuelwood. Access  to  village-proximate  forest  resources depended  on  village  residence,  although  all Tawahka had equal access to resources far from settlements. With no tradition of effective village councils or local political leadership, the Tawahka have used social sanctions to convey communal  disapproval of excessive forestproduct harvest from what is a de facto forest commons. 3   The  T awahkas'  collective  knowledge of forest resources and extraction methods are nationally renowned (Cruz and Benitez 1994; House 1997).

Over the past two decades, T awahka extraction  patterns  have  been  increasingly  circumscribed by an ever-expanding colonization front of  nonindigenous,  Spanish-speaking  farmers, who are moving into the Tawahka homeland from the south and west. Aggressive land grabs by  these  colonists  in  the  mid-1980s  led  the Tawahka to consolidate disparate homesteads into five communities within a defensible core area (Herlihy 1997), which in turn led to the 1999 ratification of the 2,300-square-km TABR.  Nevertheless,  conflicts  over  land  and timber  resources  continue,  as  colonists  clear forests  deeper  into  the  reserve  and  have charged Tawahka fees for the use of forest resources there. Although it is the responsibility of Honduras'  state forestry administration (AFE)  to  enforce  the  reserve  boundaries  and expel  new  migrants  (Republic  of  Honduras 1999), effective enforcement is lacking. In con- trast, AFE employees at downriver offices have been  relatively  quick  to  tax  the  T awahka  for small volumes of wood products (e.g., dugout canoes)  exported  from  the  reserve,  which  in some cases has raised the cost of forest-based market production.

The  T awahka  also  face  land  and  forest  resource shortages as their population grows rapidly: the median age is 12, and households are large,  averaging  7.8  members  (McSweeney forthcoming). Land was rendered more scarce when  flooding  from  1998's  Hurricane  Mitch wiped out the majority of the T awahkas' most productive riparian fields. Hardest hit were the cacao  orchards  that  had  become  increasingly important  in  T awahka  market  strategies.  Because the fieldwork on which this study is based was completed six months before Mitch, results depict economic conditions prior to subsequent agricultural  reorganization.  Nevertheless,  results attest to the flexibility of T awahka market strategies,  a  trait  on  which  the  group  leaned heavily during post-Mitch reconstruction.

The  Tawahka  have  traded  forest  products and  other  goods  with  a  neighboring  ethnic group, the Miskito, and with outsiders since at least  the  late  1700s  (Roberts  1827;  Young 1842). In common with many remote tropical forest regions, economic integration with national and international  markets  has  been highly cyclical. External demand for successive products-which in the T awahka case have included  bananas,  rubber,  and chicle (latex  used for chewing gum)-has driven so-called booms (Cruz and Benitez 1994). At the time of the study, however, the T awahka characterized the local economic climate as one of lala  apu ('no money'), or relative economic stagnation. Under  such  conditions,  participation  in  no single  market  activity  is  overdetermined,  and income portfolios among forest peoples typically broaden to accommodate market needs in  more  diverse  ways  (Pinedo-Vasquez  et  al. 2001). As a result, the T awahka earned income during  the  study  period  from  varied  sources. They  exported  forest  products,  agricultural goods, and labor to downriver Miskito communities and to farmers and river traders from upriver.  The  T awahka  rarely  migrate  seasonally for  work,  in  marked  contrast  to  the  Miskito. Some goods exported from the TABR eventually reached national markets, including beans, cacao, and gold dust. Other goods were con-

sumed within the Mosquitia, particularly lumber, dugout canoes, and perishable agricultural produce. Coastal Miskito communities, where such  products  are  scarce,  provide  a  constant market for such T awahka commodities.

The Tawahka sell a variety of goods to each other,  including  agricultural  surpluses,  forest products  (particularly  meat),  firewood,  dairy products,  and,  most  importantly,  labor.  Salaried  Tawahka-those  working  as  teachers, nurses, or NGO employees-provide a steady cash input to the local economy, as they hire neighbors to tend their fields and cover domestic work. Other T awahka use market earnings to  meet basic needs such as tools, medicines, food and other perishables (particularly cooking oil, coffee, sugar, flour, salt, soap, and kerosene), clothing, and educational expenses.

As with much of rural Honduras and forests pantropically, government involvement in the economy is minimal. There is no formal credit provisioning,  no  insurance  markets,  and  few government technical assistance services. Local shopkeepers are typically the main source of informal credit. Cash is often scarce in T awahka communities, and barter is common. As a result, this study uses the term 'market income' to refer to T awahkas' earnings from the sale of goods and services, rather than the more exclusive term 'cash income.' With few formal ways of holding wealth, the T awahka invest surplus earnings in livestock,  in  trade  (by  purchasing outboard  motors),  in  agriculture  (by  buying improved  seeds  or  herbicide  applicators),  in forest extraction (by buying chainsaws), and in their children's secondary education (by paying  school  fees,  and  room  and  board  outside the TABR).
sections.Data and Methods: To establish  a  picture  of  the  role  of  forestproduct sales within T awahka market production, I analyzed information about the sale of goods and services compiled from three household-level surveys: one conducted in 1995 by a research team from the Harvard Institute for International  Development  (HIID),  and  two that I conducted in 1996 and 1998. 4  I organized these data into two sets, one comprising a single year  of  market  production  (1997-1998)  for about 100 Tawahka households and the other covering three years (1994, 1995, 1997) for a subset of 49 households from one T awahka village. Below, I describe how the data were collected and organized.

title: MIGRATION PATTERNS DURING A PERIOD OF POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC SHOCKS IN THE FORMER SOVIET-UNION - A CASE-STUDY OF YAROSLAVL-OBLAST
abstract: This paper examines migration in Russia during the period that preceded the breakup of the former Soviet Union (FSU) and during the current transition period. An unusually rich dataset is used to conceptualize the impact that the political and economic collapse of a world superpower has on a migration system. A regional case study of migration in Yaroslavl' Oblast from 1989 through 1992 is used to examine the relevance of expected outcomes given standard theories of migration, empirical regularities found in capitalist economies, and past trends in the FSU. The data clearly show a migration system undergoing political and economic shocks. A significant decline of the volume of flows and a relative increase in the importance of interrepublic movement indicate disruptions. Increased relative mobility for those in the later years of the working-age population and increased importance of urban-to-rural migration flows are also important changes evident in this migration system undergoing shock.

sections.Data and Methods:
Migration  data  for  Phase  I 1   come  from  the annual  population  register  data  collected  in Yaroslavl' by  the oblast government. Register data  collected at the oblast level are probably of  higher  quality than  those  presented  at the national  level; by  the  time  the  national  level receives  the  data,  they  have  passed  through several  government  offices,  each  having  the potential  to introduce  error. Trained  sociologists calculated this dataset by hand  using the original registry forms. Although human error can occur in the absence of computerization in

Russia, the population accounting in this dataset is  the best available to date.

Several major drawbacks, however, exist due to the nature  of  the registry system. First, inmigration data are more accurate than outmigration data. Individuals must register as  they migrate into a  place  in order to receive social services,  including  housing, education,  and public assistance, but  no  such incentives exist to  register  outmigration.  Outmigration  data are  generally underestimated,  but  due  to  the absence of  place-to-place migration  data,  we cannot  estimate  the  level  of  undercounting. Within this particular dataset, however, we can measure 6% undercounting for intraoblast migration. Second, the urban accounting systems are  more  accurate than  the  rural  ones. Rural inmigration and outmigration are likely undercounted. Third, there are two separate counts of intraoblast migration. Differing levels of accuracy  between  urban  and  rural  accounting systems and  differing levels  of  self-reporting for  inmigration  and  outmigration  explain the latter  problem.

Accounting  and  data  quality  problems  are not  unique  to  Soviet  or  Russian  population data. These problems exist  in many contexts, particularly those with less technologically advanced data management systems. These data are,  however,  the  best  quality  and  most  detailed available on migration trends in Russia. Our approach is to analyze the time series with respect to trends without giving undue weight to  absolute figures. We  rely  most  heavily on the inmigration  data-rather than  the  outmigration  data-and the  data collected in urban places.

Because the goal of this work is to conceptualize the nature of a migration system undergoing shock and, in part, because of data limitations,  simple  descriptive  techniques  rather than causal modeling techniques were used  to describe and analyze the migration data. Other than  presenting  the  raw  data  themselves, we calculate simple ratios to describe the composition of the migration flows, such as a sex ratio and an age ratio of the 15-34  age group to the 35-59 age  group.  We  also  calculate  demographic  effectiveness ratios  to  measure  gains and  losses due to  the  exchange of  population at varying geographical levels. A high positive or  negative ratio  indicates a  large imbalance between the stream and counterstream. An in-

creasing ratio  over time  signifies regional net gains. The ratio is calculated by subtracting the counterstream  from  the  stream,  dividing  by the sum of migrants, and multiplying by  100.
sections.Yaroslavl' Case Study:
The  Russian  and  Soviet  migration  systems have undergone shocks in the past due to major  violent  events  such  as  the  I917  Russian Revolution, civil  war, and  World  War  1 1 . Characteristics of the migration system persisted  despite  these  events-the north-to-south and west-to-east flows and rural-to-urban flows.

The essential  problem  here is to conceptualize  how  the  direction  and  composition of migration flows within the migration system(s) of  Russia  may  change  during the  post-Soviet period-a time  of  instability,  disintegration, and reintegration, not a wartime period. There are likely to be several overlapping yet distinct phases  of  migration.  The reality  of  the  situation suggests that although the phases may be distinct,  no one phase will be evident in isolation  in  any one place  or at any one point in time. Phase I, destabilization, describes the late 1970s and early 1980s  when the reversal of the north-to-south  net exchange occurred. Phase I foreshadows Phase 1 1 ,  disintegration,  when the chaotic patterns occasioned by the current destabilization and politicaVeconomic shocks become evident.  The initial  period  of  destabilization  ended  in  the  late  1980s just  as pereswoyka was ending. Phase I1 migration should be  evident  in  the  1990s, with  1989 being  a transition year  when both  Phase I  and  Phase I1 patterns co-existed.
sections.Yarosla vl':
Migration  in and  out  of  Yaroslavl'  Oblast should  be  seen  as  representative of central Russia. Data on migration in the Central Economic  Region  (a  statistical  accounting region to which Yaroslavl' belongs)  for 1970 through 1989 indicates that Yaroslavl'  is not atypical for the region with respect to losses of  population

in  the  1970s due  to  migration,  gains  in  the 1980s, persistent inflows of  migrants to urban places from the  1970s through  1989, and consistent outflows of  migrants  from rural  places (Goskomstat  RSFSR 1990).  Although the Central Economic Region has received a large portion  of the forced migrants returning from the  former  Soviet republics, Yaroslavl' Oblast received  about  the  average  number  for  the region  (Vitkovskaya  1994). Despite  the  relatively  large  number  of  returning  Russians in Yaroslavl', the oblast was  not  designated as  a receiving location by  the  central  government (Schwartz 1993).

Other regional  issues also support  the  description of Yaroslavl' as typical for the region. The politics are not overwhelmingly  liberal or conservative, although the region can boast of early  'democratic' movements  (Hahn  199  I). Although the oblast capital is located within a five-hour train  ride,  Moscow does not  dominate  the  region;  the  oblast capital, Yaroslavl', is  itself  a  regional  center  due  to its  industrial importance and role as a transportation center. Industrial employment in the oblast is concentrated in petrochemicals,  machine-building, the  automobile  industry,  and  light  industry (textiles).  These industrial sectors provide the oblast economy  with the combination of growth possibilities and an obsolete, fixed capital  base.  The oblast  is  not  dominated  by  the military  industrial  complex,  although  some factories  did  produce  for  it.  Yaroslavl'  does differ  from  other  central  Russian  oblasts  in that it has a higher proportion of its population living  in  urban  areas  (about  80% urban  and 20%  rural  in  1989), but  like other  oblasts in the central region its population is mainly ethnic Russian (95% in  1989).

title: The geography of the 1994 Nordic vote on European Union membership
abstract: In 1994, support for European Union (EU) membership was highly variable across Norway, Sweden, and Finland. The ''no'' vote was strongest in rural areas eligible for substantial EU subsidies. Moreover, the majority voted against EU membership in Norway. To explain these outcomes, this article focuses on the ways in which local and national differences mediated interpretations of the issues raised during the campaign. The analysis highlights Important forces shaping northern Europe today and their implications for the EU in the years ahead.
picked: Mediating Factors at the National Level
Mediating Factors at the Local Level

sections.Mediating Factors at the National Level: Norway, Sweden, and Finland have distinctive political, economic,  social, and  cultural  attributes and, for many, these influenced how the arguments surrounding EU membership were understood  and interpreted. A brief  examination  of  the  situation  of  each  of  the  Nordic countries  that  voted  on  EU membership  can thus provide insight into the variable successes of  the  'yes' and  'no' campaigns in  northern Europe.
sections.Mediating Factors at the Local Level:
Beyond  national  differences  among  Finland, Sweden, and Norway, the remarkable continuity in  the internal  spatial character  of  the  EU membership vote across all three countries requires  explanation.  For  those  living  in  the more densely populated areas of Norway, Sweden,  and  Finland,  the  arguments  in  favor  of membership were apparently persuasive-persuasive enough  even to overcome projections that EU membership would have negative economic  consequences  for  the  larger  cities  of Finland,  Sweden,  and  Norway.  These  arguments  were  clearly less  effective in  the  rural periphery,  even when  combined with  projections  showing  the  rural  periphery  benefiting from  EU subsidies. The reasons behind  this outcome can be discerned from the preceding discussion.  The  urban areas  of  the  Nordic countries  are  dominated  by  those who  define their interests more in national terms and who therefore  were  more  easily  persuaded  by  the macroeconomic  and  political  influence  arguments  of  the  'yes'  campaign.  By contrast, those  living in  more  remote  rural  areas were more  likely to  be  swayed  by  the  prospect  of diminished local control and the restructuring of  the rural sector.

The negative reaction to EU membership in the  Nordic periphery  was  exacerbated  by  the relationship that currently exists between core and  periphery  in  Norway,  Sweden, and  Finland. The  psychological distance between those  in  the  capital  cities  of  the  European north and those in outlying areas is significant (John  1984). The extent  of  that  distance became  clear  during  the  campaign  over  EU membership.  It  manifested  itself  most  obviously in a general disuust of  statements emanating  from  Oslo,  Stockholm,  and  Helsinh about the benefits of EU membership. In particular, substate regionalism is associated with a  suspicion in  many  rural  areas  that  the  national  governments  of  Norway,  Sweden, and Finland would  use EU subsidies as  an excuse to  cut  state  subsidies (Dug ug Tid 1994a). In Norway  such  suspicions were  heightened  by decades of north-south polarization that can be traced  back  to  the  efforts  of  the  Norwegian government to develop the country's industrial potential  after World  War I1 by discouraging northerners  who  had  been  brought  to  the south  during  the  Nazi  period  from  returning

home  (Mmnesland  1994). As  a  result,  when the  Agricultural Minister  failed  to  come  forward with any information on the level of subsidies  that  Norwegian  farmers would  receive after the five-year adjustment period that Norway would have gone through had it joined the EU, those in the periphery worried  about betrayal (Nytt Fra Norge 1994). Regional antipathies were sufficiently  strong that they affected how  economic  predictions  were  understood and interpreted. For many, such antipathies led to  a  rejection  of  the  economic  benefit  argument that was being advanced by advocates of EU membership in the urbanized core.

Beyond concerns about the amount of  economic benefits rural areas might receive, many voters  were  concerned  about  the  form  those benefits  might  take  if  Norway,  Sweden,  and Finland  joined  the  EU.  In the  Nordic  countries,  particularly  Norway,  the  goal  of  state regional  subsidies  in  recent  decades has  been to sustain a decentralized settlement pattern by creating  jobs  and  production  possibilities  in rural districts (Jussila and Malinen  1993). Regional funding is  used  to compensate  for the extra  cost  of  producing  goods and  services in these regions, and selective support to firms is therefore  not uncommon. To many, the prospect  of  substituting this  approach  to  regional assistance for the  EU approach-even if  total subsidies were greater-was unacceptable (Almk et al.  1994). As  they saw it, restructuring would bring social and psychological costs that would far outweigh any theoretical shortterm economic gain.

It should be clear from the foregoing, then, that local concerns played an important role in the  campaign for  E U  membership.  They are certainly evident in the positions of particular counties  and provinces  in  Figure  3.  For  Finland, the province lying farthest below the regression line is Vassa,  a western province that is  not strongly tied to the urban core but that is  distant  from Russia  and  therefore  less concerned with Russian influence than its counterparts  farther  east. In  the  case  of  Sweden, the counties lying the farthest below the regression line  are  Jamtland, Blekinge,  and  Goteborg. Jamtland is the county  with perhaps the strongest  sense  of  local  particularism  in  the Swedish  north-a consequence  of  close  historical  ties  with  adjacaent  parts  of  Norway. The other two counties are less distinct, but in each  case  the  inhabitants  expressed  concerns over the impact of EU membership  on sensitive  local industries. As  for Norway, the counties  that  lie  the  farthest  below  the  regression line are either well north of  Trondheim (Troms,  Nordland),  in  the  remote  area  between Bergen and Trondheim (Sogn og Fjordane,  Mme og  Romsdal), or  in  the  isolated southeast (Rogaland).  There is one Norwegian county well  below  the  regression  line  that  is more  urbanized-the county  of  Hordaland where  Bergen is located-but there  are longstanding  divisions  between  the  Bergen  area and the Norwegian core. Hordaland is thus in a very different  position  from  the Norwegian counties that lie the farthest above the regression line-Akershus, Buskerud, Oppland, and Hedmark-which are in a ring around Oslo.

title: From the Right to Energy to the Right to the Countryside and Back Again: Contextualizing Rural Energy Transitions
abstract: Rural areas as well as their interlinkages with urban agglomerations have gained increasing attention as the main sites where the current energy transformation toward the use of renewable energy is taking place. Due to this, contestations over transitions and emancipatory efforts to transform energy infrastructures cannot be detached from the structural conditions of rural areas and their entanglements with other spatial scales. In this sense, sustainable energy transitions reflect various differences between as well as within rural areas. Consequently, rural energy transitions are embedded in broader processes of rural change. This contribution to the Focus section illustrates interconnections between energy transitions and rural change as they relate to issues of land-use change in rural areas, rural poverty, and marginalization, along with rural populism. In doing so, we argue that energy transition plays an important role for all these issues of rural development and advocate for a systematic integration of the transformation of energy systems and rural change. We, thereby, believe that contextualizing rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a right to the countryside and of just and sustainable rural futures within the energy sector and beyond.

title: SPATIAL ACCESSIBILITY TO HEALTH-CARE FACILITIES IN SUHUM DISTRICT, GHANA
abstract: To improve geographical accessibility to health facilities in rural Ghana, it has been recommended that additional health facilities be built. Resource constraints make this recommendation infeasible. Using location-allocation models, this paper demonstrates that in the Suhum District of Ghana substantial improvements in accessibility can be achieved with better locational choices and without additional facilities. Also, additional facilities will produce little improvement in accessibility if location is not explicitly considered. The paper demonstrates the utility of location-allocation models for improving accessibility to services in the Third World.

sections.Studv Area:
The Suhum District is in the Eastern  Region of Ghana (Fig. 1). It is  one  of  10 pioneering districts which  the government  of  Ghana  selected  to  implement  the  PHC policy in  the country.  Consequently,  it is  the  focus  of  ongoing research into the planning and delivery of health services in Ghana. In fact, at the time of  fieldwork for this research, the district was involved in a World  Health Organization  assisted project to delimit the catchment areas o f health  facilities  and  identify  gaps  in  service delivery.

According to the latest available (1  984) census, Suhum has  a  population  of  146,100 and encompasses  about 877.5 sq km (District Health Management Team 1987). The district is located  on the  edge of Ghana's forest belt. The district capital, Suhum, has a population of 19,298  and is 60 km from Accra, the national

Figure 1: Ghana and location of Suhum District.

<!-- image -->

capital. Suhum has several central place functions, including education, administration, commerce,  and  health.  Besides  Suhum,  only Nankese has a population exceeding  3,000  people  (3,414),  and  just  14 communities  exceed 1,000. The remainder of the population is located predominantly in small rural farming villages (Fig. 2). Because of  this skewed  population  distribution,  Suhum  is  the  hub  of  most activities in the district.

The district has 30 government health facilities altogether:  the  C-level  facility at Suhum, six B-level  facilities, and  23 A-level  facilities. The system is  successively inclusive; higherlevel facilities offer all the services provided at lower-level facilities in addition to services that are not provided at lower levels. Thus  there are 30 facilities providing A-level services, seven of which  provide  B-level  services,  and  Suhum hospital provides all three levels  of service. Like most other districts in Ghana, health facilities

Figure 2: Population size of villages and towns in Suhurn District

<!-- image -->

are located primarily in the larger centers with very few in the remote rural centers. Access to government health services is quite limited for rural residents.

Walking is the most popular means of travel in  the  district  because  few  people  own  any mode of transportation including bicycles. Access  to  commercial passenger vehicles is  limited. Where access is not a problem, the high fares charged, especially during the rainy season when the roads become difficult to travel, restrict use.
sections.Data Requirements and Modelling Approach:
Essential data for this study included population  and locational information  for each community.  Population  data  were  obtained  from the  1984 population  census.  Because  Ghana does not have  a  digital spatial database, locations  were  digitized  as x and  y  coordinates from the Ghana  1:50,000 map series obtained from  the  Ghana  Geologic  Survey  in  Accra. There were no major problems with the maps, but the population  data of some smaller communities had been aggregated with larger centers  close  by.  Another  minor  problem  was communities with different locations but simi- lar  names.  These were carefully organized to avoid assigning the wrong population figure to any location. A simple distance generating algorithm  was  used  to  generate  Euclidean distances between locations.

The analysis involves 150 population centers in the Suhum district as demand points and the population  at each center as the proxy for demand.  Euclidean  distances  are  used  because walking is the main mode o f   travel in Suhum district.  This  avoids the  problem  of  seasonal inaccessibility  along  different  types  of  roads. The Tietz and Bart (1968) heuristic algorithm was  used. The modelling approach treats  the three  levels  of  service  independently  and  locates an optimal system of 30 facilities in keeping with the successively  inclusive nature of the system.  Seven  of  these  will  provide  B-level services, and  one  of  these  seven will  provide C-level services.
sections.Proximity to Health Facilities:
The  immediate  question  is  proximity to Alevel  services. How  does  the  existing (actual) system of facilities compare with an optimally located set of 30 facilities? The optimal p-median system  @=30)  results in an average weighted  distance ( A m ) of  1.09 km compared  to  1.38 km  in  the  existing system,  the latter involving 26%  more travel distance than the  optimal  system (Table  1). Thus, A-level services are not as accessible as they could be. Figure 3 presents proximal (nearest facility) allocations for the actual system while Figure 4 illustrates the optimal p=30 system.  The shorter allocations and evenly spaced facilities

Also  peripheral  communities  travel much  longer  distances in  the  actual  system than  they  would  in  an  optimal  system.  For example, the maximum distance in the optimal system is 5.86 km but is 8.36 km in the actual system.

Next,  the possibility of providing the  same level  of  accessibility to  A-level  services with fewer facilities is considered. How many optimally located facilities would provide the same level of  accessibility? In  order  to  answer this question, the level of accessibility for different values of p (i.e., numbers of facilities) needs to be determined. Table 1 presents the results for p ranging between 1 and 30. The level of  accessibility provided  by  the  actual  system (a n average travel distance of 1.38 km) can be provided with only 23 facilities.  This suggests that it is possible to reduce the travel distance  in the actual system (improve accessibility) even with fewer  facilities.  Unquestionably,  therefore,  a higher  level of accessibility could be  obtained

for the same amount of investment as the actual system of A-level facilities.
sections.pMedian Accessibility to Higher-Level Se:
Next, the provision of higher-level services beginning with B-level  is  considered. Because it is successively  inclusive, seven of the 30 facilities in the actual system provide B-level  services.  In  order  to confomi  to  this  hierarchical structure, the optimal model must select seven facilities from the 30 providing A-level services to maximize proximity to users. The results are presented in Table 2. Hodgson (1  984) demonstrated  that  such  a  bottom-up  approach  can result  in  suboptimal  higher-order facilities. This effect is  evaluated by  selecting seven facilities  freely  from  the  open  system  of 1.50 demand points. This system, however, differs from the bottom-up  solution by less than 1% (Table 2). The optimal p=7 system would provide an AWD of 3.28 compared to 3.7.5  in the actual system. The actual B-level system is thus not as accessible  as it could be, since it involves 1. 5   % more  travel  distance than  the p-median system. In  fact, six optimally located facilities would provide an AWD of 3.6 km and involve less travel than  the actual system (Table  1).

Finally,  the  location  of  C-level  services  is considered. Only one facility, Suhum, provides C-level services. To conform with  this structure, one facility  to provide C-level services  will be  selected from  the  seven providing  B-level services. The  goal  is  to  verify  whether  it  is possible  to  improve  accessibility  to  C-level services. In  this  analysis, the  bottom-up  approach identified the same location, Suhum, as the  best  location  for  C-level  services. When one facility is  selected freely from the  150 demand points, however, only a  slight improvement  in  efficiency  (less  than  1%) could  be achieved.

title: Greenhouse horticulture and economic transition
abstract: Narpes Commune, South Ostrobothnia, is the center of the largest area of greenhouse horticulture in Finland. Its presence is an example of local adjustment to agricultural decline and increased population pressure. The empirical horticultural evidence is the basis for a theory of economic transition for depressed rural areas.

sections.A THEORY OF ECONOMIC TRANSITION:
The  successful evolution and  development  of  greenhouse  horticulture in  Narpes  illustrate  a  process  that  has  been  occurring  in Finland  and some other areas of  Europe.  Two excellent  examples  from other communes in western Finland are  fur  farming,  centered  on  Jakobstad,  and Konni  clock manufacturing,  in  Ilmajoki. Each  of these industries  represents  the  adjustment of a local area to  declining agricultural  resources and  increasing population, essentially  the same conditions that once  prevailed  in Narpes.

An inductive  theory explains  the occurrence  in rural areas of  highly specialized  industrial communities formed  by  similar small-scale enterprises, originally  with  quite  low  technological  levels  (Palomaki 1983). Thus far, empirical  results have  come  from Finland and from central Europe.  The  point  of  departure  is an older  agricultural  area,  where all available  agricultural  resources  have been used, so that  expansion  in  any traditional  way  is no  longer possible (Fig.  4).  The  economy  is so one-dimensional that  virtually  no other  ways  of livelihood exist.  Transportation is slow and  expensive.  No  possibilities  for  commuting  to  adjacent,  more developed  areas  exist because the  process  of urbanization  there  is still in an initial and  rudimentary phase.  Therefore,  livelihood  necessarily  remains centered on the local area.

The  population  is nevertheless  growing.  The birthrate  remains at a high  level,  but  because  of  improved  health care and  rising  levels  of hygiene  the death rate  is  decreasing.  The  rate  of  migration  is  low,  initially

FIG.  4-Model for  regional  agrarian change.

<!-- image -->

because of these conditions. As a result of continued subdivision of  land, farms  have become smaller  and,  especially during  famine  years,  production of food remains limited and  inadequate.  These conditions lead to a continually growing  population  pressure. Because an  expanded  labor force cannot be  used  in  agriculture, unemployment  with  unfavorable social  consequences  follows.

On the  positive  side,  these  conditions  sensitize  an  area to  accept changes  to  improve living  standards and the immediate economic situation. The diffusion of information about conditions  prevailing  outside the area  performs  a  key  function.  Knowledge  of  living  conditions elsewhere and information  about  possibilities  for  expansion  there  encourage mass  emigration, despite  the difficulties of  transportation.  Mainly  the young  and  more  venturesome  segment  of  the  population  departs. Though  effective,  this  pattern  is not the  most  advantageous  way  to relieve population pressure:  the area  loses the  part  of its  population  that is most likely  to  accept changes  and to  promote  in situ modifications.

At the same time, an information flow from outside  may  include the knowledge  of new  ways  of  production,  often with  details for  specific economic activities. A  person  with  special  skills and new ideas  may  come to the area or be aware of its  surplus  labor force and  tempted  to  exploit low  wage  levels. This  entrepreneur  initiates  production,  and if the enterprise  is  successful,  additional  workers  are  needed and  hired.  The  requisite skills must be communicated to these newcomers to the  industry.

<!-- image -->

1st  generation

2nd  generation

3rd  generation of economic  growth  and diffusion  in a local area. The X ind

Workers  are local  people,  most  likely  former farmers  and their  sons, who  are used  to  working  independently.  If the  firm continues  to be successful and the  original entrepreneur  becomes  financially  secure, the boldest and most  energetic  workers  may  demand an increased share of the returns.  One  way  to achieve this outcome is for  them to establish  new enterprises.  The new  entrepreneurs'  skills are  apt  to be limited to those proved  in the  original enterprise.  Therefore,  the new firm must be of the same  type  as the  original  one  (Fig. 5a).  If the  outgrowth  is  successful, additional firms will be started. The  consequences  are the  same, and a new  generation  of  firms  emerges.  The  process  can be  repeated many times.  Although  some  failures and other  interruptions  of  growth  will occur,  the total number of firms  steadily  increases.

The first  firm will  often  be  located  in  the  most  accessible  place, because  the  entrepreneur  has no  previous  ties to the  community  and makes a rational decision influenced  by  market forces  (Fig. 5b).  For the second-generation  firms of local  entrepreneurs,  the  deciding  locational factor  usually  is  prior ownership  of  the  land,  if  the  general  location satisfies other  preconditions  for the  activity.  Therefore,  the distribution pattern may  be scattered. Much later,  if  growth  is sufficient, the intense rivalry characterizing  these  pioneering  phases  will  ease  and be  supplanted by  cooperation  in  subcontracting, marketing,  traffic  arrangements, and  repair-shop arrangements.  The  changes happen  because the cost of these activities is  beyond  the economic resources of individual enterprises,  but  their  functioning  benefits  all  of  the  enterprises.  The entrepreneurs  will  find it  profitable  to start education and  training  in the field and to take care of roads, water  supplies,  and sewer  systems, as well  as other  components  of an economic infrastructure. Thus the benefits of  agglomeration begin  to  strengthen  the  position  of the new industrial area.

At the same time, other  changes  occur in the area. The  mobility  of people  increases  by migration,  because of better  information,  closer links to outside  areas,  and  greater  accessibility  to  transportation.  These same conditions  encourage  local  commuting  of workers to outside centers of employment. title: FEMALE ACTIVITY SPACE IN RURAL BANGLADESH
abstract: Mobility and employment opportunities of women have traditionally been restricted in rural Bangladesh. As poverty increases, women in poor families seek work to support families. This trend has resulted in expansion of female activity space, after many years of stability. This article analyzes female space in the context of purdah, the patriarchal family structure, and the spatial organization of rural settlements. It discusses ethnic and other differentials that influence female space. Governmental and nongovernmental organizations are urged to create additional employment opportunities for rural women, so as to expand further their activity space.

sections.BACKGROUND:
The extent  of  female  space  in  rural  Bangladesh  is  closely  linked  to the purdah, which is  deeply  rooted in Islamic doctrines. The word  literally  means curtain or  veil,  and  the  practice epitomizes  the  exclusion  of  women  from public  male  space  and  their  seclusion  in  the  home  compound,  which  is surrounded and shielded  by  houses,  foliage,  and  fencing  (Feldman  and McCarthy 1983,  949;  Chen  1986,  217).  Purdah is often one of several instruments of  patriarchal  family  structure that enable men to dominate women  in rural Bangladesh (Cain, Khanam, and Nahar  1979, 1).  Men  usually  exert  power and  authority  over  women,  because the  former control  property,  income, and women's  labor,  and because husbands  generally  are five to fifteen  years older than  their  wives.  Purdah and  patriarchal family  structure have  produced a  rigid  division  of labor  by gender  and a  system  of social stratification that makes women  extremely  dependent  on  husbands  and  places  them  at extreme  risk when  husbands  prove  unreliable  or withdraw  support.  The women's  apparent  insurance  against  such  potential  risks  is  children,  especially  sons,  the  birth  of  whom  confers  some  status and  autonomy  on  a young  woman  (Chen  1986, 217-218).

To understand the extent of sex-based  activity space  in rural  Bangladesh, it is  necessary  to have  knowledge  of the  spatial organization  of rural settlements.  Their  primary  unit  is  a  bari,  which  generally  consists  of  two  to six houses around a  square  or  rectangular courtyard.  The residents of a bari are in most instances divided  into households  living  in  separate  houses that are used  for  sleeping,  storage,  and  cooking.  If a household  has  cattle, there  is likely  to be a shed in the outer  courtyard  (Fig. 1).  There  may  also be a kitchen garden  accessible to the bari without  exposure  to the outside world. A household  usually  consists of a nuclear  family  and  represents  the  primary  economic unit,  being  the locus of  production  and  consumption.  All the residents of a bari are members  of  a  patrilinear family.  Most  daily  activities  of  married women  and  young  unmarried  girls  are confined  to a bari.

Women  perform  a wide  variety  of  jobs  and  activities  to  maintain  the family.  However,  the  existent  social  system  dictates that women  specialize

title: SPANISH COLONIZATION AND INDIAN PROPERTY IN CENTRAL MEXICO, 1521-1620
abstract: After the conquest of Mexico (1519-21), the Spaniards coopted Indian administrative structures, allowing the King and the new Colonial government to exploit traditional regional revenues. Key participants of the military campaigns were rewarded with rights to the tribute and limited labor conscription (encomienda) required of the indigenous population in a particular district. Legally, encomienda did not confer property rights, but holders of the privilege also received most of the earliest land grants and had the advantage of conscript labor during the planting and harvest seasons. As the encomienda system was gradually reformed and phased out, agriculture and stockraising became the major source of rural income for increasing numbers of Spanish settlers. Public land was overwhelmingly awarded to officials, the military, and the Colonial elite. Following the failure of the Puebla experiment (1531-34), designed to create a new class of farmers with small holdings, agricultural work was relegated to Indian labor. Property became the focus of competition between Spaniard and Indian, ending with partial dispossession of Indian lands by the early 1600s. The granting of lands (mercedes) is explicated by three examples: the Basin of Mexico, the district northwest of Puebla, and the Valley of Toluca. Archival documentation of land grants provides a powerful tool to decipher regional settlement histories and to examine the degree to which the Spanish legal system safeguarded Indian properly rights. Spanish agricultural expansion was made possible by the Indian demographic collapse, as a result of recurrent epidemics, and was facilitated by Indian settlement amalgamation (congregacion). While the processes and temporal patterns of property transfer show structural similarities in the heart of Central Mexico, settlement histories in peripheral areas are unique. The means by which Indian communities slowed Spanish expansion are discussed. The pattern of dispossession of the Indian was established during the first hundred years, setting in motion a process that culminated with the powerful haciendas of the nineteenth century.
