title: THE PLACE OF NARRATIVE IN THE STUDY OF THIRD-WORLD MIGRATION - THE CASE OF SPONTANEOUS RURAL MIGRATION IN SRI-LANKA
abstract: Studies of migration in geography have most often been based on quantitative research approaches. Such studies cannot adequately shed light on the contextuality of migration and the individual decision-making processes involved. Personal narratives express individual experiences within a social context. The story of ''Amma,'' a female rural migrant in Sri Lanka, shows the role of women in migration, the importance of family ties, the contextual causes of migration, and characteristics of the migration flow per se. Personal narratives have an underutilized potential of capturing the variety of migrants' experiences and the complexity of the decision to migrate.

sections.Methodological Considerations:
The last decade has seen an increasing emphasis on a people-centered  development process. Some researchers have stressed the role of researchers and development workers as listeners and learners, while those whose lives they intend  to 'develop' are increasingly recognized as  the  teachers  and  experts  (e.g.,  Chambers 1983, 1993). A first step  must  be  to  acknowledge and respect the predominantly  oral culture  of  many  poor  communities.  Slim  and

Thompson (1993, 20) claim that: 'If the voice of  poor  communities  is  to  be  heard  more often, it will have to be predominantly through oral  encounters  and  exchanges.'  People  are used to both telling and relating to stories, and therefore  the  narrative  approach  seems to be especially relevant in development geography. Stories  may  also  help  foreign  researchers  to understand  situations in an unfamiliar culture. In addition, the narrative has considerable potential  for  giving  the  underprivileged  a  voice to be heard. Bringing together what people say and  think  in  the  form  of  personal  narratives, and then communicating those narratives, is a way of correcting a bias that runs through the whole development debate (Slim and Thompson 1993). Langness and Frank (1  98 1, 138) put it this way:  'Ordinary people can  be seen as the small heroes they often are and may be  taken  as  the  teachers  they  can  be.'  The narrative  also provides a  dynamic view  of  the migration  process. Few other methods  (quantitative  or  qualitative)  are  able  to  convey the experience of the dynamics of stepwise migration as well as narratives. Most migration studies have  been based  on  questionnaire surveys, and  the  fact  that  Amma  decided  to  migrate might  have  been  missed  through  an  ordinary survey.  The  first  time  I  interviewed  Amma about  the  migration  she  said  that  she  came with  Gamini  when  he  left home  (women are supposed  to  be  subservient to  men).  During one of our last conversations she revealed that it  was  her  decision  to  migrate  and  that  she brought  Gamini with  her  because he was  her youngest child. This illustrates the importance of  establishing a  collaborative relationship  or friendship with the informants in order to get them to tell their stories (Oakley 1981).

In the case of development studies, the narrative is often the product  of  a complex series of interactions between the researcher and the interpreter  and  between  these  two  and  the people interviewed. There must be a sense of equality  in  the  relationship  and  both  voices (informant's and  researcher's) must  be  heard (Smith 1993). To establish a  sense of  equality is  difficult when  research  is  carried  out  by  a 'rich' white  European  among poor  Sinhalese peasants.  But  despite  the  age,  class,  and  cultural disparities, I think both Amma  and I felt a  sense  of  equality  based  on  gender  and  on telling  each  other  about  ourselves.  Our  rela-

tionship was essentially a practical one that we both enjoyed. Amma participated in the interviews because she was curious about me. Eventually our relationship became more social, and my position to Amma  changed from that of a stranger to a  kind  of  member. She said  I was like a  daughter to her.  Despite  this,  our  relationship  was  inevitably  unequal.  The  advantages and disadvantages of the researcher being in  either  an  outsider  or  insider  position  in relation to the informant are discussed by various authors. Miles and Crush (1993) assert that if we  treat the narrative as  an interactive text, then  the  question  of  whether  outsider  or insider status produces better  or more  accurate results is  of  secondary importance. They further  argue  that  the  ideal  intimate  nonhierarchical  relationship  based on  simply  gender similarity  between  researcher  and  informant may be  more difficult to attain for the insider. Stubbs (1984) claims  that a  close similarity in social situation may lead to less inhibition but increased social conformity. According to my own experience  most  people,  especially  the women,  were  very  open  to  an  outsider.  Because of this I think that I managed to establish a  collaborative relationship  with  my  informants. My interpreter played  a  decisive role  in establishing this  relationship.  She  was  a  university graduate, but she was also from a poor peasant family herself and she was remarkably sociable.  An objection especially related to the use  of narrative in development studies is the language problem. When the narrative is  constructed  via an interpreter there is a real danger of distorted reality or loosing nuances during  the  translation  from  one  language to the  other.  However,  these  problems  are  not specific for narratives; they also apply to questionnaire interviews.

One  often  expects  to  obtain  an  increased quantity and quality of data when the relationship between the informant and researcher becomes  more  established. However,  the  more formal  relationship  at  the  beginning  of  the research process may also have its advantages. At  this  point  the  informant  expects  the  researcher to have little or no knowledge about the subject under discussion; consequently the informant  may  give  more  patient  and  clearer answers and explanations to the questions. It is also important to select informants carefully in order to utilize the full potential of the narra- tive method. This means not only a cross section of the community but also various personality types. There is a  danger of  interviewing only  the  more  confident  and  articulate  persons, who may well represent a distinct group in the local community. Such persons are usually  more  accustomed to  presenting  a public image  and  may  therefore  be  less  sincere  on personal recall. Amma is the main character in this narrative. Although she is relatively talkative, she does not represent the outwardly oriented articulate group of the local community. She  is  an  elderly woman  and  women  in  Sri Lanka do not traditionally express  their views in public; the man generally talks on behalf of the family.

I did  not  explicitly use  a  narrative approach when  collecting  the  data.  The  information about Amma's migration was  collected via  an interpreter  through  in-depth  interviews  and several  informal  conversations  with  her  and other  members  of  her  family (we  visited  her home village and  her  eldest son  also).  However, many of the things she told us were formulated as  short stories. We heard  only segments  of  her  migration  history each  time we met, although more rich in detail and personal aspects  over  time.  Sometimes  we  met  her alone, at other  times Gamini  or other  family members were present. I had chosen not to use a tape recorder because I feared it might make people  uncomfortable  and  thus  restrict  their willingness  to  talk.  Sometimes  I  took  notes during the interview, at other times I wrote it down after we  had  left her  house. The main purpose of the in-depth  interviews was  to record her migration history and how her migration  had  occurred. T o  write a  narrative based on field notes and the in-depth interviews and conversations I had with Amma  seemed to be a  suitable  way  of  presenting  the  data.  This provided an opportunity to present a full case story instead of spreading the data out as short quotations in a research report. Further, I find narratives more  readable than  interview transcripts. When editing the  story the  segments were  grouped  by  topic  and  sequenced  in  a loose chronological order. The chronology is loose because neither Amma nor Gamini could remember  the exact time things took place. A few  stories  not  central  to  the  theme  of  the narrative  were  left  out  (e.g.,  about  Gamini's marriage).

Working  with  narratives  raises  questions about  the  authorship:  Whose  story  is  told? Whose  voice  is  heard?  (Personal  Narratives Group 1989). The interviewer's  influence does not  cease with  the  end  of  the  interview; she also interprets, edits, and writes the narrative. Although Amma's story was told as a dialogue between us, the narrative is  my interpretation of  that story. Thus the  story  told  here  is  my narration  of  Amma's  story, or my  experience of her migration  experience as she conveyed it to  me.  I  have  tried  to  convey  her  migration history  as  told  by  her,  not  in  detail  but  in content. As such, the narrative does not represent Amma's direct voice; this is contained in my narrative. Preferably she should have been actively taking  part  in  the  production  of  the text  (cf.  Mbilinyi  1989). However, it was  not possible for me to involve Amma in the writing of  the narrative  since this  was  done after  the fieldwork  was  completed.  In  1993  I  got  the opportunity to see Amma again. The narrative was  read  to her  and  since  it made  sense and was  understandable  to her  I think  it provides an  adequate  interpretation  of  her  migration. The  story  about  Amma  is  depicted  as  one comprehensive story with a beginning, a middle, and  an  end. Her 'real' story  is certainly not  so  streamlined.  All  assessments,  doubts, and  coincidences are not  easily  conveyed, although  I have  tried  to focus on those I heard about.  Her migration  story is necessarily not finished even though it may appear so. Migration  is  part  of  life, and she might  move  again.

Despite the problems related to narratives, I want to argue that there is an unused potential for  narrative  research  in  migration  studies. The narrative  presented  here  is  a  short  and simple one, but I think it illustrates the advantages of narratives in revealing the contextuality  and  complexity  of  migration.  In  my  research project  the narrative  approach is combined with  a more  traditional  household  survey  approach. The narrative  functions mainly as  an  illustration  or  detailed  description  of  a migrant's reason for migrating.  The information  gathered through in-depth interviews has also increased my knowledge about the migration process and thus my ability to analyze the quantitative data. I think there is also a  scope for migration studies based  entirely on a  narrative  approach,  but  then  the narratives must be more detailed than the one I have been able to provide in this  short  article. The narrative approach can provide a new way  of looking at migration  through  the  eyes  of  the  migrants. Generalization  based  on  narrative  is  difficult, but if personal narratives are grouped together carefully they can  provide a variety of  experiences around  a  theme that  can overcome the unrepresentativeness  of any  one  individual story (Bartholomew 1991).
sections.Narrative and Migration Research:
~

As  mentioned  above,  a  commonality for  the traditional  approaches to  the  study of  migration is that they are mainly based on quantitative  methods  of  data  collection and  analysis. The quantitative studies are valuable for giving us  information  about  the  magnitude  and  the spatial patterns  of  migration  streams and migration  selectivity by  age,  sex,  marital  status, education,  and  occupation.  Such studies also attempt  to  explain  the  socioeconomic causes and consequences of  migration. They may be capable of  doing this on the macro level,  i.e., by  describing  the  sort  of  societies  that  are ejecting or attracting certain types of migrants. But  these  kinds  of  study  cannot  adequately shed light on the  complexity of  the  causes  of migration  and the  individual decision-making processes  involved.  Daniels  (1985)  points  to 'the  incapacity  of standard  statistical  techniques  to  describe the  fluency of  human  life . .  .' (p.  148). Consequently,  there  is  also  a need for studies of the circumstances in a particular place that  make  a  particular individual migrate. The individuals and  their  time-  and place-specific lives  disappear  in  the  statistics. Narratives give the numbers a human face. We can  never specify the  exact set of  factors that influence the individual in his or her decision to  migrate;  we  can  only set  forth  a  few  that seem  to  be  of  special  importance.  This  has especially been the case with quantitative studies. However, if we  let people tell their stories of migration  it  may  be  possible  to  capture more of the factors involved and thus to reveal a more complete picture.

A narrative is  a  sequence of  events told  in words, and the events are ordered chronologi-

cally. The dominant form of narrative in Western culture has been  the novel, but the novel is only one of  a number of narrative possibilities. According to Scholes and Kellogg (1968), a  narrative  is  distinguished  by  two  characteristics: the presence  of  a story and  a  storyteller. Further,  Scholes (1981) claims that  any set of  events that can be sequenced and related can also be  narrated.  Consequently, narrative is also a  relevant method  in scientific writing. Often in  scientific writing,  a simple narrative in  the  form  of  a  quotation  is  used  to supplement more quantitative data. Narrative is both phenomenon  and  method.  It  is  a  reasonably well-established practice to call the phenomenon 'story' and the inquiry or method 'narrative.'  People  by  nature  lead storied  lives  and tell  stories  of  those  lives,  whereas  narrative researchers collect and tell stories of such lives, and  write  narratives  of  experience (Connelly and Clandinin  1990).

Feminist  research has emphasized narrative as an alternative form of producing knowledge in academia (e.g., Gluck and Patai  1991).  The Personal Narratives Group (1989,4) maintains that:  'Since  feminist  theory  is  grounded  in women's lives and aims to analyze the role and meaning of gender in those lives and in society, women's personal narratives are essential primary documents  for feminist research. These narratives present  and  interpret  women's life experiences.' It has also been argued by some that  narrative  is  particularly  appropriate  for capturing  women's  knowledge  and  forms  of expression  (see  Belenky  et  al.  1986). Several authors  argue  that  story is  central  to the  organization of  knowledge and is  a  natural  and common way  of  thinking  for  human  beings (e.g.,  Mitchell 1981;  Sarbin 1986;  Polkinghorne  1988; Carter  1993). In creating stories, people are able to impose order and coherence on the  stream  of  experience and to work out the meaning of incidents and events in the real world.  Stories are  a  means of  interpreting  or reinterpreting events by  constructing  a causal pattern that integrates what is known about an event,  as  well  as  that  which  is  uncertain  but relevant  to  interpretation.  Stories  are  always subject  to  reformulation  in  the  face  of  new stories. Further, what we  tell and how we  tell it is a revelation of what we believe, and therefore a story is also a theory of something (Carter  1993). A story  is  a  construction  and  is  as much  about  social  perception  as  it  is  about reality. As told, it can be assumed to lie somewhere  between actual behavior and  social expectations, with possible added  distortions over time through subsequently changing values  and  norms  that  may alter  perception. To tell one's story is not only to talk and remember, but to reconstruct the meaning of the past from the viewpoint of  the present  and  also to give  meaning  to  the  past  in  a  way  that  has meaning  for  the  present (Stubbs 1984). Further, Stubbs claims that the subjectivity  or bias in a  life story  (what  the  informant chooses to remember and to tell or not tell, or what she believes and why)  can  be  as  significant as  the facts elicited.

There  are  certain  limitations  of narrative that need to be considered. First, narrative may give the illusion of presenting a complete story with  a  beginning, middle, and end, while real life  is  unstructured and  continues  after  the story is told. Thus  the narrative's representation  of  reality may be questioned. White (1973) raised the issue of  whether  a  narrative might  be  best understood  as the  construction of a  story about reality rather  than  as a direct representation  of  it. He claims that narratives can best be understood as a literary reconstruction of the reality that includes the ideological perspective of the author. Thus narratives have a moralizing value. 'It is only by virtue of what it teaches about moral wisdom, or rather about the irreducible moralism of  a life lived  under the  conditions  of  culture  rather  than  nature, that narrative can claim cognitive authority  at all' (White 1981a, 253). Mink (1981) opposes this  view  and  says  that  narratives  might  be presented  as  moral  tales,  but  most  are  not. This controversy is probably based  mostly on different  definitions  of  'moral.'  Most  narratives have  an explicit or implicit message. Storytellers have  their  own  strategies when  they tell  their  stories,  and  the  perspective  of  the researcher is present in the narrative. The results of narrative research cannot claim to correspond  exactly  with  whxt  has  actually  occurred,  ie., they  are  not  'true'  if  'truth' is taken to mean exact correspondence to reality.

The aim of narrative research is verisimilitude,  or  results  that  have  the  appearance  of reality  (Polkinghorne 1988).  White  (1981b) distinguishes  between  life  and  narrative;  he says that in narrative reality wears the mask of

a  meaning  that  we  can  only imagine but  not experience. According to Polkinghorne (1  988), White uses  the written  text  as  his  model  of narrative, and  in contrast to the written  story where all threads are tied up, life as lived seems confused and unstructured.  In contrast, Polkinghorne (1988,68) maintains that 'experience forms and presents itself in awareness as narrative.'  We  find  meaning  and  identity  as  a result  of  the  stories  we  tell  about  ourselves. Narrative  provides neither  an  'accurate' nor LLina~~~rate' description of preexisting real experience,  but  rather  helps  to  give  experience form. Therefore, a narrative approach to selfunderstanding is not a distortion of  reality but a  confirmation  of  it.  However,  the  narrative structuring of  experience is different from the narrative structuring of a written text. In a text all  the  'noise'  is  cut  and  only  those  events necessary to move  the  plot  along are related. A similar selection occurs in experience through the human capacity for attention, but the self is in the middle of its story and has to revise the plot constantly without knowing the end  of  the  story.  Despite  these  differences, there is  a  continuity between life as  lived  and the formation of  a written narrative (Polkinghorne  1988).

Narratives may also be criticized for emphasizing the individual at the cost of  social context.  However, the  power of  narrative is precisely its capacity to express life experiences in meaningful ways.  Further,  language in  narrative,  compared  to  other  scientific writing,  is less  abstracted from the  meaning of everyday life  because  it  is  mostly  conversational. The narrative is  constructed by  the researcher and the informant, and it functions as an argument in which we  learn something essential by understanding a life as lived. Geertz (1988) claims that the reader's acceptance of the text occurs not  because  of  its  factual weight  but  rather because of  its narrative strength,  i.e.,  by  convincing the  reader  that  the  author  was  really there.

Another objection to narrative is that it may give  an  illusion  of causality  because  of  the chronological order of events. However, there is  also  the  opposite  problem,  which  Sayer (1989) draws attention to: a tendency to underspecify causality in the  processes described in narratives. This is  partly  because narrative  is not  primarily  concerned  with  explaining the nature  and  implications  of  social  structures, and partly  because  the difference  between mere temporal succession and causality may be difficult to see. According to Sayer (1989), narratives  also  have  a  tendency  to  neglect  synchronic  relations  at  the  expense  of  temporal successions, because given the linearity of narrative,  it is  inevitably more  difficult to represent the  synchronic dimension than  the  temporal.  However,  Sayer  adds  that  these  criticisms  of  narrative  are  not  intended  to  imply that explanations of concrete situations through  conventional  analysis  are  necessarily better. Sayer (1989) argues for the realist concrete  study, which is  an  attempt to construct theoretically informed narratives that give appropriate  weight  to  the  synchronic  and  the temporal dimensions. However, he admits that this is  more easily said than done.

Despite  the  critique,  I think  the  narrative method  is  relevant  and  useful  in  migration studies and in development geography in general. According to McDowell (1992), we have reached a self-reflexive moment in human geography, influenced by  feminism, the  literary turn in ethnography, and postmodernism. Feminist geographers argue for a human geography that  is  based  on the  recognition  of  diversity, for theories rooted  in personal experience, and for a greater tolerance of difference. Narratives could  be  central in such a  geography,  since  narrative  techniques,  according to Miles and Crush (1993), have considerable potential  for  recovering hidden  stories, contesting academic androcentrism and eurocentrism, and reinstating the marginalized as makers of their own past; i.e., giving them a voice to be heard.  How people  understand  and  relate  to the opportunities and constraints they are facing are essential factors for the understanding of migration. Thus, in migration studies, people's stories are important. Narrative is a useful method  for  understanding cases  because  it seeks people's own formulations of  their  situation and how people come to make the decisions they make.  Elbaz (1993) claims that narratives are  needed  to explain connections between thought and action. The narrative unites thought  and  action in  an  intuitive and  direct way;  it  conveys how  humans  experience the world. Narratives can illuminate both the logic of individual action and the effects of structural constraints  within  which  life  courses  evolve.

Narrative  is  held  to  combine  things  that  are determined  by  general  laws  with  things  that are contingent,  producing  a plausible, because followable, story (Abbott 1992).

Further, narrative  includes  the  time and place  aspects to a greater  extent than  do data based  on questionnaire  interviews. By  using a questionnaire we  will most often get brief answers to the questions we pose, while through the narrative method  we  will  get the  informant's own  story, which relates the phenomena to  time  and  place.  Connelly  and  Clandinin (1990, 8) claim that 'Time and place .  .  . work together  to  create  the  experiential quality  of narrative.'  Place  is  where  the  events  occur, where  individuals  live  out  their  stories,  and where  socioeconomic  and  cultural  contexts play constraining  and  enabling roles.  Place is not  always  evident in  a  narrative,  but  a  good narrative should make clear from where people are speaking because place is central for understanding  action  and  thought.  According  to Connelly and Clandinin (1990), it may be that place is the more difficult  construction for narrative  researchers.  The  reason  for  this,  they argue, is that the necessary field notes for constructing the place are often lacking, due to the fact  that  during  data  collection  one  tends  to concentrate  on people rather than things. Geographers should  have an advantage  here, since  we  have  a  tradition  of  including  place characteristics in our  work.  Brown  (1991) stresses the need  for a  research approach that is  more  idiographic  than conventional  approaches to  migration  studies-both in  sense of  place  and  individual  level.  This  is  where narratives  may  contribute.  Narrative  is  one relevant way  of  trying  to grasp  the  combination  of  structural and individual causes of  migration,  i.e.,  the  ground  level  context within which  migration takes  place.  According  to Sayer (1989), narrative has the ability to capture and communicate processes and change in concrete  situations.  Narrative  explanation  is primarily  contextual,  not  causal;  it  explicates meaning through context. The personal narrative  conveys  how  the  individual  copes  with society, and also how society influences a person's life. Narrative explanations  are retrospective; they draw together events into an account that  makes the ending reasonable and believable. According to Polkinghorne  (1988,  171), they  'are genuinely  explanatory, for they  can answer  the  question  of  why  something  happened.' Further, the reasons a person gives for doing something are acknowledged as the impetus for the action.  The  insights  gained through  narratives may pose new avenues for inquiry,  as  well  as  inform  on  the  analysis  of quantitative data.

Narratives do not replace surveys in migration  research,  but  combining  these  methods will  increase the understanding  of  the migration  process  under  study.  Miles  and  Crush (1993)  emphasize  that  the  collection  of  migrants' stories will  increase the  sophistication of  the analysis and  also increase the  explanatory value of more quantitative data. Although surveys give room for exploring the motives of migration,  narratives make it possible to look at actual decisions and actions and to perceive behind  these  practices  the  network  of  social relations that allowed them to take place (Bertaux-Wiame  1982). By  linking individual stories into a group biography (e.g., collecting the stories of people migrating from the same village), one gains further insight into the social structures  underlying  the  migration  process. The  social  networks  change  over  time  and most  often  they  are not  formally established, i.e.,  they do not leave any trace behind  them. Hence the relevance of  the narrative method. The methods employed in migration research will  largely  be  determined  by  the  research questions addressed. I think  the  narrative  approach  is  especially  relevant  when  studying topics  such  as  the  meaning  of  migration  to migrants, gender relations of migration, social networks  (narratives  may  disentangle  men's and women's individual motivations and aspirations within a family context), the motivation and  multiple  reasons  for  migrating,  and  migrants' sense of  place. Further, a narrative approach  can  increase  the  researcher's  knowledge and understanding  of  the  places of  outand  in-migration.  The narrative  approach  allows one to take a new  look at old questions, to open new fields for inquiry, and to explore new  approaches  (e.g.,  an  ethnographic approach to the study of migration) (Bertaux and Kohli  1984).

title: The Rise and Fall of a Timber Baron: Political Forests and Unruly Coalitions in the Carpathian Mountains of Romania
abstract: Concerns over deforestation are growing along with the climate crisis. This is particularly unsettling in relation to the rise of populist authoritarian regimes. In this article I reveal the connections between forests, neoliberalism, authoritarianism, and cronyism, through an in-depth ethnographic study of the Romanian Carpathian forests after the fall of socialism in 1989. The study examines the intricate entanglements between forest extraction, party politics, and informal territorial governance that emerged over the last thirty years. It argues that unruly coalitions shaped forest history. It focuses on the central figure of the timber baron, who ran businesses in connection with state office politics and maintained provincial authoritarian control over resources by tapping into paternalist dependencies of rural mountain dwellers. The article uses the analytic tools of political ecology and the conceptual framework developed by studies on resource frontiers and political forests combined with the anthropology of postsocialism. I draw on field research from 2004 to 2016, in which I collected data through systematic fieldwork, interviews, and surveys, complemented with official reports and media coverage. The article uses a narrative ethnographic writing approach.

title: Challenges to family farming in China
abstract: China's agricultural sector requires reforms to assure farmers and consumers of fair prices while protecting the environment and permitting sustainable growth in the coming years. The affluent eastern province of Jiangsu is an appropriate site in which to explore the effects of agricultural reforms on rural households and, in turn, the effects of these households on the environment. We compare two surveys (1987 and 1996), of too households each, of farmers in Huaiyin and Huai'an Counties, Jiangsu Province. Indicated are chronically low economic returns on grain, moderate returns for livestock, and the highest returns for vegetables. Unfortunately, the production of livestock and vegetables requires more farm chemicals, inorganic fertilizers, and placement of field plastic-all of which are associated with greater environmental problems.
picked: PREDICTING  FARM INCOME FROM CROP SALES

sections.HOUSEHOLD SURVEYS IN JIANGSU PROVINCE:
We selected  northern  Jiangsu  Province  for our case  study  for a variety  of reasons. First,  the province  was one of the earliest  to introduce  rural  reforms  in the early 1980s. During  our  first  survey, in  1987, the  entire  province  had  been  operating  under reform  policies for at  least  four  years.

Jiangsu  is a highly productive  agricultural province  with rich endowments  of prime,  well-watered  alluvial  land.  After  decades  of water-management projects  on the  Huai  River  and  Hongze  Lake, flooding  is  much  less  often  a  problem  than  it  was  in the  past,  and  canal  systems  (equally important  for  irrigation and  for  transportation) are  excellent  throughout  most of the province.  Except  for  minor  local issues  of soil quality  and  drainage,  environmental  conditions  seldom  affect  crop-selection  decisions.

At the same  time, elevated  yields  associated  with high-quality  land  throughout the region  mean  that  capital  is  usually  available for  farm  chemicals, field  plastic,  and other modern inputs. These products,  in conjunction  with inorganic fertilizers, have  made  possible  rapid  increases in output  during  the  past  two  decades. They  also bring  environmental  problems,  the  most  significant  of  which  is  pollution  from  field runoff. Residual pesticide on produce and the growing volume of plastic film plowed into the soil are  other  concerns  that  our respondents  cited  frequently.

Another factor  that makes  Jiangsu  an excellent  location for research  is the increasingly  significant  commercial  bond  between  the  advanced southern  third  of the province  (Sunan)  and  the  poorer  northern  portion  (Subei),  an  important  and  welldeveloped aspect of what is representative of China's  emerging  "new"  integrated farm  economy.  Long-distance  commercial  relationships  in agriculture are  becoming more and more common throughout  China.  They  diversify  the rural  economy and  thus  improve  the  quality  of  life  for  farmers  in  prosperous areas. This  geographical aspect-larger markets  for  a more  diverse  group  of products  that  can  be sold at increasingly  distant  places-is  often overlooked  by  studies  outside  geography. The reduction in the "time-space continuum'"  brought about by significantly  better transportation  systems  and  capital  from  distant  markets, is  crucial  to  the  farmers in

our sample.  Admittedly,  the commercialization that  has  played  such  a  major  role  in Jiangsu's success  remains  a  distant  goal  for  farmers  in the  interior  provinces.  Farmers  in  less-advanced  areas  have  seen  onlyvery  limited  improvements in  the  quality  of their  lives  since the early  1980S  (Lin,  Cai,  and  Li  1996,  219-220).

Jiangsu,  however,  is a vanguard  province,  and what has happened there  will spread  to other  places.  Although  not ranked  first  in  any  single  measure  of  economic activity-total value  of exports  or  gross  value  of industrial  output,  for  example-Jiangsu is often considered China's  "richest" province thanks to sustained strong performance  in numerous  economic  areas (Cartier 1995;  JTN 1995). Differences between the Jiangsu  counties north and south of the Yangtze River  are  significant  in our study because they have led to distinct development  strategies  and histories, creating  what may easily  be thought of as the province's  "core" and "periphery."
sections.SOUTHERN JIANGSU:
For  much  of China's history  southern  Jiangsu, or  Sunan, has  been  an  important  agricultural  region (Eberhard 1977).  At one time it constituted  a  significant  portion of the historic Chinese granary,  Jiangnan,  which also included the fertile plains of northern  Zhejiang  Province  and  extended  south  to  Hangzhou.  The  agricultural surplus generated  by Sunan's  farmers  earned  the southern  third  of Jiangsu  the name "Land  of Fish  and Rice"  (Zhou 1992).  The name underscores  the renowned  longterm stability  of southern  Jiangsu,  an agricultural production  that  has  long distinguished it from the poorer, northern portions of the province (Li  R.  X. 1996,13-15).

Southern Jiangsu has changed radically  since reforms were instituted, and township-village  light industrial  manufacturing  now accounts  for the bulk of the region's output  value (Fan 1995;  Marton 1995). The path to prosperity is paved with proceeds from the production of myriad  items, including  computer  components (CD-ROMs and hard  drives),  electric  fans,  bicycles,  automobiles,  refrigerators, and washing machines. Remarkably, the people of the land of rice  and fish must now import food, as their standard  of living  has skyrocketed  on the strength  of the industrial and commercial sectors and as their numbers  have risen in accord  with stepped-up demands for labor. Foodstuffs for Sunan are increasingly  imported from the northern two-thirds of the province  or from  beyond its borders.

Sunan's  growth  has  had  a  cascading  effect  on the  household  economy  of the Subei  farmers  in  our  sample.  Since  the  early  1980S,  rapid  growth  in  purchasing power  of Sunan  consumers  has  spurred  the  agricultural transformation of  the  poorer  north.
sections.NORTHERN JIANGSU:
The northern two-thirds of the province,  or Subei,  which includes Huaiyin and Huai'an  Counties,  was historically  plagued  by natural  disasters  and renowned  for great poverty  (Cheng  and Lu 1984;  Rozelle and Jiang 1995, 60-63).  Although  it lags behind Sunan in economic development,  Subei  has made great  strides  since 1949, particularly since  1985, when  provincial  leaders began  to  invest  in  transportation and infrastructure  (FBIS  1982, 81-86).

The investments in Subei infrastructure  reflect not provincial  largess  but a changed  role of the north in long-term  provincial  interests.  As Sunan  has  increasingly  committed  effort  and  resources to industrial  production,  losses  of arable  land and a  shift  of comparative  advantage to nonfarm  activities  have  resulted in the  stagnation of grain  production  since the late 1980s. Provincial  shortfalls  vis-a-vis nationally generated production "targets"  cause tensions between the provincial government  and  Beijing.  Jiangsu's  olution  has  been  to shift  tax  revenues  from  rural industries  located throughout  the province  to finance  improvements  in railroads, roads,  irrigation  systems,  and grain-handling  and -storage  facilities  in Subei,  thus aiding  production  in the north.
sections.PREDICTING FARM INCOME FROM CROP SALES:
In  1996,  mean  grain  sales  accounted  for  just  over  36.2  percent  of  the  value  of off-farm sales  of  agricultural products  by  the  households  in  our  sample.  The  proportions  varied widely,  from  less  than  1  percent  of household  income  to almost  82 percent.  Our preliminary  analyses  found no correlation  between  the  value  of grain  sales  and  the gross  value  of agricultural sales  by  household.  That  is,  for  most households  selling grain  was  unimportant  in  determining  the  total  value  of off-farm  sales,  a  conclusion supported  by interviews  with farmers  and consistent  with the results  presented  in Table  II.  Other  household characteristics may  predict  farm  sales  more effectively.

Toward  this end,  we evaluated  five  independent  variables  that  we hypothesized would affect  the annual  value  of off-farm  sales  (our dependent  variable)  for 82 of our original  sample  of loo households (the remaining  18  households reported  no off-farm  sales): LANDAREA,  the area of contracted land per household;  MEANDIST, the mean  distance  from  home to the  fields  contracted  by  the  household;  ECONAREA, the  amount  of  land  sown  to  economic  (nongrain)  crops;  ANIMALSAL, a  dummyvariable  reflecting  off-farm  sales  of  livestock  or  fowl  amounting  to more  than  loo yuan; and FAMSIZE, the number  of people  in the  household  (Table  III).  Of  these  variables, we hypothesized,  LANDAREA,  ECONAREA, and ANIMALSAL would positively affect the gross  value  of sales,  because  greater amounts  of contracted land  and  more  land  sown to more  profitable economic  crops  should  boost  the  total  value.  The  sale  of  livestock also represents  some measure  of value added  from  on-farm  processing,  which  we believed  should also  boost the  gross  value  of sales.  On  the  other  hand,  we  hypothesized that MEANDIST and FAMSIZE would negatively  affect sales,  because distant

Finally,  we assumed that large  families  need more grain,  reducing  the amount of arable  land that  can  be committed  to other  ventures  and,  as  a  consequence,  deducting  from  the value of sales.

We divided the households  by county to determine  whether  results  would vary by location. They do, significantly: The model for Huai'an  achieved  a much better level  of explanatory  power  (adjusted  R2 =  0.71)  than  did  that  for  Huaiyin  (adjusted R = 0.38). For  the  five  independent  variables, across  the  two  locations,  only  one  variable,  ECONAREA, was significant  in both places  (even at p = .11, when the signs reverse).  Still,  two of five  hypothesized  variables are  significant  for  Huaiyin  (at .05 or better),  and three  of five  are  significant  for  Huai'an  (at .05  or better).

In  sum,  the  models  are  significant  and  stable,  although  the  explanatory power  of the Huaiyin  model is limited.  What  is most clear  is  that  although  these  two  counties are  adjacent,  Huaiyin  and  Huai'an  are  different  places-and that  their  farm  households  have  adopted  very  different  strategies for  generating income from  agriculture. The following scenario  emerges.

For  the Huaiyin sample,  the highest reported  sales  of off-farm  products  come from  households  that  grow  grain  but  use  their  surplus  for  feeder  operations  at  home

and  sell  no grain  to  the  state. This  is  the  way  to  live  in  a  rice-growing district  and  still make  some money:  One grows  grain  as  required, but one does  not sell  it-one  converts it to pork.  A further  measure  of Huaiyin's focus on livestock  is that the area sown to economic crops is actually  a drag  on maximum  sales  per household (the coefficient  for  ECONAREA in Huaiyin  is  negative). With  prices  for  quality  feed  at  levels  at  or  above  mean  prices  for  rice  and  wheat,  farmers gain  the  most  by  raising  livestock  and  feeding  them  surplus  grain,  even  though  rice  and  wheat-the  major  grains of these farms-are  extremely  inefficient  feedstuffs.  This is reasonable  from the household's  perspective  but a poor use of resources.

The results  for Huai'an  are  markedly  different,  for farmers  there  are  utilizing increasingly  unique income-generating  strategies;  and whereas  Huaiyin  farmers concentrate  on livestock,  those  in Huai'an  concentrate  on vegetables.  Huai'an  specializes  in selling  vegetables  to cities,  and the sale of livestock  is not a significant contributor  to the  gross  value  of sales.  Significant relationships  for  Huai'an  include total  crop  area,  area  sown in economic crops  (p = .11), distance  to fields,  and  size  of the household. The larger  area  sown to nongrain  crops  translates  to a  higher  gross value for  vegetables  sold by Huai'an  farmers.  Greater  sales  mean  higher  incomes.

Commercialization  of agriculture  has helped farmers  in Subei,  but their incomes lag when compared  with those of factory  workers  (Su and  Veeck  1995).  Reported  per  capita  incomes,  adjusted for  inflation,  for  the  Huaiyin  households  in the survey  rose  only  34 percent,  from  u.s.$187.oo  in  1987 to  U.S.$251.00 in  1996. In Huai'an,  beyond  the reach  of legislation  that  makes  grain  growing  mandatory, the increase  was  also  34  percent, but  the  mean  absolute  per  capita  income  was  25  percent greater there than in Huaiyin, because per capita income increased from u.s.$235.00 to U.S.$314.52.  This compares with an urban per capita income  in Jiangsu in 1987  of u.s.$350.OO,  which  increased to u.s.$625.54 in 1996 (ZTN  1988, 199;  1997,  300).

title: Digital technology and post-rural: rural restructuring in guangzhou, china
abstract: Globalization and digital technology have restructured rural spaces in China, engendering intricate rural dynamics. Based on the urban-rural continuum theory and adopting the post-rural perspective, this paper conducts empirical research in Conghua, Guangzhou, to analyze the multidimensional mechanisms through which digital technology reconstructs rural space. The findings reveal that in urban-rural fringe, digital technology serves as a catalyst for the transition of conventional agriculture toward refined, digitalized, and multifaceted management approach. Consequently, the trajectory of rural development is transitioning from a simplistic, productivist model toward a complex paradigm emphasizing postproductivist considerations. Top-down policy directives integrate the digital framework into rural spaces, while local actors facilitate rural production and reproduction through spontaneous and informal digital practices in their daily lives, constituting a consultative neoendogenous rural development. This paper integrates digital technology into the desakota model, underscoring the interplay among globalization, networking, and locality. It enriches the understanding of rurality in the digital epoch, and proposes a novel spatial paradigm that encompasses the dimensions of production-consumption, tradition-modernity, and the coexistence of multiple subjects and meanings. It offers a new theoretical perspective for comprehending the integrated development of urban and rural areas, and carries practical implications for rural vitalization.

title: LANDSCAPES OF CULTIVATION IN MESOAMERICA ON THE EVE OF THE CONQUEST
abstract: Pre-Columbian Amerindian agriculturalists developed technologies and management practices with which to crop a wide range of ecological conditions, giving rise to a multiplicity of cultivated landscapes. This variety was particularly evident in Mesoamerica, where agricultural practices ranged from swiddening to multicropped, hydraulically transformed wetlands. Here we explore these indigenous cultivated landscapes as they existed about the time of the Columbian Encounter. We illustrate them through the examination of three transects approximating the courses of the initial Spanish entradas through this diverse region: the first extends from the Gulf coast to central Mexico; the second traverses the Yucatan peninsula from north to south; and the third climbs into highland Guatemala from the Pacific coastal plain. Second, we broadly sketch the major changes that took place in these landscapes during the first phase of Spanish domination and some of the forces that shaped these changes. Three processes were especially significant: the Amerindian depopulation, the introduction of exotic biota and technologies, and the reordering of land and the rural economy. Ultimately, however, reconfigured hybrid landscapes resulted that reflected the union of cultures. Last, we argue that the scale of environmental transformation of Amerindian agriculture has not always been fully appreciated, the scale of environmental degradation associated with Spanish introductions has been overstated at times, and the contrasting ideologies of nature between the two cultures has been over-simplified.

sections.The Cortes Transect:
Cortes and his small band probably first saw the snowcapped summit of Orizaba (5,639 m) from ship's  deck in the vicinity of modern Veracruz, Mexico.  From that vantage point, they were observing the eastern flanks of the Aztec empire, a domain that stretched east-west  from the  Gulf  of  Mexico to the Pacific Ocean and north-south from the  Bajio to the  Isthmus of Tehuantepec (Figs. 1, 2). More properly identified with the 'Triple Alliance' of the city states of  Tenochtitlhn,  Texcoco,  and  Tacuba  in the Basin of Mexico (Gibson 1964, 17), the empire has taken its popular name from the dominant Mexica (Tenochtitlhn)  and their mythical homeland, Aztlan. The Alliance commanded a political and  economic realm unparalleled in Mesoamerican  history,  complete  with  a  supreme  ruler,  professional  armies  and  merchants, and a system of taxation and marketing that siphoned the wealth of the empire into its lacustrine heart. Population estimates for Central  Mexico,  roughly  corresponding with  the empire,  range  from <I0 million->50 million (Denevan 1976, 77-84;  1992).

This  transect  parallels the Cortes route and crosses virtually every major climatic and agroecological zone in Mesoamerica: the hot and  humid  tierra  caliente  of  the  Gulf  Coast Plains, the tierra templada (temperate land) of the  coastal  piedmont  and  the  basins  on  the altiplano or  Mesa  Central,  and  the  upper reaches of the sierras that separate the basins from  one  another  (Figs. 2, 3). Each  of  these broad realms,  with the exception of the cold lands and steep slopes of the sierras,  was  or-

sections.The Montejo Transect:
The Yucatan Peninsula, home to the lowland Maya, provided a radically different experience for the Spaniards (Figs. 1,4).  As in  the Mexican case,  the northern Yucatan was well peopled, and the Maya were both skilled cultivators and active  in  long-distance  trade  (Andrews  1983; Chamberlain 1948;  Farriss 1984). Nevertheless, by such  measures as  the number and spatial domain of city-states, and level of sociopolitical organization and affluence (as measured by the scale and quality of monumental architecture),  the  condition  of  the  lowland  Maya  in

Yucatan at the time of contact was not on par of years  earlier  (Chase  and  Rice with that  of  their  Classic  Period ancestors some  500-700 1985;  Jones 1989;  Turner 1983a, b).

The  Yucatan  is  composed  of two environmental domains (Figs. 4,  5) over which a common set  of  cropping  practices were  differentially  employed  in  association  with  differing intensities  of  occupation. The  peninsula  is  a large limestone shelf with extreme karst conditions,  dominated by a tropical wet-dry climate (tierra caliente) in  which rainfall increases considerably from the northwest to the southeast (Finch 1965; Wilhelmy 1981; Wilson 1980). The northern periphery of the peninsula is a relatively  flat, lowly  elevated  plain, but  starting with the Puuc Hills (Figs. 3, 4),  a rolling hill or upland area extends southward into the P6ten (Guatemala).  Everywhere in  the  north, extremely shallow and rocky soils, an absence of surface  water,  and  a  pronounced  dry  season impeded agriculture.

At the time of the Columbian Encounter, the northern low plains were moderately to heavily occupied.  In  contrast, the central and southern uplands, an area that was once the heart of the Classic Maya civilization (Culbert 1973;  Turner 1990a),  were  very sparsely settled in  1492 (Jones 1989;  Means  1917;  Scholes  and  Roys 1968;  Turner 1990a,  b).
sections.Alvarado Transect:
Pedro de Alvarado led the  Spanish entrada into the highland Maya realm of Guatemala in 1524,  charting a route southeastward from the Mesa  Central,  following  the  Pacific  coastal plain,  before turning northward into the welldefended highlands of present day Guatemala (Figs. 1,6). Following the experience of Cortes, Alvarado brought  thousands  of  Aztec and Tlaxcalan warriors  to  subdue  the  Maya,  who fought  the invasion in a  series of  bloody battles. The Spaniards found a  populous highlands divided  into  provinces  of  different  ethnolinguistic Maya stock. Each province had hereditary rulers, but no overarching state was  present,  nor were  there  many  large cities of  the material majesty found in the Aztec realm. The region, however, contained some of the finest agricultural soils in Mesoamerica and the lowlands of its Pacific versant gave the Spaniards a preview of yet another source of wealth-estate production of cacao.

The  climb  from  the  Pacific  Coast  to  the homelands of the highland Maya  transverses an array of broad agroecological  zones associated with elevation (West 1964a,  373). The  Coastal Plain (La  Costa) and the  Boca Costa or  piedmont comprise a 40-50 km-wide strip between the  ocean  and  highlands proper  (Figs.  6,  7).

Figure 6.  Alvarado Transect, showing southwestern Guatemala, and the path of the Alvarado  Profile, A-A' (see Fig. 7). Sources: adapted from U.S. Defense Mapping Agency (1978) as  a base map and Bergmann (1969) and Orelanna (1984) for other locational information.

<!-- image -->

The coastal plain (up  to about 100 rn elevation) and the lower Boca Costa (about 100 m-460 m elevation) are  tierra  caliente while  the  upper Boca Costa  (about 460-1500 m elevation) is tierra templada.  Precipitation increases inland and with elevation, such that  portions of  the Boca Costa receive in excess of 2000 mm annually (Viv6 Escoto 1964, fig. 10). Around 1000 m elevation,  the  mountain front  rises steeply to cinder cones and composite volcanos, some o f

Above the 1500 m contour and to the  interior of the versant  is Los Altos,  the highland volcanic axis,  composed of small depressions and calderas surrounded by volcanoes  (more  than  twenty  in  Guatemala alone). Lake Atitldn occupies such a caldera at 1566 m. The peaks are in clouds and mist much of  the time and  average annual  precipitation there  reaches  3000  mm-4000  mm.  To  the northern end of the Alvarado transect the volcanic axis gives way to the lower-elevated and drier central highlands.

title: This land is ours now: Spatial imaginaries and the struggle for land in Brazil
abstract: In recent years, scholars of contentious politics have paid increasing attention to the dynamics of space and place in the construction of organized resistance. To date, however, the literature has tended to focus on the social construction of space rather than the equally important spatial constitution of the social. In this paper, I analyze how particular understandings of space, or what I call spatial imaginaries-cognitive frameworks, both collective and individual, constituted through the lived experiences, perceptions, and conceptions of space itself-influenced the formation of the largest grassroots social movement in Brazilian history, the Movement of Rural Landless Workers (the MST). I analyze the decision to join the MST among small family farmers in southern Brazil and rural plantation workers in northeastern Brazil. People from both groups decided to join the movement, but the farmers from southern Brazil used their spatial imaginaries to embrace the act of occupying land and to create new frontiers for colonization while the rural workers from northeastern Brazil overcame the spatial imaginaries produced through the plantation labor system and joined the movement because they had few other options available to them. Because such imaginaries stay with people long after they engage in the initial acts of mobilization, incorporating this sort of analysis introduces an important dynamic component into the analysis of movement formation.

title: Regional Drinking Water Supply in Pakistan: Regional Disparity, Inequality, and Development Pattern
abstract: This article explores the regional disparities in water supply coverage in Pakistan in the context of intraregional development patterns. We applied the Gini index, Esteban and Ray index, and Moran's I to measure regional development patterns in terms of inequality, polarization, and spatial concentration and build an integrated framework combining them with other widely accepted factors to understand regional differences in water coverage quantitatively. Our results show that improved water (tap and pump water) is more widely supplied in Pakistan with lower inequality but higher spatial concentration than tap water supply coverage, although the patterns differ by urban-rural divisions and provinces. Western regions with smaller populations tend to have higher tap water coverage, and eastern regions with large populations are more covered by improved water. The regression models show various mechanisms of improved water and tap water coverage. Both are related to local economic conditions but tap water coverage is more related to local environmental conditions, and improved water is more related to local demographic conditions. Strong and dense population centers decrease improved water coverage but promote tap water coverage. Urban planners and policymakers should address polycentric regional development to fulfill various development targets and improve regional equity of drinking water coverage in terms of accessibility, availability, and quality.

title: From Street View Imagery to the Countryside: Large-Scale Perception of Rural China Using Deep Learning
abstract: Evaluating residents' subjective perceptions of the rural environment is crucial for formulating effective rural planning. Due to the difficulty in obtaining rural data and the limitations of traditional questionnaire survey methods, existing research mostly focuses on small-scale perception evaluations in specific areas, making it difficult to reveal rural perception characteristics at the regional scale. To address this issue, our study proposes a rural living environment perception evaluation model based on street view images and deep neural networks, achieving a quantitative evaluation of rural perception in 118 cities nationwide. We collected a large data set of rural street view images nationwide through crowdsourcing and established an index system comprising five subjective perception dimensions: wealthy, tidy, lively, habitable, and terroir. By training a multidimensional quantitative evaluation model, we comprehensively evaluated residents' subjective perceptions of China's rural environment. Furthermore, we explored the relationship between these subjective perceptions and objective socioeconomic indicators. The model achieves an average evaluation accuracy of 75 percent across five dimensions, with the wealthy dimension exceeding 80 percent. Rural environment perception is comprehensively influenced by various factors such as economic base and traditional feature protection, showing significant differences between different regions. The perception of rural environment in the eastern region is closely related to economic levels, whereas perception in the western region is more affected by infrastructure improvement and social development. Overall, this study provides scientific evidence for formulating more targeted and effective rural planning.

title: The Making of White Water Citizens in Australia and the Western United States: Racialization as a Transnational Project of Irrigation Governance
abstract: This article examines the role of settler irrigation systems and water governance in establishing and reinforcing tenacious imperial geographies of whiteness. Through an analysis of the lives and work of two powerful men who made foundational contributions to establishing irrigation economies and water governance systems in Australia and the Western United States, we investigate the racialized sociospatial processes that bound whiteness to water. Alfred Deakin (1856-1919) and Elwood Mead (1858-1936) were men of science, technology, and politics who actively circulated in and shaped transnational flows of knowledge about whiteness and racial hierarchies. As Deakin and Mead vigorously promoted particular social and political systems associated with irrigation, steering water flows toward uses regarded as modern and productive according to taken-for-granted norms, they imagined, naturalized, and privileged a white water citizenry. In the process, they contributed to the dispossession and displacement of Indigenous peoples as well as marginalizing Other water users, most notably Asian migrants. These men's hydro-imaginaries, which were endorsed and enacted by their respective governments, served to motivate a form of state protection of family farms, inculcate civic self-reliance and local organization, and establish the white water citizen, a baseline against which others were expected to conform. By examining the making of white water citizens, we hope to contribute to Indigenous geographies and studies of racialization in rural places, as well as the effects of irrigation in settler nations.

sections.Alfred Deakin and Elwood Mead: Transnati:
The man who is acknowledged as the father of Australian irrigation and water law is Alfred Deakin (Gabay 1987). Deakin grew up in an inner Melbourne suburb in a family of modest means. Although he studied law, he spent more of his working life in politics than serving at the bar, entering the Parliament of the state of Victoria when he was twenty-two. For a short time before that, he was a journalist. His principal interests were literature and spiritualism (Gabay 1987).

Deakin is a well-known figure in Australian political history for the many contributions he made, not only to irrigation but to Australian federation and the creation of several national institutions. He played a crucial part in bringing the British colonies into a federation in 1901 under an elected prime minister. Deakin served in that role on three occasions when the bulk of the Commonwealth's foundation legislation was initiated (Gabay 1987). One biographer described him as a 'commanding orator, an energetic administrator, and an innovator in public policy' (Macintyre 2004, 4).

As a colonial nationalist, he pursued an ideal of duty to his nation and an abiding belief in the destiny of the 'Anglo-Saxon race' (Gabay 1987). Believing that Australia was 'reserved for Anglo-Saxons only' (Murdoch [1923] 1999, 94), he actively pursued one of Australia's founding acts of racial exclusion, in the radical form of the White Australia Policy, which prevented immigration of non-whites, especially targeting Asians. It also expelled Pacific Islanders who had been brought to Australia as laborers for tropical sugar plantations (Lake 2003). For Deakin, this doctrine was 'a reasoned policy which goes to the roots of national life, by which the whole of our social, industrial and political organisation is governed' (cited in Macintyre 2004, 7).

Deakin is also well known to scholars of Australian water governance, primarily recognized for having rejected British common law water doctrine and setting Australia on its path of state-administered water management. In his time, he was the 'foremost authority' on Australian water management (Rankin 2013, 128), doing more than any other statesman and lawmaker to shape a set of distinctly Australian governance arrangements through the development of state water institutions. Deakin was a leader in forging water ideologies adapted to a modern nation moving toward independence from Britain and one that needed to develop agricultural production to absorb the population boom following the Victorian gold rushes.

Deakin introduced the colony's first irrigation law in 1883 and built on that contribution throughout the next decade. While attorney general in the Victorian government, he served as the chair of the internationally celebrated Royal Commission on Water Supply (1884-1887). That inquiry recommended legislation to nationalize water by transferring rights to all water of the colony to the Crown and establishing a state system to license private diversions (Harris 2007). Deakin brought to that commission a comparative approach to the global study of irrigation, examining the water cultures and institutional frameworks of southern Europe, Egypt, Italy, India, and the United

States. During the 1880s he wrote two books: Irrigation in Western America , which was for many years a standard textbook in the United States, and Irrigated India: An Australian View of India and Ceylon . His extensive tours and correspondence significantly influenced Australian water policy (Rankin 2013).

Deakin was particularly interested in the merits of 'new world' experiences in irrigation: the circumstances of 'every country in which the practice of irrigation is grafted upon agriculture for the first time' (Deakin 1885b, 10). Strongly affected by his tour of the U.S. West in 1885 (Deakin 1885a), Deakin saw similarities that were significant to his water policy reform agenda (Harris 2007) and, ultimately, Australia's (Rankin 2013). Deakin identified with U.S. manhood, which he equated with the republic, at a time when 'manhood was enshrined in the Anglo-Saxon world as a key political value' (Lake 2007, 36). He deemed the U.S. irrigation experience a suitable model for the state of Victoria because of its comparable place in the white man's world, a world that was taking shape during the nineteenth century as globalizing theories of race, gender, and nationhood were being refined in transnational exchanges (Lake 2003).

His tour of California, Colorado, New Mexico, and Mexico altered his perception of the inherent value of irrigation such that he became an 'enthusiastic believer' and 'at once embarked on an irrigation crusade in his own country' (Murdoch [1923] 1999, 93; see also Rankin 2013). Irrigation would secure continuous agricultural development: 'We have evidence to show us,' said Deakin, 'that irrigation . . . is at least calculated to make agriculture a sure and certain calling, with profits that could be relied on whatever the seasons might be' (cited in Rankin 2013, 122). Irrigation would also serve to fulfill the Jeffersonian ideal of a virtuous rural society, as the following speech by Deakin (1912) shows:

No pursuits are more attractive than horticulture, agriculture, grazing, fruit-growing, and beef farming. Nothing is more beautiful than the healthy and natural labour by which upright and honest people obtain a sufficient living. . . . [They] are in touch with nature . . . their homes are healthy and restful, their freedom and independence making their citizenship a far greater prize than it is in city communities as we know them. (2940)

When in California, Deakin witnessed the irrigation enterprises established by the Canadian Chaffey brothers and he later negotiated an agreement that would enable them to establish Australia's first large-scale irrigation colony at Mildura on the Murray River. The Chaffey brothers adapted plans and systems from their U.S. enterprises to the Australian site, which was to become a model for others around the country.

Examination of his U.S. diary gives reason to suggest that Alfred Deakin most likely met Elwood Mead in Colorado, but long before this Mead identified with agriculture. He was the first of seven children born and raised on his parents' prosperous farm in Switzerland County, Indiana, on which the Mead family grew tobacco and corn and raised sheep and a few cattle. As a youth, he was disturbed as many nearby farms were sold by their owners to speculators and then rented to tenants, tenants who Mead thought did not tend the soil properly and cared little about local affairs, religion, or their children's education (Kluger 1992). His distrust for systems of farm tenancy and his motivation to promote small farm ownership were constants throughout his life. He dedicated himself to agricultural reform and 'helping men own farms,' which became the title of one of his many publications. As a reformer of men, farms, and society, Mead was passionate about the yeoman agrarian ideal (Teisch 2011). By the end of his career, Mead's zeal led him to serve in one of the most significant water leadership positions in the world, the U.S. Commissioner of Reclamation.

Mead started his career after college with a brief stint at the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers, followed by a professorial appointment at Colorado State University (Kluger 1992). He spent his thirties in Wyoming as its First Territorial Engineer, during which time Mead tried to organize and bring order to irrigated agriculture throughout the state. To that end, he drafted Wyoming's constitutional provisions relating to water rights (Teisch 2011), which later became a model for other Western U.S. states. In 1899, he took a position as the lead irrigation investigator for the U.S. Department of Agriculture, a role in which he reviewed irrigation projects across the country. Mead's contention that states should take the lead in irrigation and water initiatives rather than the federal government was not favorably received in Washington, however, so he left to teach at the University of California at Berkeley (UC Berkeley), where he became Professor of Rural Institutions and the Practice of Irrigation (Powell 1982).

Although Mead started off focused on the material and technical issues that enabled and constrained irrigation, throughout his life he became increasingly involved in irrigation governance, particularly its social and financial dimensions. He also pursued

opportunities to promote irrigated agriculture as a means of social engineering; for example, immigration policy favorable to farmers. His was an ideology of a nation made strong through rural communities of small white farmers who sustained themselves by means of irrigated agriculture (Tyrell 1999). While irrigation was a key to democracy in Mead's view, he was not alone in his thinking or actions. Progressivism, fueled by the growth of cities and paranoia associated with increasing southern European immigration (considered non-white at the time), along with reported declines in white birth rates, sought to make rural conditions more attractive and efficient. Within Progressivism, the Country Life Movement reinforced rural nostalgia, humanitarianism, and scientific and technological efficiency (Powell 1982). As a middle-class, well-educated, white man with a Protestant belief system, MidWestern roots, and a strong belief in the yeoman agrarian ideal, Mead fit the profile as a crusader in this movement (Powell 1982).

Mead's work was known to Australian water administrators (Powell 2002), who considered him perfectly placed to invigorate and restructure their water sector following the reforms undertaken by Deakin. In 1907, he and his family moved to Australia, where he became the first chair of the State of Victoria's Rivers and Water Supply Commission (SRWSC) and assumed several related professional responsibilities. He was to play a central role in establishing irrigation settlements in Australia and the content of their water rules. Mead's large-scale program of closer settlement based on irrigation was pursued for decades in Australia (Davis 1968). Completing the circle of transnational transfers that started with Deakin's tour of the United States, Mead 'brought the Victorian formula back to the United States where he was influential in securing land use legislation' (Davis 1968, 658). While in Australia, Mead explained U.S. irrigation practices and water governance and, in turn, when he returned to the United States he promoted the closer settlement policies and irrigation practices that he had worked on in Australia (Mead 1920; Powell 1982). Returning to UC Berkeley, Mead continued to advocate for governance arrangements and ideologies associated with irrigated agriculture as a means of bettering society, not only through his teaching, professional lectures, and writings but also through his work as an irrigation consultant in Mexico, Hawaii, Australia, and Palestine, along with two Californian irrigation demonstration projects he initiated (Kluger 1992).

title: Reparation Ecologies: Regimes of Repair in Populist Agroecology
abstract: Amidst the backdrop of attention to populism in general, it is instructive to understand populism through social movements focused on food and agriculture. Agrarian populism is particularly salient in agrifood movements. Agroecology has been widely identified as a domain of populist claims on environmental and social governance surrounding agricultural-ecological and political-economic systems. As authoritarian populist leaders gain power throughout the world at a time of expanding economic globalization and contingent socioecological crises, contests over populism in agrifood regimes can highlight current dynamics relevant for formative evaluation of alternative political agroecology strategies and of populist environmental governance more broadly. Can populism be harnessed by radical political agroecologies to simultaneously contest the hydra-headed nature of capitalism, authoritarianism, and pollution and implement forms of environmental governance based on repair? We argue that populist agroecology has untapped potential for repair and that the mechanism of focusing social movements on repair might help address some of the more problematic authoritarian tendencies of populism.

title: Introduction to Focus Section: The Geographies of Crime and Policing in the Global Countryside
abstract: This focus section aims to identify, conceptualize, and understand the emerging geographies of rural crime, in particular those of globalized rural crime, and evaluate their impact on different rural places. Contributions to this focus section reflect an interdisciplinary array of fields from geography, economy, and criminology to rural studies, fully engaged with pertinent theories and state-of-the-art literature. The focus section also critically examines how security and policing of rural areas is delivered by existing and emerging agencies, drawing from evidence from different country contexts in Brazil, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Sweden.
picked: Framing the Contributions to the Special Section

sections.Framing the Contributions to the Special:
The first article by Richard Yarwood introduces the special section by providing an overview of work that has examined the geographies of crime and policing in rural areas. It starts by examining the significance of organized and serious crime in rural places using the United Kingdom as a jumping-off point and argues that global rather than community-based perspectives are needed in its study and policing. This global perspective opens up a number of opportunities, including for ' care of others ' beyond the locality.

This theme is developed and exemplified by Susanne Stenbacka, who examines the challenges faced by police officers when dealing with crimes that are committed against rural populations but are global in nature and perpetrated by people in other places. Given a lack of clear global policing strategy, this article draws on interviews to examine the experience of policing local crime in a global context.

The third article draws on evidence from the Global South to examine the commodification of rural security. High rates of crime, an ineffective criminal justice system, and failing policing practices have driven some people to seek self-protection in Brazil. Using data from the Brazilian National Household Sampling Survey, James Temidayo Aransiola, Vania Ceccato, and Marcelo Justus assess the determinants of adopting safety devices in different urban and rural contexts. Their article draws attention to the unequal commodification of security across the country that penalizes the rural poor.

The fourth article is devoted to an underresearched area of study, namely vandalism in rural areas. The empirical material reported in the article by Donna Yates, Diana B  erzina, and Aaron Wright was gathered from a series of interviews with managers of rock art heritage in the Southwestern and Western United States. Yates and colleagues first describe the nature of heritage crimes to provide a context to discuss the complexity of policing in these types of rural landscapes in the United States.

With an increasing awareness of animal rights and of the environmental impact of consuming animal products, conflicts between animal rights activists and those who defend ethical animal production have increased worldwide. Drawing on answers from a national survey directed to animal farmers in Sweden, Vania Ceccato, Peter Lundqvist, Jonatan Abraham, Eva G € oransson, and Catharina Alwall Svennefelt characterize farmers ' victimization with a focus on crimes related to animal rights activists. Long distances and poor police presence are often associated with high rates of underreported crimes against animal production. In this final article, Ceccato and colleagues also highlight the importance of incorporating farmers ' safety needs into sustainable rural development policies. /H17039

title: How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm, After They've Seen Paree? World War I Overseas Military Service and Rural Americans' Postwar Occupational Mobility
abstract: In the aftermath of World War I, U.S. discourse was animated by the concern that demobilized soldiers, having experienced the world outside of their hometowns, would resist returning to farms and to their preinduction occupations. Did military service really encourage an occupational shift? Were rural individuals especially susceptible to and was emplacement in foreign locales especially culpable for this change, as popular culture suggested? Focusing on North Dakota, a state with unusually detailed World War I records, this article uses a novel linked census-military data set and statistical analysis to examine how individuals' place-based military experience might have inflected their postwar occupational mobility. Whereas univariate models support the contemporary perception that farm boys with overseas service were less likely to remain in agriculture, increasingly complex models suggest more nuanced interpretations, with civilian individual and contextual characteristics and their interaction being significantly predictive of farm leaving. Addressing substantive gaps in World War I historiography by contextualizing neglected subpopulations, this research also shows the value of using quantitative methods to engage with critical military geographies. Operationalizing theories of place-individual co-constitution through the analysis of longitudinal, individual data demonstrates how interest in soldiers' experiences and in the spatiotemporally distant effects of war can be productively intertwined. ????????, ??????????????????????, ??????????????????????????????????????????????????????????, ??????????????????????????????, ??????????????????????????????????, ????????, ???????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????, ?????????????????????????????????, ????????????, ??????????????????????????????????, ???????????????, ?????????????????????????, ?????????????? Inmediatamente despues de la Primera Guerra Mundial, el discurso norteamericano se animo con la preocupacion de que los soldados desmovilizados, habiendo experimentado el mundo que existe mas alla de sus pueblos natales, se resistirian a regresar a sus granjas y a sus ocupaciones anteriores al enlistamiento. Realmente el servicio militar estimulo un cambio de ocupacion? Los individuos de origen rural fueron especialmente susceptibles a este cambio y fue el emplazamiento en locales extranjeros especialmente culpable de ese cambio, como sugiere la cultura popular? Enfocandose en Dakota del Norte, un estado que dispone de registros inusualmente detallados de la Primera Guerra Mundial, este articulo usa un nuevo conjunto de datos censales y militares, y analisis estadistico, para examinar como la experiencia militar basada en lugar del individuo podria haber modulado su movilidad ocupacional en la posguerra. Mientras los modelos univariados soportan la percepcion contemporanea de que los jovenes granjeros que prestaron su servicio militar en el extranjero estuvieron menos inclinados a seguir en la agricultura, modelos cada vez mas complejos sugieren interpretaciones mas matizadas, siendo los individuos civiles y caracteristicas contextuales y sus interacciones significativamente predictivas para dejar la granja. Abocando brechas sustantivas de la historiografia de la Primera Guerra Mundial, contextualizando subpoblaciones olvidadas, esta investigacion muestra tambien el valor de usar metodos cuantitativos para comprometerse con las geografias militares criticas. Operacionalizando teorias de co-constitucion lugar-individuo a traves de un analisis longitudinal, los datos individuales demuestran como el interes en las experiencias del soldado y en los efectos espaciotemporalmente distantes de la guerra pueden enlazarse productivamente entre si.
