title: Rural Ruins in America's Climate Change Story: Photojournalism, Perception, and Agency in Shishmaref, Alaska
abstract: This article provides a visual analysis of a set of peopleless photographs taken in 2006 of a falling home erosion in the village of Shishmaref, Alaska, that have been widely circulated in reporting about the relocation of the village due to climate change. It asks whether the visual contract between spectator and absent climate change victim extends beyond an empathetic response to action toward restoring the lost home. The article explores the relationship of contemporary scholarship on postmodern ruination in U.S. Rust Belt cities and the Shishmaref fallen home photograph as a means to analyze the work done by rural ruination.
picked: Understanding Shishmaref: Physical Positioning the Falling House Photograph

sections.Understanding Shishmaref: Physical Posit:
The village of Shishmaref is located on a barrier island, Sarichef Island, in the Chukchi Sea roughly five miles from mainland Alaska. It is separated by a lagoon and lies within the Bering Land Bridge National Preserve and has been inhabited for at least 500 years (Marino 2015). The population of Shishmaref is roughly 600 people and is mainly Inupiat Native Alaskan. Erosion is nothing new for Shishmaref. The land on which the village thrives is part of a dynamic barrier island chain. Residents have noted land lost to the sea from natural trends for hundreds of years -it is an impermanent and ever-changing landscape. For most of its history, though, the community ' s mobility throughout the

Figure 2. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers constructed a rip rap sea wall to protect much of Shishmaref from 2005 to 2009. The project is the latest in a number of sea walls constructed to try to slow the rate of erosion on Sarichef Island. Credit: Eli Keene, 2016.

<!-- image -->

year was also dynamic and seasonally patterned. Their movement and building of camps was flexible, and was made dependent on an analysis of weather and ice conditions. This high amount of mobility proves a successful adaptation strategy to protect the community against flooding and erosion, as movement off of Sarichef Island could be done quickly and efficiently (Marino 2015). In the mid-twentieth century, however, as a federally funded school was built on Sarichef Island, the community of Shishmaref consolidated more permanently to adhere to the mandated attendance policy. This eroded the flexibility of the community, replacing it with immobile infrastructure, often prefabricated further south and shipped north.

As climate change and warmer air and sea temperatures are accelerating the speed and extent of shoreline erosion, this fixed infrastructure of Shishmaref and the community have become more vulnerable to environmental and climatic hazards. The consequences of recent warming have resulted in a loss of three to five feet of shoreline per year, with a single severe storm washing away fifty feet of land (Natural Resources Conservation Service and Shishmaref Erosion and Relocation Coalition 2003). Storms caused such severe erosion in 1997 and 2002 that some homes fell into the ocean and several more needed to be moved. Shishmaref has voted to relocate twice in the past twenty years. The first, more informal vote took place in 2002 after a particularly bad fall storm. Although a new site to relocate the village further inland was scoped, it was eventually dismissed due to hazards of permafrost thaw. On 16 August 2016, residents again decided in a ninety-four to seventy-eight vote to relocate (Hovey 2016).

The vote to relocate was the latest media event that brought the fallen house photograph to the forefront of climate change reporting. Although ' The Melting Arctic ' event at COP22 provided the personal impetus for this article, it is the constellation of news reports on the August 2016 vote that

Figure 3. Shishmaref, seen from just south of the seawall, in August 2016. Credit: Eli Keene, 2016.

<!-- image -->

provide the basis for this visual analysis. The 2016 vote was widely covered by major news outlets, with many choosing to use the fallen house photograph. In print media, The New York Times (Mele and Victor 2016), Huffington Post (Sheppard and D ' Angelo 2016), and the Guardian (Holpuch 2016) used the photograph; on television CNN (Sutter 2017), ABC (Thorbecke 2016), and Fox News (via Associated Press 2016) used the image; and even in radio reporting, National Public Radio (NPR; 2016) and PRX (2016) both recycled the falling house. All of these news reports use one of two photographs of the fallen house in Shishmaref. One is coursed by the stock photo site AP Images. Titled ' Alaska Eroding Village, ' it was taken 8 December 2006 by Diana Haecker, a reporter for the Nome Nugget , for the Associated Press and intended for editorial use only, meaning that it cannot be used for commercial advertising purposes but instead only for a newspaper or magazine article or for descriptive purposes on Web sites and blogs.

The second set of photos comes from Getty Images and was taken by Gabriel Bouys, an Agence

France-Presse photographer based in Los Angeles, on 28 September 2006. This photograph is also tagged as editorial rights with possible use for commercial or promotional uses. As noted, both photographs were taken in 2006 at a particular moment in Shishmaref ' s history. Over ten years later, the fallen house has been cleared, a rock revetment wall now extends the length of the shoreline pictured (Figure 2), and the beach beyond the wall has been eroded by increasingly intense fall storms (Figure 3). Its visual immobility, the canonical prewall image of Shishmaref, and construction as a near still life allow the photograph to easily function as document and archive of the village despite material changes over the past decade. The image, and village, are anchored to the meaning of climate change impacts, textually layered on in each of its uses with additional signs of the most recent climate-induced relocation event or story.

The sections to follow deconstruct this composition in three readings of the image through its visual signifiers. In parallel to this more Barthesian semiotic analysis, the photograph ' s performativity is

also considered. The reception of the photograph by its audiences and how those audiences initiate its performing force and meaning are probed within a frame of social justice. In particular, the article asks whether the visual contract between spectator and absent climate victim outside the frame of the photograph extends beyond an empathetic response to action toward restoring the lost home. In short, does the image exceed the status of testimony by calling for action on part of the viewer? To do this, first a framework for analysis at the nexus of ruination and material decay, representation and landscape, and postcolonial analysis in photography is laid out. Most notable, the following sections explore the relationship of contemporary scholarship on postmodern ruination in U.S. Rust Belt cities and the Shishmaref fallen home photograph as a means to analyze the work done by rural ruination in on the Arctic, Native agency, and Western philosophical sentiments toward a warmer world. Using this scholarship as a foundation, it then delves into an visual analysis of the Shishmaref fallen house photograph and offers three readings of the image: (1) a narrative tension between the romantic aestheticization of decay and an active engagement with the socioenvironmental issues of climate change; (2) the return to nature in postmodern ruination as commentary on nature -human relationships in an era of manmade climate change; and (3) the disordering of normative conceptions of time and materiality in connection to indigenous or peripheral agency.

title: A LiDAR-Based Analysis of Stream Channel Cross Section Change Across an Urban-Rural Land-Use Boundary
abstract: Little is known about the downstream propagation of stream channel alterations initiated by urban flow regimes. In this study, freely available Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data were combined with ground survey data to derive information on changes in stream cross sections in a North Carolina watershed, moving downstream across an urban-to-rural land-use boundary. Regression analyses relating LiDAR model and ground survey data exhibit poor relationships for all channel morphometric measurements except reach-average channel capacity. Application of the channel capacity regression reveals a negative power function pattern of downstream decline in channel enlargement. The largest declines occur before streams enter the rural landscape, with more gradual declines afterward. The largest declines in channel size might be attributable to reservoir effects along reaches with wide floodplains. Model results indicate no discernible enlargement once rural land covers and percentage impervious areas of about 60 percent and 16 percent of watershed area, respectively, are reached.

sections.Methods:
Field Surveys

Ground surveys using meter tape and leveling (Abney or theodolite) were conducted to acquire data on the dimensions of twenty-six channel cross sections from ten different stream reaches (one to five cross sections per reach, spaced 20-30 m apart) along NBC and one cross section at one reach downstream of the NBC-SBC junction (Figure 1). Surveys were conducted over a period of three years from 2005 to 2008. Sites were chosen to avoid the spatially immediate effects of tributary junctions, bridges, and culverts. Bankfull elevation heights were estimated at each site using morphological criteria, including the top of well-developed point bars and prominent benches (when present) and, more commonly in the absence of such indicators, the elevation of the apparent floodplain (top of lowest bank; Harrelson, Rawlins, and Potyondy 1994). Morphological evidence of bankfull stage was emphasized due to the unreliability of features like temporary scour lines and vegetation zones along eastern streams (Harman 2000; Doll et al. 2002; U.S. Department of Agriculture 2003). Bankfull stages thus identified were judged on the basis of gauging data and postflood field evidence to be reached by flows typically occurring every one to two years, the most common frequency cited for bankfull flows in eastern U.S. streams. Bankfull channel capacity, width, and depth were calculated from the field data for each section.
sections.Field Area:
North and South Buffalo creeks head in Greensboro, North Carolina (population 250,000; Figures 1 and 2), a medium-sized city in the Piedmont physiographic province. The area falls within the humid subtropical climate zone, with an average annual temperature of 14.5 ◦ C and an average annual rainfall of 1,074 mm. Vegetation consists predominantly of mixed deciduous and coniferous trees. Upland soils are formed in residuum from metamorphosed felsic rocks and contain a clay-rich Bt (argillic) horizon. North and South Buffalo creeks (henceforth, NBC and SBC) exit the urban boundary at drainage areas of approximately 65 and 75 km 2 , respectively, and join in

Figure 2 Selected images of North and South Buffalo creeks. Names refer to stream reaches displayed in Figure 1. NBC = North Buffalo Creek; SBC = South Buffalo Creek. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

rural eastern Guilford County to form Buffalo Creek (total drainage area of 230 km 2 ). Total relief in the watershed is 76 m. The majority of the municipal area within the NBC and SBC

catchments has been fully urbanized since the 1960s and 1970s, respectively; thus, there has been some time for a new quasi-equilibrium state under urban conditions to be achieved.

Data on stream bankfull cross-sectional area (capacity), width, and depth for large numbers of both rural and urban streams in the North Carolina Piedmont demonstrate that urban streams typically exhibit an increase in channel dimensions relative to rural streams of equivalent drainage areas (Doll et al. 2002). Regional hydraulic geometry curves derived from these data display an average channel capacity enlargement ratio (the urban capacity divided by the corresponding rural capacity at the same drainage area) of 2.6. The channels surveyed in this study are partially confined to unconfined and increase in sinuosity downstream, reaching values of 1.4 to 1.8 near the NBC-SBC confluence. Some upper urban reaches have been dredged for flood control as recently as 1986. Elsewhere, deliberate direct modification of channels is uncommon, particularly in areas downstream of the urban boundary. Based on maps of historical land uses in 1895 and 1908, and subsequent 1951 and 1994 U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps, four mill ponds existed on the main stem of NBC and one on SBC at different times prior to 1951. No impoundments on the main stems of either stream were documented for subsequent decades.
sections.Topographic Measurements from LiDAR: LiDAR technology allows the rapid remote acquisition of highly accurate elevation points at high spatial resolution. Expected horizontal and vertical root mean square errors are frequently less than 1 m and point spacing of refined data sets is commonly less than 4 m (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Baltsavias 1999; Hodgson et al. 2003). Several important limitations of LiDAR exist, though. For example, even at 4-m resolution, LiDAR returns might be ill-suited to defining features with precise boundaries such as the tops and bottoms of stream banks, necessitating manual input of breakline data derived from other sources (Maune 2001). Automated methods for filtering buildings from bare-earth surfaces tend to also filter or smooth natural features with similarly sharp topographic breaks (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Maune 2001; Bowen and Waltermire 2002; James, Watson, and Hansen 2007). LiDAR returns from water features are generally unreliable, due to the absorption and scattering of pulses (Maune 2001; H¨ ofle et al. 2009). In densely vegetated areas, a nearvertical pulse is needed to effectively penetrate canopy and generate a true bare-earth return (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Hodgson et al. 2003). The mean distance to the nearest LiDAR point might be closely tied to land cover class, with the greatest point spacing in deciduous, mixed, and scrub or shrub environments (Hodgson et al. 2003).
sections.Morphometric Analyses with LiDAR:
Despite the limitations, useful geomorphological analyses have been conducted using LiDAR data. An early application of LiDAR technology involved the measurement of channel and gully morphology. Ritchie et al. (1994) made rough estimates of river channel widths and depths by connecting minimum elevation measurements with straight and curvilinear lines using 'best judgment' practices. Bowen and Waltermire (2002) sought to identify the types of river corridor terrain most commonly associated with the largest measurement errors in the Western United States. Large LiDAR elevation overestimations were found to be common in areas with both dense vegetation and steep banks. Charlton, Large, and Fuller (2003) evaluated the abilities of LiDAR to map a gravel-bed wandering stream in the United Kingdom and found that error was introduced by both the presence of vegetation and by deep water, which tended to produce gaps in the point spacing. James, Watson, and Hansen (2007) used LiDAR to map gully networks and headwater streams under forest canopy in South Carolina. Their model captured the location of gully networks accurately but not gully channel dimensions. Overestimation of channel width and underestimation of channel depth were tied to point spacing. The authors recommended the incorporation of ancillary data such as breaklines to explicitly delineate the rims and bottoms of channels.

These studies illustrate that accurate measurements of channel width and depth are difficult to extract from LiDAR data sets. If the limitations of the methods with respect to topography and land cover are consistent or constant, however, then scaled relationships between model and nature might be obtainable. In this study we create and field-calibrate a LiDAR-based model of downstream change in channel dimensions and particularly channel capacities at higher resolution than could be obtained by field studies alone in a similar time frame. We use this model to test the hypothesis that decline in channel enlargement ratio downstream of urban headwaters is directly proportional to the proportion of watershed area that is urbanized, a value that declines exponentially with downstream distance from the municipal boundary.

title: Finding a Disappearing Nontimber Forest Resource: Using Grounded Visualization to Explore Urbanization Impacts on Sweetgrass Basketmaking in Greater Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina
abstract: Despite growing interest in urbanization and its social and ecological impacts on formerly rural areas, empirical research remains limited. Extant studies largely focus either on issues of social exclusion and enclosure or ecological change. This article uses the case of sweetgrass basketmaking in Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina, to explore the implications of urbanization, including gentrification, for the distribution and accessibility of sweetgrass, an economically important nontimber forest product (NTFP) for historically African American communities, in this rapidly growing area. We explore the usefulness of grounded visualization for research efforts that are examining the existence of fringe ecologies associated with NTFP. Our findings highlight the importance of integrated qualitative and quantitative analyses for revealing the complex social and ecological changes that accompany both urbanization and rural gentrification.

sections.Case Study and Methodology:
Sweetgrass, as noted earlier, is a key natural and signature resource used in basketmaking, which, according to popular discourse, is being destroyed by rapid residential and commercial development (Hunt 2006). Baskets sewn by enslaved Africans were once essential to the rice economy that helped fuel the early growth of Charleston and its rural surroundings (Pollitzer 1999; Carney 2001). By the end of the twentieth century, despite the disappearance of rice production almost a century earlier, the descendents of these slaves and their hand-built stands had become a regular site along U.S. Highway 17 in the Mt. Pleasant area and in key tourist areas in peninsular Charleston. Basketmaking remains an important part of the household economies of many African Americans (Derby 1980; Coakley 2006) in the settlements that were once rural outposts of a then smalltown Mt. Pleasant (today referred to as the 'Old village'; Figure 2 inset). What was once

Figure 2 Development trends in Charleston County, South Carolina, for the period since colonial establishment, highlighting significant hurricanes in 1911 and 1989.

<!-- image -->

a small town has become South Carolina's fifth largest city and one of the state's fastest growing cities (U.S. Census 2000), complete with numerous upscale gated communities, some with golf courses and waterfront parcels with private docks. Residential subdivisions increasingly surround historic rural settlements and, in at least one case, largely have replaced an entire community, leaving only a few small pockets of homes with land-use patterns that are more rural in character and that are mainly invisible to passersby (see Figure 3 inset). Beyond its impacts on land ownership, residential and associated commercial development in the greater Mt. Pleasant area also have transformed patterns of land use and land cover associated with many former agricultural and timber land holdings.

Residential growth in South Carolina has outpaced the national average. In the greater Mt. Pleasant area, this rapid residential growth has transformed the area's socioeconomic and racial demographics. First, South Carolina's coastal counties, which comprise a large por- tion of the area known as the Low Country, experienced a 151 percent increase in population between 1950 and 2000, compared to a nationwide increase of 86 percent (National Park Service 2005). Growth in developed acres grew by 256 percent between 1973 and 1994, whereas the population grew by only 41 percent (Allen and Lu 2003). Conservative estimates suggest the Low Country's population will grow by another 500,000 people over the next thirty years (Coastal Conservation League 2006). Meanwhile, Mt. Pleasant's population grew from 30,108 in 1990 to an estimated 59,113 in 2006 and the town's area has grown to encompass 41.89 square miles (U.S. Census 2000). Second, over a century ago, African Americans comprised roughly 70 percent and whites just 30 percent of the population in South Carolina's coastal counties (U.S. Census 2007). By 1990, the percentage of African Americans in Charleston County and Mt. Pleasant had declined to 34.9 and 15.7 percent, respectively (U.S. Census 1990). Today, African Americans comprise 31.9 percent of

Figure 3 Development trends in the greater Mt. Pleasant area, including changes to the boundaries of historically African American communities: 1-Ten Mile, 2-Phillips, 3-Seven Mile, 4-Six Mile, 5-Snowden, 6-Four Mile, 7-Green Hill, 8-Remley's Point, 9-Old Village, 10-Two Mile.

<!-- image -->

Charleston County residents (U.S. Census 2006) and just 7.3 percent of the population within the town of Mt. Pleasant (U.S. Census 2000). Third, whereas the median household incomes were $37,810 (in 1999 dollars) in Charleston County, with 12.4 percent of families below the poverty line, median household incomes in Mt. Pleasant were $61,054, with 3.2 percent of families below the poverty line (U.S. Census Bureau 2000). Thus, as Mt. Pleasant has grown, public discussions about the threats to basketmaking have grown to include concerns about the vulnerability of these stands and the physical communities where basket makers live (Behre 2006; Dixon 2006; Hunt 2006) to the conditions that are resulting from the processes of capital investment and displacement that characterize gentrification, such as the inability of some landowners to keep up with increasing property taxes or for community members to afford to purchase new property. For example, basket makers and concerned citizens met in a

December 2005 workshop to discuss 'Sweetgrass Basketry: A Tradition Under Fire' at the Avery Research Center in Charleston, where many of these issues were raised. Certainly, urbanization and gentrification pressures hold potentially important implications for sewing and selling (see, e.g., Halfacre, Hurley, and Grabbatin 2008; Hurley and Halfacre forthcoming), but here we focus on the consequences of development for gathering activities that are central to basketmaking.

Although basketmaking relies on sewing raw materials into a final product and selling baskets at various market locations, the process begins with the gathering of four key natural materials from local Low Country woodland and wetland ecologies. Specifically, basket makers use blades or 'threads' of sweetgrass ( Muhlenbergia sericea ), strips of the leaves of palmetto trees ( Sabal palmetto ), needles of the longleaf pine ( Pinus palustris ), and cuttings of black rush ( Juncus roemerianus ). Historically,

the plants necessary for these materials appear to have been widely available in local settings, either through collection or via cheap purchase from collectors (Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004). Today, sweetgrass is needed in the greatest quantity and currently is the most difficult to obtain (Derby 1980; Ohlandt 1992; Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004; Grabbatin 2007). Importantly, sweetgrass occurs naturally in clumps landward of the second dune line at beaches as well as in the boundaries between marsh and woods (Rosengarten 1986; Gustafson and Peterson 2007). Thus, the preferred habitats of sweetgrass potentially occur in the very areas that have become highly sought after for their attractiveness by developers and new residents who are able to pay high prices for waterfront land. Yet, the current extent of sweetgrass habitats in the South Carolina Low Country largely is unknown, as is the extent to which the ecological and social dimensions of urbanization have altered potentially suitable habitat and shaped conditions of access.

To explore the extent to which sweetgrass is disappearing and the role social and ecological dimensions of urbanization play in this disappearance, we use the grounded visualization approach described by Knigge and Cope (2006). Grounded visualization builds on the grounded theory approach described by Glaser and Strauss (1967) and Strauss and Corbin (1990) by bringing together ethnographic and GIS methods. Over a forty-year period, social scientists have regularly used the grounded theory approach, where researchers ground (or base) their theoretical development within data analysis, as opposed to a priori theorization within data collection. Through this method, themes and trends can be identified in a manner that allows for more nuanced understandings of dynamics. The marrying of ethnographic and geographic data to examine land use trends provides unique insight into the processes at play. Specifically, grounded visualization relies on recursive integration to analyze these normally disparate data. With recursive integration, researchers first create maps to look for patterns and new opportunities to pursue strategic fieldwork. Second, information from key informants is used to develop new maps that expand the understanding of particular processes and resulting patterns. Third, these maps are used to pursue new questions with key informants; this information is then used to develop more helpful maps. In this study, we began with early efforts to both map known distributions of sweetgrass and potential collecting sites. Next, we pursued key informant interviews to build a more grounded understanding of sweetgrass collecting in Charleston County. We used this information to revise our maps and develop our ecological model. Subsequent interviews incorporated these data to further explore urbanization and its impacts on collecting with basket makers and members of the area's historically African American communities. Coupling these analyses with fieldwork, we helped further develop our understanding of spatial dynamics of sweetgrass use and accessibility.

Ouruseofgroundedvisualization is intended to address two interrelated and overlapping difficulties that we see with finding disappearing resources in an area experiencing urbanization and the potential pressures associated with rural gentrification. First, from an ecological change perspective, assessing the status of sweetgrass is a difficult and expensive but relatively straightforward methodological proposition. In fact, there are a number of different approaches one could take, including the use of air photos, satellite data, or hyperspectral imagery (Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer; Hirano, Madden, and Welch 2003) combined with rigorous ground truthing that is sensitive to land-use patterns (see, e.g., Fox et al. 2002), to measure the current extent of sweetgrass in the study area and begin tracking this over time. To date, no comprehensive remotely sensed data set exists to conduct this analysis for the area. This is due to two factors: (1) the resolution of available remote-sensing products is too coarse, and (2) the use of air photos is prohibitively expensive, given the six-week time window when sweetgrass is readily identifiable from the air. Likewise, there is no comprehensive historical data set to evaluate ecological changes to the area and, thus, to assess the impact of development on Low Country sweetgrass habitats. Given the expense and the difficulties involved, we use a GIS to model existing environmental parameters to characterize potential sweetgrass habitats. Second, there are no straightforward data sets on property regimes , or the combination

of ownership of land and the rights of access or use associated with a given parcel. One can map privately versus publicly owned land, but mapping property regimes is more complicated, as it involves understanding the terms under which nonowners may access resources.
sections.Ethnography: Our ethnographic methods rely primarily on semistructured in-depth interviews, document analysis, participant observation, field research, and attendance at key community events. Our results present data from interviews conducted during June 2002 and January 2003 that were collected for an initial study that examined basket makers' views of and roles in past and current sweetgrass management (Hart 2003; Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004), interviews in the summer of 2003 about collecting strategies, and data from an ongoing study that specifically examines basket maker responses to urbanization. The 2002-2003 study included a total of twenty-three Charleston area basket makers (sixty were invited to participate), including basket makers from the three main locations in the Charleston area (see Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004 for complete details). The summer 2003 interviews included fifteen respondents from the same locations, and the 2006 data collection efforts included interviews with twenty-six basket makers (out of eighty-four who were invited to participate) from the same three sales locations as well as a newer sale site at the local farmer's market (located at Marion Square in downtown Charleston). In all three studies, participants were identified using both convenience and snowball sampling, with most identified specifically through field excursions to basket stands and additional interviews coming from referrals by participants. A variety of other ethnographic data also inform this research. Over the course of several years, we have observed local government meetings, visited with basket makers in their homes and stands, toured local communities with residents, and conducted field visits to numerous local subdivisions. We analyzed government documents related to land-use decision making, community workshops associated with planning processes, community governance in area subdivisions, Web sites and marketing materials for these same subdivisions, and newspaper stories and popular magazine articles about growth and sweetgrass basketmaking.
sections.GIS:
To explore the intersection of ecological and social change resulting from residential growth in the area and the implications for basketmaking, we created a series of maps that provide information on (1) the distribution of sweetgrass using both the botanical literature and information provided by basket makers themselves, which provides some baseline information on areas that have been accessible in the past; (2) land development trends in Charleston County since the South Carolina colony was founded, highlighting the relationship of recent development and parcels that allow access to deep water and spectacular views; (3) land development trends and changes in the boundaries of African American communities in the greater Mt. Pleasant area, which allows us to explore the socioeconomic demographics of the incorporated and the unincorporated portions of the Mt. Pleasant area; and (4) a model of suitability and accessibility that is derived from information about environmental conditions associated with habitat suitability, land ownership, and parcel sizes that suggest the likelihood that sweetgrass on a given parcel would be accessible for collection. On the face of it, the GIS component of our analysis might be seen as merely corroborating the stories told by basket makers. Yet, it is important in a rigorous critical GIS to seek correspondence between empirical observations made by researchers, key informants, and GIS data. We agree with Knigge and Cope (2006) that this process is also about finding areas of correspondence and important disconnects. This includes using the habitat model in discussions with informants that move beyond popular discourses about collecting. Importantly, we note that these maps integrate information from scientific experts with the local knowledge and experiencesboth ecological and political-of basket makers themselves.

Wereconstructed the historic distribution of sweetgrass according to herbaria records from in-state and out-of-state museums, a review of existing literature, and using information gathered from interviews with basket makers in 2002 about places where they were able

Figure 4 Known distribution of sweetgrass ( Muhlenbergia sericea and synonyms) according to herbaria records and interviews with basket makers.

<!-- image -->

to collect 'sizable quantities' of this resource (Figure 4). Three important points about using these types of data should be noted. First, herbaria records reflect the sampling priorities of prior research projects and available funds. Second, given a variety of methods, published literature is helpful in filling in gaps. Third, the locations identified by interviewees ranged from specific areas, such as an area along a particular creek or along a specific road, to more general locations, such as indicating an entire island. Read together, however, these three data sources point to areas that once supported important sites where harvesting took place or to sites that were potential collection sites.

Next, we examined the development trends in Charleston County over time (Figure 2), tracking the period prior to 1911, between 1911 and 1989, and since 1989. The period breaks were chosen to mark two periods when major hurricanes in 1911 and in 1989 (Hurricane Hugo) came ashore just north of the city of Charleston, both of which caused tremendous flooding and storm surge-related destruction to the area's developed and undeveloped environments (South Carolina Department of Natural Resources 2006). The 1911 hurricane is associated with the demise of the rice economy (and some argue the rice culture; see Edgar 1998) and a subsequent 1916 hurricane is often identified by members of the basketmaking community as a major impetus for the beginning of local basket sales to the public. The post-Hugo period is often described as the beginning of a dramatic increase in development in the greater Charleston area (Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004; Hurley and Halfacre forthcoming). Figure 2 was constructed using Charleston County's parcel database and tax assessor's database, together with data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, to map jurisdictional wetlands. Importantly, Charleston County does not keep track of dates associated with the construction of commercial structures. Thus, commercial development is mapped separately from area residential development. This means that our analysis potentially underestimates the extent

to which sweetgrass habitats and access to existing habitats may have disappeared.

In addition, we specifically examined development trends in the greater Mt. Pleasant area, focusing on the relationship of recent development to the historically rural African American communities that are home to most basket makers (Figure 3). These maps include information about what members of these communities consider their historic (pre-1989 development) and current boundaries (see inset). Using these boundaries, we are able to explore the extent to which racial differences within Mt. Pleasant and across the greater Mt. Pleasant area are related to urban change and the communities where basket makers live (Figure 5) and how these patterns relate to the location of potentially suitable habitat. We also use this information to examine differences in property values for all residential parcels in the Mt. Pleasant area as well as two of these communities more specifically, which represent different development dynamics, based on current figures (Figure 6) and according to historical trends (Figure 7). These examples suggest the ways that processes of gentrification and enclosure differentially influence these places.

Finally, we estimated the disappearance of sweetgrass using a comparative model approach. Figure 8 considers current sweetgrass suitability and accessibility to basket makers. In mapping suitability and accessibility, we model the distribution of key ecological conditions that are, in the absence of development, believed to be controlling factors for the presence of sweetgrass together with pertinent information about land ownership and parcel size (Table 1). We followed a three-step approach to create our model. First, we overlaid information about soil composition, hydrology, and proximity to water using the ratings described in Table 1. Second, we identified and classified three land types by using information from Charleston County's tax assessor and GIS parcel databases (Table 1) to group private; nonprofit and churches; county, municipal, public utilities, state, and federal; and unknown lands into classes that attempt to capture the potential

Figure 5 Comparison of 2000 Census block data with the current boundaries of historically African American communities in the greater Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina, area.

<!-- image -->

Figure 6 Property values for all residential parcels and parcels in subdivisions in Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina, and residential parcels inside and outside of the historically African American rural communities of Snowden and Seven Mile.

<!-- image -->

of basket makers to access these properties. We assessed the total acreage of all parcels, with land classified using three categories (categorized into less than ten acres, ten to ninetynine acres, and greater than one hundred acres). Third, this information was integrated with data layers on past and current sweetgrass habitat (Figure 2). When all three steps are combined into the final model (Table 2), the resulting map depicts the potential for sweetgrass habitat and the likelihood of accessibil- ity. This information allows us to compare area estimates of sweetgrass to assess disappearance of the resource during different time periods.

title: Household Water Insecurity in the Global North: A Study of Rural and Periurban Settlements on the Texas-Mexico Border
abstract: This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas-Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected findings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a significant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as universal water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North.

sections.Household Surveys: Qualitative research was conducted in Hidalgo County during nine visits between January 2009 and August 2011. The fi rst author led a research team, including a local community health worker ( promotora ), as they conducted forty-one semistructured interviews and two focus groups. The fi rst author used qualitative information to develop a household water security survey, which was then completed for seventy-one households in Hidalgo County (sixty-eight households used in study) in July 2012. The second author conducted sixty-six household surveys in El Paso County and Do ~ na Ana County (New Mexico) in July 2013. We used the State of Texas colonia classi fi cation system to stratify our sample of households (Parcher and Humberson 2009). We selected households in eleven different colonias in eastern Hidalgo County and fourteen different colonias in eastern El Paso, with households representing each colonia classi fi cation: red, yellow, green, and unclassi fi ed (Table 2). We also surveyed colonias not classi fi ed in the Texas database. We removed six household surveys from adjacent counties in New Mexico when we ran the logistic regression models to limit our analysis to Texas counties. The surveys were conducted in Spanish or English with the available head of household. The survey, which took between thirty and forty- fi ve minutes, was divided into four parts: (1) household demographics (age, occupation, health care access, country of origin, etc., for each household member), (2) water usages and practices, (3) series of yes -no questions related to the three water dimensions, and (4) income and wealth. Descriptive statistics of households are provided in Table 3.
sections.Data Analysis:
We analyzed household survey data using three techniques. First, we used an experiential scalogram technique (Guttman 1945) to draw inferences about a latent variable (water insecurity) in the observed data (Guttman 1945; Guest 2000). In this study we created three scalograms for each dimension of water security. Guttman scalograms provide a measurement of cumulative or progressive objective, subjective, and biocultural experiences; it has been particularly useful when related to domestic water access and food security (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Hadley and Wutich 2009; Stevenson et al. 2012). For Hidalgo County, we used household scales and classi fi cations from previously published data (Jepson 2014), and we followed the same procedure to create the water security scales and classi fi cation for households in El Paso.

Survey item responses were entered 0 or 1 into a respondent-by-item matrix for each dimension of water security, with each row representing a household respondent and each column representing an indicator for each dimension of water security (water access, water quality acceptability, water distress). Guttman scalograms order item responses such that the individual who responded more positively will rank higher than an individual who responded negatively, and the positions of the item responses and individuals are given numerical values. Three conventional measures of reliability for each scale were calculated: coef fi cient of reproducibility (CR), coef fi cient of

2A

scalability (CS), and minimal marginal reproducibility (MMR). The CR should be greater than 0.90, CS more than 0.60, and MMR less than 0.90 (Guest 2000; Peregrine, Ember, and Ember 2004; Table 4). 2

The experience-based indicators that correspond with survey item responses used in scale development are described in the idealized Guttman scales (Table 5). For example, households that experienced the lowest water access reported the presence of all the indicators, but households with the most water access experienced none or the fi rst listed indicator. In addition, Table 5 reports the number of households that positively responded to the presence of each indicator. For example, water was not affordable in 84 percent of Hidalgo County households and in 91 percent of El Paso households. Similarly,

Second, we clustered households into four groups of water security using the three scale scores by applying the centroid method and squared Euclidean distance measurement to create a dendrogram in S C software (TIBCO 2010). The four household water security groups or classes are (1) water secure, (2) marginally water secure, (3) marginally water insecure, and (4) water insecure. We used R software to test the hypothesis of no difference between two or more groups among the four groups using the nonparametric

title: Settin' the woods on fire: Rural incendiarism as protest
abstract: Fire is a fundamental tool within a broad spectrum of vegetation-management strategies, from swidden agriculture to plantation forestry. Through the seemingly pyromanic activity of incendiarism, fire assumes additional significance in the human-environment relationship. Case studies from England, Algeria, and the southern United States serve to illustrate the circumstance of fire as an indication of agrarian discontent and a weapon of peasant resistance. Other documented cases of incendiarism reveal that use of fire in the landscape has expanded from a constructive ecosystem-manipulation technique to a destructive form of protest undertaken by the oppressed or disempowered.

sections.FORMS OF INCENDIARISM:
An incendiary  fire  has  been defined  as  a  "wildfire willfully  set  by  anyone  to  burn,  or to spread  to,  vegetation  or  property  not owned or controlled  by  him, and  without consent of the owner or his agent"  (Forest  Service  1978, 9). Although  the popular Hank  Williams  song  used  "settin' the  woods  on  fire" merely  as  a  metaphor, these  illuminating  lyrics  are  clearly indicative  of  actions  familiar to  many  rural  residents.  Motives for  such actions  include  personal  grievances  against  landowners,  attempts  to devalue  property  for  speculative  economic gain,  incidents  of arson  by  unemployed firefighters who seek  work,  and  the  pyromanic  activities  of demented  individuals. The focus of this article  is on incendiarism  as  a tool of protest  or resistance.

Arson is  listed  by  James  C.  Scott  as  one of the  "weapons of the  weak"  that  "relatively  powerless  groups" utilize  against  ",those who seek  to extract  labor,  food, taxes, rents,  and interest  from  them"  (1985,  29).  Rural  incendiarism,  according  to George

Rude,  belongs  "to  that  shadowy  realm  between  crime  and  protest  where  it  is  often  no easy  matter  to tell  the two apart" (1978,  4). In  cultural-ecological terms,  destructive burning of the landscape  represents  seemingly  maladaptive behavior,  as  a result  of which the perpetrators themselves  become  victims.  But  a review  of the  literature of peasant resistance  stamps  this type of incendiarism  an act of desperation,  which must be seen as  part  of a  "rebellion  of hopelessness" (Scott  1976, 195). In  many  cases it is  a  refractory phenomenon that  occurs  wherever  an  established  agrarian order  is forced  to undergo change  that threatens  to disrupt  its particular  subsistence  ethic and its  traditional  resource-use  patterns.  These  inflammatory reactions  range  from isolated  incidents  of arson  to jacquerie,  or full-blown  peasant  revolt,  during  which incendiarism  may be widespread.  Frederick Gamst  found that "such  uprisings  of peasants  often  stem  from  increased rates  of  extraction of  the  fund  of  rent,  or  from  attempts to alter  the nature  of their  ties to the land"  (1974,  48).

In the wake of commercial agriculture,  the rise of export-driven  plantation space-economies,  and  postcolonial  modernization  of the  peasantry, rural  incendiarism persists  as a political-ecological  trait  operating  in defiance  of unpopular  government  policies  or  as  a  symbolic  and  immolatory  act  of  protest.  The  representative case studies reviewed  below, followed  by a brief assessment  of incendiary  activity elsewhere  around  the world,  serve  to illustrate  this idea.
sections.A GLOBAL ASSESSMENT:
Incendiarism  as a  tool of protest  or resistance has  been a  recurring, albeit  sporadic, phenomenon across  the globe,  although  certain  areas  are  more  prone  to experience this activity  than  are  others  (Figure  5).  A sampling  of documented  cases  reveals  the following situations,  beginning  with several  locations once subsumed  within the British  Empire.

During  the 1920S, in Kenya, the encroachment  of European  colonists  into areas of traditional  pasture  for  tribal  livestock  led to a government-sponsored  program known as kifagio,  a  Swahili  word  for  "broom," referring to the  sweeping  away  of native stock. Resistance  to kifagio included acts of incendiarism,  involving  settlers' crops  and  the  forest  reserves in  which  indigenous  people  were  forced  to  relocate.  The ensuing poverty  led to militancy,  and "acts  of terrorism  against  settlers  and their property  increased," part  of a  peasant  movement  that  found  ultimate  expression  in the  Mau  Mau  rebellion  (Kanogo  1987,140).  To  the  south,  in  neighboring  Tanganyika during the 195os,  a mandatory government soil-conservation  program  that included a ban on burning  elicited  an incendiary  response:  "Ribbons  of smoke  rose defiantly  all  over  the  Uluguru  Mountains....  Rules  against  burning  were  no longer enforceable,  and the peasants  now openly flaunted  authority  by firing the hills" (Young and Fosbrooke 1960,  157).

In India,  forestry  programs  under  the British  Raj  included  suppression  of fires, often to the detriment  of both economic and  ecological  functioning.  Protest  over these  policies  took  the  form  of "spectacular outbreaks" of incendiarism,  along  with a "relentless insurgency  of small  firings" (Pyne  1995,  166).  And  in the Indian  Hima-

laya,  peasant resistance  to commercial  forestry  ignited "outbreaks of planned incendiarism"  as the attempted  government  repression  of traditional  annual  forest burning had the opposite effect  (Guha  1990,  52).  Incendiarism  in the state  of Uttar Pradesh  was  especially  common in 1916,1921,  and  1930-1931.  The  situation  in India, particularly, suggests  that a distinction should be drawn  between  incendiarism  as strictly  a destructive  form of protest  against  any  manner  of injustice  and  the insistence on utilizing  fire  as  a constructive  tool of resource  management  in the face  of criminalization  or restrictions  on its further  use.

The  island  continent  of  Australia has  been  occupied  by  its  aboriginal  inhabitants for tens of thousands  of years.  Burning  was an essential  component of the human ecosystems  for  these  antipodean  hunter-gatherers, whose culture  so carefully  managed  the environment  for  broad-spectrum  food production  that  it earned  the epithet "firestick  farming," a descriptive  term  first  ascribed  to Rhys  Jones  (Pyne  1991, xii). In the Aborigine  worldview,  frequent  burning  was absolutely  necessary,  not only for subsistence  but also in order  to take  care  of the land (Lewis  1989;  Kohen 1995).  With the inevitable  and  unavoidable  clash  of cultures  associated  with incursions onto native  lands  following  the 1788 British  convict  settlement  at  Botany  Bay and the subsequent  colonization of the frontier  beyond,  the Aborigines  naturally used fire  as  a  tool of resistance: "They  fired  wheat  shocks  as  they  did  tussocks.  They hurled  fire  sticks  as  though they  were  warding  off night demons escaped  from  the Dreamtime.  Fields  and paddocks  they  burned  like  favored  hunting  grounds.  They set decoy fires  to distract  settlers,  then plundered  their  homesteads  and barns  for food" (Pyne 1991,  192).

In the compartmentalized  geography  of modern Australia,  where "ecosystem management"  is at  once  the  tenet  and  the  responsibility of government  scientists,  an attempt  has been made to incorporate  Aboriginal  burning  practices  and environmental  knowledge  as part  of the management  plan for Kakadu National  Park.  But different  perceptions  and  ideas  about  proper  fire  intensity  and  seasonal  restrictions have  contributed  to misunderstandings between  park  personnel  and  resident  Aborigines.  In one case,  a ranger  reported  an antagonistic  attitude  on the part of one landowner  who vehemently  insisted on his right to burn;  the ranger  commented that the resultant  fire  "was  almost a form of protest  against  us"  (Lewis  1989,  952). Less  ambiguous  is  the  situation  documented  by  Jeff Collmann  for  an  outback  settlement of Aborigines  near  Alice  Springs,  where  land rights  were  perceived  as being threatened  (1988).  Collmann,  using the pseudonym  "Mt.  Kelly" for this particular community of "fringe-dwellers," wrote of one individual  who, on 21-22  May  1975, burned a large  area  of surrounding  land:  "George burnt  the bush  around  Mt.  Kelly when the basic  assumptions  of power,  responsibility, and  independence,  which  underlie  bush-burning  and  the identities  of the  Mt.  Kelly domestic  groups  as  a  whole, were under assault  and subject  to grave  compromise  from  outside  forces"  (p. 208). The boundaries  of this burned area  corresponded  to what the people felt  were  the true  claims  for  their  settlement.  The  fire  was  an  attempt  to assert  control  over  space that the people believed  rightfully  belonged  within their  domain.

Several  traditions  of rural  incendiarism  have  been documented  in continental Europe.  Andre Abbiateci  linked fire with the changing economic geography  of eighteenth-century  France  and  noted  that,  "for  the  most  part,  rural  crimes  of arson were committed by landowners  and tenant farmers  whose land was threatened" (1978,  170).  In  operation  was  the  peasant  tradition  of perpetual  leasehold:  A tenant could  not  be forced  to  leave  the  land  held  under  lease  and  had  the  right  to  a  moderate rent  and  the right  to purchase  the  land  if the  owner  offered  it for  sale  (first  refusal). Violations  of these  rights  would often  result  in retaliation by arson,  and  "rural society during  the  Ancien  Regime  ...  was  an  anxious,  threatened  and  fragile  one,  living in dread of fire and the firesetter" (p. 176).  This incendiary  tradition  among the French  peasantry  was roughly  contemporaneous  with the English  use of fire as a weapon of agrarian  protest,  but it does not appear  to have  been as  widespread  or as politically  charged.  Following  the institution  of French  forestry  codes,  authorities who attempted  afforestation during  the  late  1800s  blamed  the  "malevolence of shepherds"  for frequent  outbreaks  of incendiarism  (Clout  1983, 134).

The lack  of organized  resistance  to agrarian change  also  characterized the  use  of incendiarism  by  German  peasants  in the  latter  half  of the  nineteenth  century,  which Regina  Schulte  found to have  been predominantly  a situation  of individuals  acting from a sense of personal  injustice  (1994).  Writing  about  both "accidental" and incendiary  blazes,  Cathy  Frierson  elucidated  what  seemed  to be an  "epidemic  of fire" that captivated  local narratives  and discourse  during the same period in Russia (1996, 1997). And in the forests  of Poland,  incidents  of incendiary  fires  in 1947 accompanied Ukrainian  resistance  to government  relocation  efforts:  "The  fires  were said  to represent  a  new strategy  by  the  stubborn  Ukrainian  bands,  which at  present are Poland's  biggest internal  security  headache"  (New York  Times 1947).  Farther east,  in  China,  during  a  period  of forest  fires  in  1953, it  was  reported that  "some  trees were  deliberately burned  because  of 'dissatisfaction' with the  Government  takeover of privately  owned forest  land"  (New  York  Times  1953b).

As might be expected  given  the  unique  pyrophytic  ecological  conditions,  Mediterranean  lands  in addition  to Algeria  have  witnessed  the destructive  use of fire.  In Cyprus,  for example, British  forest laws imposed in the late nineteenth century clashed  with the traditional  use of a "common"  resource.  Restrictions  on grazing and fuelwood gathering  led to incendiary  reactions  by shepherds  and others  who to 'dis(1997, 135). A  vicious cycle  of of  the Cyprus  Republic,  and  "the  tradition  of firing  the forest  in times  of stress  and  as  po- felt  they  were  being  deprived  of their  rights.  As  Pyne  expressed  it,  "attempts cipline'  Cypriot  pastoralism  only  led to incendiarism" arson  followed  by  further  restrictions prevailed beyond  the  1955 establishment litical  protest  continues"  (Thirgood  1981,  147).

The Spanish  countryside  during  the 1930S was in the grip  of "rural  anarchism" that induded burning crops and woodlands, a phenomenon that seems to have diffused  from a heartha:  "In  the fall  of 1933 a series  of farm  burnings,  which originated  in the Jerez  de  la Frontera-Medina Sidonia  region  of Cadiz,  spread  rapidly  to other  parts  of Spain.  From  August  to November, several  hundred  farms  and  forests,

though apparently  relatively  few  farm  buildings,  were  set on fire"  (Malefakis 1970, 301).  Post-Civil  War  government  reforestation programs  became  the  target  of  political  agitation,  largely because  of the  requisite linkage  of state  control  with  plantation establishment: "A  protest  against  one is a  protest  against  the other;  both often  come in the form  of fire" (Pyne  1995, 122). Other  resource  issues  have  incited  similar  strife. Paul  Starrs  and Lynn  Huntsinger  noted  variations  among  the autonomous  regions of Spain  regarding the regulation  of hunting  practices; in some areas  the continued application  of a 1970 law  allowing  landowners  to post their  lands  and  close  them  to hunting  has  resulted  in  numerous  fires  set  by  villagers in retaliation against  such  restricted  access  (1991). The problem  of incendiarism  in Spain  lingers,  as reported  in the New York Times:  "The  settling  of accounts  by  setting  fire  to a neighbor's land is common practice  in Galicia" (New York  Times  1989).  Where  once fire  was a useful tool of ecosystem  management,  destruction  for  its  own sake  is now  the order  of the day.  "Increasingly, the demise  of traditional  burning  is replaced  by incendiarism  as protest,  vandalism,  revenge,  and  terrorism. Each  site  of change  becomes  a  potential flashpoint.  The sharper  the change  the more  likely  the spark" (Pyne  1995, 124).

Throughout  the greater  Mediterranean region,  the  practice  of "politically motivated  arson"  remains  rampant  (Pyne,  Andrews,  and  Laven  1996,  636).  Portugal  was the  scene  of incendiary fires  in  1975, reportedly part  of a  "right-wing offensive  to create  political  chaos"  (Howe  1975). More  than  1oo,ooo  acres  were  burned  by  midsummer,  and some fires  were  reported  to have  been  set  by  aircraft dropping  incendiary bombs. Israel  also has been plagued  by arson  attacks  on its forests.  In 1988  nearly 50,Ooo  acres  of woodland  and  pasture  were  destroyed by  proponents  of the Intifada (New York  Times 1988).  This region  had  previously  suffered  incendiary  activity  as well:  During the late  1930S forests  near  Nazareth were  a frequent  target  of Arab  arsonists (New York  Times 1937, 1939).

Greek  incendiarism  was  so rife  in  1981 that  it  was  the  subject of an  editorial  in  the New York Times  that  began,  "Democracy  is a Greek  word.  So is  anarchy. So is pyromania"  (Ebon  1981). The  following  summer  seemed  no different, as  the  government "blamed  organized  arsonists  or  political  extremists  for  a  series  of devastating forest fires" (New York  Times  1982). But  neither  is  incendiarism new to Greece,  which  encountered  such  acute  problems  in  1900  that  the  Orthodox  Church  threatened  arsonists  with  excommunication  (Pyne  1982, 165). Characterizing the  country  as  one  with "a  history  of hostile  fire,  of fire  used  violently,  of a  malevolent  and  vindictive  burning'" Pyne  graphed  the  total  burned  area  from  1922 through  1990.  He  noted  a  "strong correlation  between  fires  and  periods  of social  unrest" and  found  that  the  amount  of burned area  was especially  high during  election  years  (1995,  97-105).

Beyond the Mediterranean  region,  the world's  islands,  as microcosmic  metaphors  for  a  closed  system,  seem  particularly prone  to outbreaks of incendiarism.  On Madagascar, for  example,  grass  and  brush  fires  were  commonly  set  as  a  "subtle  form of political  protest"  (Mohr  1971). But  such  actions  have  increased  to the point  that they are  not so subtle anymore,  for Daniel Gade  writes  that "incendiarism of the land  rages  over  Madagascar as  a  way  of  expressing political  or  social  discontent" and

further  comments  that  these  fires  maybe  "away for  a  repressed culture  to  externalize their  emotions and  hostilities"  (Gade  1985, 1ggo).  The  Edenic  paradise  of Mauritius was transformed  by colonial  invasion  and  indiscriminate burning  (Pyne  1997, 406410).  Lorded  over  in its  time  by  a  succession  of European masters,  the  tiny  island  ultimately witnessed large-scale sugarcane operations, and in 1937  labor strikes against  plantations  escalated into  protest  incendiarism. After  several dissidents  were gunned down on one estate,  "the  crowd  retreated, setting  fire  to the cane  fields  as they fled"  (Storey  1995, 172). On the  densely  populated  island  of Java, in addition  to woodland clearance  and  pasture  maintenance,  fire  has  been used "for  hunting,  for pleasure,  for pestering  neighbors  or neighboring  villages"  (van Steenis  1965,  33). Here  too, Nancy Peluso  found that  "historically, the state,  the  peasantry,  and other external  interests  have  acted  out their  tensions  in the natural  theatre  of the forest" (1992,  4).  Questions  of access  and  control  over  resources  hearkening  back  to Dutch colonial regulations  remained  contentious  issues  during  the 1946  revolution,  when peasants  resisted  state  control  over  forest  use  and  nearly 250,000 acres  were  torched. When  the  revolution  ended  in  1949, control  of state  forestlands passed  to  Indonesian hands, although "to forest-dependent  villagers  there was little change[;] ... restricted  forest  access,  whether  imposed  by the Dutch,  Japanese, or fellow  Indonesians,  constrained  their  lives  and  livelihood"  (p.  102).  During  the  1970s,  protest  over the  establishment  of pine  plantations  and  government  prohibitions  against  clearing swiddens for agriculture  resulted  in further  incendiary  activity:  "As  fires  flared  on the forest  lands,  'no one knew'  who started  them"  (p. 194).  Wolf Donner recounts frequent  fires  on the outer  islands  of Indonesia,  citing  "arson and  negligence  on the part of peasants  as  well as foresters" (1987, 246).

In  the  1930S the  Philippines  was  the  scene  of  peasant  uprisings,  as  tenant  farmers sought greater  tenure security  from landlords  and protested  eviction from their lands (Kerkvliet 1971, 176).  Destructive burning  of cane  fields  was  a  common occurrence,  a  tool of protest  that  continued  to be used  during  the  Huk  Rebellion  of 19461954  (Kerkvliet  1977,  37). Although unsuccessful  in their attempt  to bring about change,  the Huks'  use of incendiarism  was  aimed  at "the  redress  of agrarian grievances"  (Lachica  1971, 11).  Problems  persist,  and the government's  Social Forestry Program,  established  in  1982, has  attempted to  alleviate the  threat  of incendiary fires. Research  in the Ifugao  region found that swidden  cultivators  regularly  use fire  to clear  new plots for planting  and resent  what  they  perceive  as unnecessary  government intervention  in their  farming  traditions:  "They  believe  that  common law  dictates  that  kaingins  [plots]  are  made  in 'open  areas' regarded  as  'public  land'...  [and] do not understand  why  they  should  be  prohibited  from  burning  or  utilizing  fire  as  a tool in their kaingin  practice" (Codamon-Quitzon  1991,  416).  As a way  around  the rules,  these  farmers have  even  instituted  a  taboo  against  anyone  observing  nighttime burning,  lest the fire  be reported  to authorities.

On the nearby  islands  of Palau,  Kenneth  Brower noted  that  "there was  once  forest  here,  but  it  burned  away in  fires  set  by  Palauan arsonists" (1974,124).  Calling  these fires  the "worst  conservation  problem  in the Palau  islands," he wrote:

Pyromania is a  strange aberration anywhere, but  in Palau it is  especially strange. Here, as  in  the  other small  islands of  Micronesia, the  traditional view  is  that  land, in its scarcity, is precious. Within  such  a tradition, then,  arson  seems  a peculiarly mindless and  self-flagellatory behavior, like  that  observed sometimes in  caged animals.  If  it  does  not  hint  at  something dark and  unhinged in  the  new  Palauan psyche, the  widespread occurrence of the  fires does  at  least  suggest that,  after a  century of foreign  rule,  the old systems  are  breaking  down. (Brower  1974,  124)

It  should be remembered,  however,  that  the fires  of Palau  are  not pyromania  at all but,  in  fact,  represent a  redirection of  traditional burning  practices toward  a  political ecology of protest.

In another  part  of Oceania,  a  number  of sugarcane fields  in Fiji  were  destroyed by  fire  following  the  1987  military  coups  d'etat  that  left  the  Indo-Fijian  leaseholders without secure  access  to farmland. Controlled  burning  of cane  is  a  common  harvest technique  for  removing  leaves  from  the  stalk,  but these  fires,  sparked by anger  over the  tortured  political  affairs of the  country,  were  deliberately set  to destroy  the  crop. Later  that same year,  as reported  by Michael  Howard,  "arson,  a common form of political  protest[,]  ...  [was]  becoming  another  serious  concern  in Fiji's pine  plantations";  by  November  more  than  25,000  acres  of trees  had  been  damaged  by  incendiary fires (1991,  305).

Halfway  around  the  globe,  and  a  century  earlier, another  island  dominated  by  the sugar  economy  witnessed  fires  of protest.  Commenting  on the agrarian unrest  during  the  188os and  189os  in  Cuba, Louis  Perez  Jr. characterized the  disturbances as  "not quite  an  organized peasant  rebellion [;]  ... rather, it  was  an  improvised assault  against the  dominant  social  class,  and  no  planter or  plantation was  safe" (1989,  29). Throughout the island,  agricultural interests-often financed  by foreign  capital- were  consolidating  lands into large  estates,  forcing  a transition  in the mode of production from  smallholder to  wage  earner. The  reaction  of displaced peasants  was  decisive  and deliberate: "They  torched  the  canefields-again,  again,  and  again" (p.  30). During  the 1910S the inexorable  expansion  of sugar  latifundios  rekindled  the flames  of protest across  Cuba:  "Incidents of  arson  increased, and  cane  field  fires  in  particular" (p.  179).

Continental Latin  America  has also experienced  outbreaks  of incendiarism, though  not nearly  as  often  as  the  Mediterranean area  or  insular lands.  In  1943  a  series of mysterious  blazes  burned  in  the  rubber-growing region  of the  Brazilian  Amazon, and officials  there  suspected  saboteurs  (New  York Times 1943). In 1953  vast  prairie fires  in Buenos  Aires  Province, Argentina,  were  thought  to have  been "the  work  of opposition  elements seeking to discredit the government of President Juan  D. Peron"  (New  York Times  1953a).  And  the  occurrence  of ecoterrorism in  Colombia  in 1990  included incendiarism  as a tactic:  "In a series of arson attacks  in July  and August,  one guerrilla  unit set fire  to 262 acres  of pine plantations" (Brooke  1990).

title: Challenges and Opportunities for Coping with the Smart Divide in Rural America
abstract: Recent success in the many applications of information and communications technologies (ICTs) in urban settings largely defines our understanding of sustainable development in the context of smart societies and communities. The footprints of such smart transformation barely imprint in the countryside, however, where rural communities face tremendous barriers, such as the absence of ICT infrastructure, geographic isolation from technological advances, and various social inequalities. The conventional wisdom of smart societies and communities built on well-established broadband access and ICT applications in urban hubs might not be suitable for decentralized rural regions. We contend that a new form of digital divide in the context of recent ICT advancement-a smart divide-is evolving into a new challenge to smart societies and communities. This study aims to characterize the smart divide, an emerging type of social inequality. To address this aim, we conduct a literature review with a focus on the technological aspects of the smart divide in rural regions and identify potential gaps in smart infrastructure and smart applications and services between urban and rural America. The article culminates in a synthesis of potential strategies for bridging the smart divide in rural America. The study is expected to benefit scientists, planners, entrepreneurs, and policymakers interested in smart rural development.

title: Biodiversity and land-use change in the American Mountain West
abstract: Rural private lands in the Mountain West of the United States are undergoing a profound land-use conversion, from agriculture to low-density residential or exurban development, though little scientific study documents the ecological consequences of this change. Nongovernmental conservation organizations are working with ranchers to keep rangeland out of development and in ranching, ostensibly because these organizations believe that biodiversity is better protected on ranches than on exurban developments. We compared plant and wildlife communities across the principal rural land uses in the Mountain West: protection, livestock ranching, and exurban development. Native plant and faunal biodiversity was better maintained on ranches and protected areas than on exurban developments. Exurban developments favored species that were nonnative or adapted to human-altered environments. The continued conversion of ranches to exurban development suggests a long-term alteration of the region's natural heritage.

sections.STUDY AREA AND SITE SELECTION:
We conducted  our  study  from  May through  August  during  2000  and 2001 in the foothills  along  the  Front Range  of the  Rocky Mountains  in  northern  Larimer County, Colorado  (40050'  N, 105°15' W).  The  study  area  is  approximately 40  kilometers northwest  of Fort  Collins, the  nearest metropolitan area.  The  land-use  matrix  of the  region is a  blend of  private  ranchland, public  protected  areas,  and exurban  developments. The  vegetation is  a  mosaic  of  shrubsteppe and  mixed-grass prairie. Dominant  grasses include needle-and-thread  (Stipa  comata  Trin.  &  Rupr.  var.  comata),  blue  grama (Bouteloua  gracilis  [Kunth]  Lag.  var.  gracilis), western  wheatgrass  (Elymus  smithii [Rydb.]  Gould),  and  cheatgrass  (Bromus  tectorum  L.).  Shrubs  include mountain mahogany (Cercocarpus montanus  Raf.  var.  montanus),  skunkbrush  sumac  (Rhus trilobata Nutt.  var.  trilobata), and  bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata [Pursh]  DC.).  Common forbs include  fringed sage (Artemesia  frigida Willd.)  and  hairy goldaster (Heterotheca villosa  [Pursh]  Shinners  var.  villosa).  Average  annual  precipitation ranges  from  33  to  46 centimeters,  with  75  percent  of it  falling  between  April  and September  (Moreland  1980).

The  study  was  restricted to sites  with similar  physical  characteristics, including the  same  shrubsteppe  plant  community, with  elevations  between  1,740  to  2,200 meters,  and similar  soil  types  to reduce  natural variability  among  sites.  Study  sites had to  comprise  at least  1,ooo  hectares  in order  to minimize the influence  of surrounding  land uses.  We  used  1:24,000  orthophoto-quadrangle maps  and  plat  maps from the Larimer County  Assessor's Office  to determine  potential  sites.
sections.STUDY DESIGN AND DATA COLLECTION: We  compared  songbird,  mammalian  carnivore, and  plant  communities  across  three land uses:  public protected  areas  (Colorado  Division of Wildlife's  State  Wildlife Areas)  whose  principal use  was  outdoor  recreation and  wildlife  protection  (no grazing, logging, mining,  or water  development);  private-land  livestock  ranches  with cattle;  and  exurban  developments  with one house  per  14-20 hectares.  We  randomly selected  ninety-three points  across the three land uses to  survey songbirds  and mammalian  carnivores  and  sixty-nine  points  to  sample  the  plant community.1 At each  point  we  sampled  communities  using  75-meter  fixed-radius point  counts for songbirds,2  scent stations for mammalian  carnivores,3  and 20-by-50-centimeter quadrats  for  plants.4

title: Countryside recreational access in the United States: A statistical comparison of rural districts
abstract: This comparative study employs the concept of physical rigor to map and measure recreational routes and zones available to the public. The comparison is made for 20 representative countryside districts in five regional settings (Northeast, Midwest, South, Great Plains, and California). Five of the districts are national parks, while the rest are 40 x 25 km settled areas chosen to typify landscapes of their region. Statistical measures of access availability are derived from 1:24,000 topographic maps for five levels of access rigor. Access was determined for small quadrats (500 m square) on a presence/absence basis, beginning with the easiest access mode (passive) and then testing for increasingly rigorous modes (casual, vigorous, rugged, arduous, and closed). Polynomial regressions show strong relationships between levels of access and the independent variables of topography, land cover, road density (a surrogate for land-use intensity), and natural vegetation. In highly utilized areas of low relief there is plentiful access via the road network, but few trails, and much closed land. By contrast, remote wilderness areas, exemplified by national parks, offer little road access, but provide ubiquitous cross-country access for a small minority of specialized or expert recreationists. Regional variations in access availability are also tentatively related to the scale of original landholdings, in turn related both to date of settlement and type of land allotment and survey. For given levels of land-use intensity, areas of large-scale landholdings have fewer public rights-of-way, and more land closed to the public.

sections.The Study Areas: Selection and Appraisal:
The  only  feasible  way  of  measuring access availability nationwide  is  through  the  use of topographic maps combined with field verification.  Since the great bulk of recreational activity  takes  place  in the  settled or  semi-settled countryside,  our interest focuses  on these areas.  More  specifically, the  study  areas  selected are located in regions having  continuous blocks of ecumene with rural densities exceeding  t w o  people per square kilometer (as shown in Figure 1) (Espenshade and Morrison 1986:86). Extensive  areas of desert,  mountain, and northern forest  are  excluded from  study, as  are regions containing only small pockets of scattered  settlement.

To  facilitate  analysis  and permit comparison with  other  studies,  the  United States  was  divided  into five  regions  differentiated  with  respect to their  natural vegetation,  dates  of settlement,  and  culture.  The  five  units  range  in size from 100,000  to 500,000  square  km,  and their boundaries are drawn  through  thinly populated  areas  or  along  major  rivers  (Figure 1).  Within  each  region,  three  representative  settled  areas  were  selected,  each  being 1,000 square  kilometers  in  area  (40  km  by 25 km).  The study areas met three criteria;  they are:  1) largely  rural with a few  tracts  of urban or suburban development;  2) mixed in topography,  water  features,  land  cover,  and  settlement types,  while accentuating features typical of the local setting;  and 3) representative of  the landscape mix in each region and of the nation as  a  whole.  The  fifteen  selected  areas,  which are  named  after  their major  settlement,  are mapped in Figure 1  and listed in Tables 1  and 2.

The  study  areas  in  the  Northeast  afford  a variety  of topography  (see amplitude  of relief, Table 2),  ranging from coastal plain (Plymouth, Massachusetts)  to  the  incised  Allegheny  Plateau  (Corning,  New  York).  They  also  vary  in settlement  vintage,  from  the  early  1600s (Plymouth), to the early 1700s (Red Lion,  Pennsylvania),  to the  early  1800s (Corning).  Irregular survey schemes and road layouts are typical in all  three  areas.  Pennsylvania's  Red  Lion  is the most intensely agricultural,  with a strong orientation to dairy farming.  Plymouth and Corning are  less  agricultural owing to the  reversion  of farmland to forest-a process that has been extensive  in Plymouth and moderate  in Corning (see  percent  land  cover, Table  2).  Plymouth has also experienced considerable exurban development.

The  Midwest study  areas  are  less  diverse topographically,  save for  the ridges and knolls of the  Hocking Hills in Ohio's  Lancaster  area. The latter's natural woodlands were divided by irregular  survey  in the  early  18OOs,  while  the tall-grass  prairie  of  Mattoon  (Illinois) and  the parkland  of  Portage  (Wisconsin)  were  partitioned  by sectional  survey  in the  mid-I  800s. Some land abandonment has occurred in LanMattoon (feedgrain) and Portage (dairying) remain over- caster's hills, but the lands in whelmingly agricultural.

The  three  Southern  study  areas  exemplify t h e  region's  diversity.  Danville  (Kentucky) was settled  earliest  (c. 1790); it  occupies  a  portion of the  well-settled Bluegrass Plateau in the north  (mostly livestock  and  tobacco  farming) and  a  section  o f the  indented  and  heavily wooded  Cumberland  Plateau in the  south. Statesboro (Georgia) includes swampy coastal plain  in  the southeast and gently rolling coastal terrace  in  the  northwest. The latter  was  wellsettled in the  early 1800s, and  remains  in mixed farming. Clarksdale (Mississippi)  lies entirely  in the Yazoo Basin floodplain (the Delta), which is heavily farmed for cotton. Both Statesboro  and  Danville exhibit  irregular  surveys, while Mississippi's Clarksdale area, settled around  1840,  has  a  modified  version  o f the sectional survey.

On the  Great  Plains,  Meridian  (Texas) was originally open woodland, while Bedford (Iowa) and  Healy  (Kansas) were tall-grass  and short-grass  prairie,  respectively.  Meridian  and

Bedford were  settled  at  moderate  densities around 1850, while Healy's more marginal  environment was thinly settled in the 1880s.  Sectional  surveys  were  used  in all  three  areas, though  with  many  irregularities  in  the  hillier sections  o f Meridian.  Farming  specializations are beef cattle (Meridian),  feed-grain (Bedford), and wheat (Healy).

The  California study areas  exemplify  the naturally wooded coastal valleys and hills (Watsonville) and the natural grasslands o f   the Sacramento Valley  (Maxwell)  and San Joaquin Valley  (Delano). Lowland  portions o f   Watsonville, settled around 1860, are characterized by fruit and  truck  farming  with  some  exurban  development. The Maxwell and  Delano areas,  settled by means o f   sectional survey around 1870 and  1880, respectively,  are  now  irrigated  for orchard and field  crops.
